q: When did Western Europe actually start to become rich?

answer.short: Income per head first pulled ahead in the north-west after the Black Death, roughly 1350-1500, when a third or more of the population died and wages and diets rose. The medieval boom of 1000-1300 was mostly more people, not richer ones. The lead then widened in the Low Countries and England through the 1500s-1700s, with Atlantic and Asian trade and institutions that protected merchants' gains, before steam. Industry made the gap huge after 1800, but it did not start it.
answer.frame: Western Europe's rise in wealth is debated between medieval growth, the post-Black Death shift, and the Atlantic and industrial divergence, so we must find when income per head actually pulled ahead.

steps.title: The famine that loaded the gun
steps.text: Before 1348, northwestern Europe was already crowded and fragile. The Great Famine of 1315-1317 began with cold, endless rain, and cattle plague followed it. Bruges and the Flemish cloth towns were hit hard, and Ypres lost roughly a tenth of its people. DeWitte and Slavin (2013) found that children who survived this famine died at higher rates in 1348, so hunger had already weakened the people the plague would meet. Land was dear and labour was cheap, which is the Malthusian trap before it snapped. Wealth per head could not rise much in that world, because every gain was eaten by more mouths.

steps.title: One in three gone: labour becomes scarce
steps.text: The map shows the plague reaching Messina in October 1347, Marseille in November, Florence in March 1348 and Melcombe in June. By 1351 Europe had probably lost a third to a half of its people, though the range is wide and local figures vary. Land was suddenly plentiful and hands were scarce. English labourers could demand more, and landlords answered with the Ordinance of Labourers (1349) and the Statute of 1351, which failed to hold wages down. The Economic historian will show the silver and the wage series; what the plague data adds is the cause of the jump. Real wages roughly rose by half or more in a few decades, a shock to the price of labour that no policy produced.

steps.title: Cold centuries, and the west pulls ahead
steps.text: The Little Ice Age (c.1300-1850) hit the whole continent, with a very cold 1600s when the Thames froze and glaciers advanced. Yet the rich northwest, Holland and England, withstood it better than the east and south, and the Great Plague of London in 1665-66 was England's last big plague. The plague data suggests that the high-wage world born in 1348 persisted, pushing employers toward capital, trade and later machines. In Italy, plague in 1630 and in Naples in 1656 helped drag the south down, so the shock was not equal in effect. My reading is that 1348 opened the door, and cold and later pandemics sorted who walked through it. I cannot prove causation here; historians still argue whether the plague or institutions did the main work, and the Political scientist should press on that.

steps.title: Cities before the plague: Europe is crowded, not yet rich
steps.text: By 1348 Western Europe had spent three centuries filling up. Our index gives Paris about 210,000 and Milan 125,000 around 1400, with Venice at 113,000 and Florence at 53,000. Many of these figures are post-plague values, so the 1348 peak was higher still. Europe's total population roughly doubled between 1000 and 1300, to perhaps 70-80 million. That is growth by adding mouths on marginal land, which is Malthusian, so more people did not mean more income per head. Córdoba shows the opposite curve: 400,000 in 1000 down to 96,000 by 1400. The urban centre of the west had shifted north and east, but this is still a crowded, poor-per-head world. Numbers here are estimates, and city figures for 1000 and 1300 are very uncertain (Bairoch's and Chandler's series disagree).

sources.cite: Paul Bairoch, Cities and Economic Development (1988)
Tertius Chandler, Four Thousand Years of Urban Growth (1987)

steps.title: The Black Death empties Europe and fills the wage bill
steps.text: The plague of 1347-51 killed perhaps a third to a half of Europeans, and England's population fell from roughly 4-5 million to about 2.5 million by 1400. London sits at 72,000 in 1400 in our index, and Florence at 53,000, a fraction of its earlier peak. Fewer people meant land became cheap and labour dear, and survivors ate better. The Economic historian will show the wage series; what the demography adds is that this was income per head rising because heads fell, not because production per worker jumped. The Epidemiologist will cover the mechanism. What matters for me is that population stayed low for about 150 years, so the higher incomes were not instantly competed away. That is the classic Malthusian windfall, and it made wages higher in the Low Countries and England than the Mediterranean.

steps.title: The north-west pulls away: Antwerp, Amsterdam, London
steps.text: Here is the demographer's tell. London goes 72,000 (1400) to a figure of 1 million (1800), the most spectacular urban climb in the index, and Amsterdam to 220,000 and Antwerp to 591,000 by 1800 by the index's reckoning. Bruges, at 52,000 in 1400 and 96,000 in 1800, was the early star that stalled. Cities in a Malthusian world can only grow if rural productivity feeds them, and the Dutch and English did so; de Vries and van der Woude found the Dutch Republic about 1500-1800 had roughly 30 percent urban population, among the highest anywhere. Italy's big cities stagnated relative to this. Treat the index's 1800 values for Milan (2.5 million) and Prague (910,000) with caution; those look far too large and may reflect regional or metro definitions. My reading: the sustained per-capita lead showed first in the Low Countries from the 1400s-1500s, then England, well before industry.

steps.title: England's income barely moves for 300 years
steps.text: Maddison's UK series starts at $1,151 per head in 1000 and is still only $1,193 in 1329, so three centuries of medieval growth were mostly more people (2.0 million in 1000) rather than richer ones. Windmills (Weedley, Yorkshire, 1185) and watermills (London, 1086) are real, but they raised totals, not income per head. The medieval boom is a boom in headcount. These are reconstructions from sparse data, not measurements, so treat the flat line as 'no strong evidence of rising income' rather than proof of stagnation.

sources.cite: Bolt and van Zanden, The Maddison Project: Maddison-Style Estimates of the Evolution of the World Economy (2020)

steps.title: After the plague, the survivors are richer
steps.text: The UK series jumps from $1,193 in 1329 to $1,552 in 1408 and $1,696 in 1486, about +42% in 160 years, which is the first sustained rise in the whole window. Fewer workers meant higher wages per head and cheaper land, and Bruges (hub 1280-1490) plus Hanseatic cloth and grain trade gave them things to spend it on. The Epidemiologist will show the 1348 mortality and the climate shock; what the income series adds is that the gain persisted and did not revert once population began regrowing. Caveat: this is a per-head rise from a smaller economy, and England is one country, not all of Western Europe.

steps.title: Atlantic silver, steam, and the pull from India
steps.text: England hits $1,839 by 1565, dips to $1,725 in 1643, then reaches $2,636 in 1722 and $3,343 in 1800. India over the same span slides from $1,264 in 1600 to $1,068 in 1750. The crossing of the two lines falls in the 1600s, when Amsterdam (hub 1585-1795) was running the Atlantic and Asian trades, and the Dudley engine of 1712 comes just after. So per-head income pulled clearly ahead of Asia around 1650-1750, well before steam did much, and the 1800 level is nearly triple 1000. I go beyond my data here: Maddison India figures are thin estimates, and Allen's wage-based comparisons show similar but not identical timing.

steps.title: Magna Carta: the king can be sued
steps.text: The Law layer lists Magna Carta (1215) as the first stop. Its clause 39 (no free man seized except by lawful judgment) and clause 12 (no scutage or aid without common counsel) are not democracy, since they bind the barons, not peasants. But they establish the principle that a ruler's taking needs consent. The Kingdom of England (936-1708) is flagged fragile at 24% on the model, so this was order secured by bargaining rather than by strength. The Economic historian will show whether income per head moved then; what I can show is that the legal precondition for merchants keeping gains appears about 130 years before the plague.

steps.title: Bruges, Venice, Genoa: merchants who ran the state
steps.text: In 1348 the map's richest commercial cities are Venice, Genoa and Florence in the north, and Bruges in the south. All were run by guilds or merchant oligarchies, not by landed kings. Venice's Serrata (1297) closed its Great Council to a fixed set of families who all had a stake in trade; Florentine guilds held the Signoria. Where the Holy Roman Empire (fragility 17%, watch) was too loose to tax them, merchants wrote the rules themselves. The Epidemiologist will show the plague emptying these cities; the institutional question is why they refilled. Most likely because courts and credit contracts survived the deaths. I'm inferring this, not reading it from the map's data.

steps.title: 1689: Parliament holds the purse
steps.text: The Law layer lists the Bill of Rights (1689) and the Toleration Act (1689). After 1688, the Crown could not tax or suspend laws without Parliament, and creditors sat in Parliament. The Bank of England followed in 1694, and North and Weingast argue that borrowing costs fell, since a king who can't repudiate debts gets cheaper loans. This came after the Dutch Republic's similar bargain with its provincial estates. Meanwhile the Law layer shows Fontainebleau (1685) and Louis XIV's Kingdom of France (fragility 20%, watch) pushing Huguenot merchants out, and England and Holland took them in. This is a story about the 1700s lead, so the Economic historian's date for income divergence tells us whether institutions caused wealth or only protected it. Historians contest North and Weingast's causal claim.

links.why: The 1348 mortality made labour scarce, and the UK income series shows the resulting jump from $1,193 in 1329 to $1,552 in 1408 and $1,696 in 1486 persisting rather than reverting.
The medieval doubling of Europe's population to perhaps 70-80 million lines up with England's flat $1,151 to $1,193 income, so the boom added mouths, not income per head.
Low population kept wages high for about 150 years, and the north-west turned that windfall into urban growth, with London going from 72,000 to roughly 1 million.

Parliamentary control of the purse and cheaper credit after 1689 came after the income lead over India was already visible in the 1600s, which suggests institutions protected and extended the gains more than they started them.

whatifs.q: What if the Black Death had killed far fewer people, say a tenth rather than a third or more?
whatifs.a: Land would have stayed scarce and labour cheap, so the post-1348 wage jump and the cheaper-capital pressure would likely have been much weaker. Western Europe might have stayed Malthusian longer, and the Low Countries' and England's lead might have formed later or not at all. That is speculative, because institutions and trade could have produced some divergence anyway.

q: Why did China keep coming back together after it broke apart?

answer.short: China kept reassembling because its core was one open arena (the North China Plain, wired to the Yangtze rice basin by canals) with no internal wall to shelter a lasting rival, and because Qin-Han institutions, a shared script, exams and the Mandate of Heaven made unity the default that every claimant had to copy. Rivers and the steppe frontier could hold the pieces apart for generations (Red Cliffs 208, Fei River 383, Xiangyang until 1273), but each reunifier found a way to master the water, and the Yellow River's need for plain-wide repair kept rewarding whoever held the whole center. Geography made unity cheap, institutions and ideas made it expected.
answer.frame: China fractured at least five times (220, 316, 907, 1127, 1279 CE roughly) yet reunified each time, unlike Europe after Rome, so what made the center of gravity so strong?

plan.frame: China fractured at least five times (220, 316, 907, 1127, 1279 CE roughly) yet reunified each time, unlike Europe after Rome, so what made the center of gravity so strong?

steps.title: Two rivers, one plain
steps.text: Look at the North China Plain (34.8N, 116.6E): a flat, loess-fed floodplain several hundred kilometres across with no mountain wall inside it. Xi'an (Qin's Chang'an) and Luoyang sit 300 km apart on the Wei-Yellow River line, and Kaifeng sits at the plain's centre. Whoever held that corridor held the biggest concentration of farmland and people in East Asia, and an army can march or float across it with almost nothing to stop it. Europe after Rome had the Alps, the Pyrenees and the Channel inside its core; China's core had none. That is my first answer: the plain is a single arena, so a rival state there has no natural border to hide behind.

steps.title: The canal that stitched north to south
steps.text: China's problem is that rivers run west to east, but the money and the politics need to move north to south: the Yellow River basin holds the armies and the Yangtze basin holds the rice. The Sui dynasty (581-618) joined them with the Grand Canal, running from Hangzhou toward Luoyang and later Beijing, over 1,700 km in its full later form (my figure from memory, treat as approximate). After the Tang fell in 907, a Kaifeng and Hangzhou linked by that canal could be one economy, and the Song capital sat on it. So when the empire broke, the south was already wired to the north, and reunifying meant switching the connection back on, not building it. I'm going beyond the map's data on canal length; the places shown are the canal's anchors.

steps.title: The river that kept breaking the center
steps.text: The same plain that unifies is also fragile: the Yellow River carries so much loess silt that it builds its bed above the fields and bursts its banks, repeatedly changing course. The great breach of 1344 flooded the Shandong and Huai region, and the Mongol Yuan court's labour on the dikes and canal helped trigger the Red Turban revolt of 1351. The Economic historian will show the silver and paper money; what the geography adds is that the river's repair was a job only a state spanning the whole plain could do, which is why every new dynasty had to rebuild the dikes and why rebels rose when it failed. I'm confident about the 1344 breach and the 1351 revolt; the causal weight is debated.

steps.title: Red Cliffs: the river that split a continent
steps.text: My data shows the first lesson of division: a river can stop a steppe-fed army. In 208 Cao Cao's northern infantry and cavalry, victors at Guandu (200), reached the Yangtze and lost at Red Cliffs to Sun Quan and Liu Bei, which 'stopped the north from reuniting China'. Horses do not fight well on water, and the south's fleets turned the Yangtze into a moat. The same fortress-city at Xiangyang (Changban 208, Fancheng 219) guards the Han River road between the two worlds. The Geographer will show the rivers as a pull toward the core; what war adds is that the same rivers are walls until someone masters amphibious logistics.

steps.title: Fei River: when the south holds the line
steps.text: At Fei River in 383, a small Eastern Jin army routed Former Qin and kept China divided 'for two more centuries'. Fu Jian's army was multi-ethnic and stretched over a thousand kilometres of supply line from Chang'an; sources claim hundreds of thousands, but I'd treat that as unknown, and the point is the tail. Division persisted when defenders sat on the Huai and Yangtze with short interior lines and the invader's grain had to travel far. The map's border layer shows the reverse in 265 and later, when a single state, Western Jin, absorbed Cao Wei's land and briefly rejoined the pieces. The Political scientist will explain why elites wanted reunion; I say the south could resist until a northern power built enough boats and grain barges.

steps.title: Xiangyang 1273: the siege that reopened the Yangtze
steps.text: The last reunification is the clearest case. Song's Yangtze defence rested on Xiangyang, which held out about six years until 1273, when Persian counterweight trebuchets broke it. Kublai then combined northern cavalry with Chinese and Korean river fleets, and the Yangtze stopped being a wall, so Hangzhou fell in 1276 and Yamen in 1279. Note the contrast with 938 and 1288 at Bach Dang, where stakes in a tidal river beat Chinese fleets: water defence still worked, but only on small rivers far from the core. The Economic historian will show the silver and grain, and the plague layer, which the 1340s Yuan collapse invites you to read, is beyond my evidence; I only know the Ming then reunified from the south in 1368-75.

steps.title: Qin builds a state that can be copied
steps.text: In 221 BCE Qin replaced inherited lords with appointed officials in about 36 commanderies, and Cliopatria shows the state at 1.523 Mkm² by 222 BCE. The key move was institutional: the same weights, measures, script and law applied everywhere, and officials were rotated and could be dismissed. Qin itself lasted only until 206 BCE, but Han kept the template, which is why the Han (peak 4.583 Mkm² in 91 CE) looked like a restoration rather than an invention. Once a reusable blueprint of centralized rule exists, every later warlord can reunify by copying it instead of inventing something new. I'm leaning on standard scholarship for the commandery count, not on the Atlas data.

steps.title: Exams and the Tang Code make talent a state asset
steps.text: The law layer marks the imperial examinations beginning in 605 and the Tang Code in 624, right after the Sui (581-618) ended roughly 270 years of division. Exams meant ambitious families gained rank by serving a single center rather than a regional lord, so elites had a career stake in unity. The Tang Code then gave later dynasties a common legal grammar, and it was copied as far as Japan's Taiho Code (701). The Tang peaked at 8.731 Mkm² in 661, and Cliopatria's Northern Song (961-1138) and Southern Song (1139-1278) follow the same civil-service model. The Historian of faith and ideas will show the Confucian canon that exams tested; what only the law lens sees is the incentive that turned that canon into careers.

steps.title: The Mandate makes chaos a verdict, not a norm
steps.text: The Mandate of Heaven treats collapse as proof that a ruler lost legitimacy, which makes a successor's claim to rule all of China a duty rather than an ambition. Cliopatria's Yuan Dynasty (1294-1374) peaks at 14.252 Mkm² in 1352, so on this map in 1348 it looks strong, yet within 20 years the Ming (1368) replaced it from Nanjing. The Mandate does not explain why that happened: the Economic historian will show the money and the plague data adds the shocks. What this lens adds is the rule of the game: each failure is read as a reason to restore a single center, not to accept several. My caveat is that the Mandate was partly retrospective propaganda written by winners, and I'm going beyond the Atlas data on that point.

steps.title: One script, one canon, one empire in the mind
steps.text: The Jixia Academy at Linzi (318-221 BCE) shows how many rival schools China once had, with Xunzi among them. Legalism, the doctrine of Qin, won by force and then standardised the script in 221 BCE. The Qin state is also said to have burned books in 213 BCE. Whatever the Qin did to the old states, it left one writing system that could be read from the Wei valley to the coast whatever people spoke aloud. That is the first thing my lens sees: after 221 BCE a Chinese official could read an edict from anywhere, so division looked like an interruption of one literate world. The Political scientist will show how the Han turned this into exams and the Mandate of Heaven; I only add that the script came first.

sources.cite: Mark Edward Lewis, The Early Chinese Empires: Qin and Han (2007)

steps.title: Buddhism fills the gap and does not break the frame
steps.text: The strongest test is the age of division after 220, when a foreign faith entered China. Kumarajiva, a monk from Kucha (344-413), translated the Lotus Sutra into Chinese in Xi'an in 406, and his versions are still the standard ones. Buddhism spread in the Han successor states, yet it came in Chinese words, through Chinese monasteries. Faxian walked to India in 399-412, and Xuanzang returned in 645 with 657 texts, both of them Chinese pilgrims rather than a rival state's envoys. The Diamond Sutra printed at Dunhuang in 868 is the oldest dated printed book, and it shows a faith that used Chinese script and print rather than breaking away from it. Buddhism gave no region a separate written identity, which is part of why the political order could reassemble. This is my judgment from the pattern; I know of no count of how many Buddhists thought of the empire as a single unit.

steps.title: Zhu Xi and the canon that outlived the Mongols
steps.text: Zhu Xi (1130-1200) restored the White Deer Grotto Academy at Mount Lu in 1179 and synthesised Neo-Confucianism, whose commentaries became the civil exam syllabus for six centuries. Song fell in 1279 to the Mongols, who ruled China as the Yuan, and still the canon survived the conquest. The Mongol rulers brought back state examinations in 1315, so even foreign rulers adopted the same reading list. In 1348 the Yuan is weakening, and the Ming under Zhu Yuanzhang will reunify in 1368; its rebels invoke the Mandate of Heaven. The Geographer and Military historian will show the rivers and the steppe frontier; what the plague data adds is a stress test, since the great epidemics of the 14th century hit alongside famine and flood, but I cannot say how much they weakened the Yuan. What my lens sees is that each rival claimant needed the same texts to look legitimate.

links.why: A single open plain meant a Qin-style centralized state could administer the whole core with one template, so the blueprint was practical as well as imaginable.
The Sui canal tied the Yangtze's grain to the northern capitals just before the exams and Tang Code gave elites a career stake in that single center.

The Yangtze wall that stopped Cao Cao in 208 was only broken once Kublai combined cavalry, river fleets and siege technology at Xiangyang, so division lasted exactly as long as defenders had a military edge on water.
The standardized script of 221 BCE made a shared canon possible, and Zhu Xi's syllabus then forced even Mongol and rebel claimants to use the same texts to look legitimate.

views.name: Ge Zhaoguang / Chinese-civilization continuity school
views.claim: A shared script and canon made division feel like an interruption of one world, so elites kept aiming at restoration.
views.for: Every conqueror dynasty, including Yuan, adopted the canon and examinations, and Buddhism entered in Chinese words.
views.against: Script unity coexisted with centuries of division (220-589), so it was not sufficient alone.

sources.cite: Ge Zhaoguang, What Is China? Territory, Ethnicity, Culture, and History (2018)

views.name: Walter Scheidel
views.claim: China's core geography lacked internal barriers, and Europe's had many, so empire kept recurring in one and not the other.
views.for: The North China Plain and canal-linked Yangtze lack Europe's Alps, Pyrenees and Channel, and steppe threats rewarded large states.
views.against: Southern China's rivers and mountains did sustain division for centuries, and geography alone does not explain Europe's Rome-sized outcome.

sources.cite: Walter Scheidel, Escape from Rome (2019)

views.name: Victoria Tin-bor Hui
views.claim: Unification came from ruthless self-strengthening and coercive strategy in a competitive system, not from inherent cultural unity.
views.for: Qin conquered through war and reform, and later reunifiers won on logistics, as with Xiangyang.
views.against: It gives little weight to why successors kept the same imperial template after each collapse.

whatifs.q: What if the Yuan had not broken Xiangyang and Song kept the Yangtze line in the 1270s?
whatifs.a: The Song might have survived as a southern state for decades, and the pattern of 383 and 938 suggests the water line could hold against a cavalry power. But the Mongols' naval adaptation was already underway, so this likely delays reunification rather than preventing it, leaving a Nanjing-Hangzhou state alongside a northern Mongol one.

q: Why did India rarely consolidate into one state?

answer.short: India rarely unified because it is several granary-cores (Indus, Ganges, and separate Deccan and southern deltas) divided by deserts, plateaus and ghats, so grain could not be carried far and each province could pay for itself. Armies could take the northern plain in one battle through the Khyber and Bolan gates, but the south needed endless garrisons, and sea trade gave coastal kings their own income. Political culture reinforced this: kings sought overlordship and tribute, not absorption, so empires like Maurya, Tughlaq and the Mughals stretched wide but dissolved into their subordinates within a few generations. The north is the exception that can be conquered whole; the all-India moments were short because the south never needed the north.
answer.frame: Why did the subcontinent's geography, economy, and politics repeatedly yield regional kingdoms, with only brief all-India empires like Maurya, Delhi Sultanate under Tughlaq, and Mughal?

steps.title: Two rivers, two cores
steps.text: The north is not one plain but two cores stitched together. The Indus system (Punjab and Sindh) opens to the Khyber and Bolan passes, so it faces Central Asia. The Ganges plain, fed by monsoon rain that falls heavier the farther east you go, faces Bengal and the sea. The Maurya built from Pataliputra (Patna) on the Ganges, the richest rice and river-traffic core, and it is no accident that the capital sat at the wet eastern end. The Thar Desert, at about 27.6N 71.9E, pushes the two systems apart in the middle, and Delhi sits in the narrow gap between desert and Himalayan foothills. The Maurya hold at around 320-185 BCE is the first time one center reached both cores, and it lasted about 140 years.

steps.title: The Deccan wall and the Vindhya line
steps.text: South of the Vindhya Range (23.1N) the land changes: the Deccan Plateau (around 17.6N 79.4E) is a tilted, drier, hard-rock tableland, fenced on the west by the Western Ghats and on the east by the Eastern Ghats. Its rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) run west to east and cut the south into separate river-delta cores, each with its own rice land. Armies from the Ganges end up marching over 1,500 km through thin-soiled country to reach the Kaveri delta. The Chola, c.848-1279, show the alternative: a state built on the southeast coast that projected power by sea to Sri Lanka and beyond. The Military historian will show why that march so often failed; what the terrain adds is that the south never needed the north, and the north could not feed an army on the way down.

routes.label: North-south route over the Deccan
Chola sea reach to Sri Lanka

steps.title: 1348: Delhi's reach and the new south
steps.text: On the 1348 map the Delhi Sultanate is at its widest reach, and the Vijayanagara Empire (founded 1336) at Hampi (15.3N, 76.5E) already stands against it on the Tungabhadra, just where the Deccan opens. Muhammad bin Tughluq tried to cure the distance problem in c.1327 by making Daulatabad, about 1,100 km south of Delhi, a second capital; the experiment was abandoned within years, which is the geography talking. A single center cannot sit in both the Ganges-Yamuna core and the Deccan. The Economic historian will show the silver and the Political scientist the overlordship; what geography adds is that Hampi chose a defensible granite basin and a river barrier, which is why the south regrouped here and not further north. I can't say from my data how the plague of 1348 reached India; the evidence is thin there.

routes.label: Tughlaq's forced move, Delhi to Daulatabad (c.1327)

sources.cite: Burton Stein, Vijayanagara (1989)

steps.title: The north is a highway, the gate is Khyber and Bolan
steps.text: Every conqueror of the north came through the same two gates, Khyber (34.1,71.1) and Bolan (29.6,67.4), and fought on the same dry plain: Tarain 1192, Panipat 1526 (29.4,77.0), Delhi 1398. The Mughal Empire held both passes by 1707, which is why the map shows the north as the one place where steppe cavalry and then guns could repeatedly reset the board. Horse archers from Ghazni and Ghur could live off Punjab grain and Rajasthani pasture, so one decisive battle often decided who owned the Indo-Gangetic plain. The Economic historian will show the grain and tax base that paid for these armies; what the war layer adds is that the plain is a single killing ground, so the north can be conquered quickly and consolidated in a way the south cannot.

steps.title: Warangal to Dwarasamudra: raids that never became rule
steps.text: The map shows Delhi besieging Warangal in 1310, 1318 and 1323, and Dwarasamudra in 1311. The repeat sieges are the tell: each win extracted treasure and tribute, but garrisons 1,500 km from Delhi could not be fed or reinforced, and the Sultanate lost the south within a generation. Northern armies depended on Central Asian horses, which breed poorly in the humid south and arrived by sea at high cost, while southern states fielded elephants, forts and monsoon-swollen rivers as defence. By 1336 Vijayanagara (15.34,76.46) was founded, and the Sultanate's reach under Tughlaq was already receding, as the 1342 battle at Kannanur (10.9,78.7) hints. I am going beyond the data on the horse-import point, which is well argued by Gommans and others; the numbers are approximate.

steps.title: Talikota and the sea: the south's own gunpowder frontier
steps.text: In 1565 the Deccan sultanates broke Vijayanagara at Talikota and sacked Hampi, yet they did not unify the south either; they were rivals who divided the spoils. In 1509 Portugal won at Diu (20.7,71.0) and held Indian Ocean sea lanes for a century, so the coast became a separate military system from the plain, with its own naval power and trade forts. The Mughals took the Deccan in stages, culminating under Aurangzeb around 1686-87, but the Deccan ulcer of constant sieges tied up huge armies and treasure, and Maratha raiders operated behind the lines. The Political scientist will explain why local elites accepted overlordship; the military point is that holding the south meant garrisoning hundreds of hill forts against an enemy who could simply wait out the monsoon.

steps.title: Many granaries, no single purse
steps.text: Start with the fiscal problem. India's surplus sits in separate pockets: the Ganges plain (the data puts iron and rice there from about 1200 and 2000 BCE, Patna from 490 BCE), then the Krishna-Godavari and Kaveri deltas, each fed by its own rivers and monsoon rhythm. Under the Maurya (322-185 BCE) Patna taxed its core, but grain is bulky and cheap per kilo, so carrying it across the Deccan by ox cart costs more than it is worth. An empire must therefore pay governors from the region they sit in, and a governor who eats the local surplus has the means to go independent. That is the economic reason Maurya reach outran Maurya control, and I am inferring this from the structure of the economy, not from a surviving budget. The Geographer will show you the rivers that make the pockets; what money adds is that each pocket was self-financing.

routes.label: Ganges river grain and tax to Patna

sources.cite: Romila Thapar, Early India: From the Origins to AD 1300 (2002)

steps.title: Pepper and horses pay the coasts
steps.text: The Indian Ocean monsoon route (100 BCE-1500) gave southern kingdoms an income that bypassed the Ganges heartland. Muziris was a top eastern hub from 100 BCE to 400 CE, and black pepper from Malabar (data: reaching Berenike in 20 CE, Rome by 92) paid in Roman gold. Later Calicut (1300-1500) and the Chola state (848-1279) did the same with Srivijaya and Song China. A ruler on the coast taxed ships and weavers directly, and had no need to send a cut north. Imported war horses were the one thing the south could not breed, so cavalry cost silver, which the sea trade supplied locally. Ports gave regional kings both revenue and independence from any inland capital; how much of that was tax versus royal temple spending I can't say from this data.

steps.title: 1348: the Tughlaq stretch snaps
steps.text: 1348 is the moment the Delhi Sultanate's reach reverses. Muhammad bin Tughlaq moved his capital to Daulatabad in 1327 and issued token coinage, yet the Deccan broke away anyway: Vijayanagara rose in 1336 at Hampi and the Bahmani Sultanate in 1347. Revenue had to cross about 1,100 km of plateau, so each province was worth more kept than remitted. Vijayanagara then built its own purse from cotton, spices and the horse trade through west-coast ports. The Military historian will cover why force could not hold the south; the plague data adds a question, since I find no record in this dataset of a Black Death in India, so I won't claim one. Even the Mughals (1526-1707) were the exception that proves the rule: they integrated silver inflows and a land-tax system, but within a few decades of 1707 the provinces were again acting as separate states.

steps.title: Ashoka's edicts: an empire of persuasion
steps.text: Maurya peaked at 3.946 Mkm² in 256 BCE, yet it ran as a hub-and-spoke system: a Gangetic core at Patna, a few viceroys (kumaras) at Taxila, Ujjain and Suvarnagiri, and loosely tied territory between. Ashoka's Edicts (-260) are telling: he must plead, in rock inscriptions, for dhamma, because administrative reach was thin. The empire then lasted barely 137 years (318 to 171 BCE by the Cliopatria record, 322 to 185 on the polity index), and the model rates it 15% fragility, 'watch'. Its legitimacy rested on one person's conquest and charisma, with no institution to renew it. The Military historian will show how it was won; what the law layer adds is that nothing here made the provinces stay. Confidence is moderate, since the Arthashastra's date and how far it describes real practice are both debated.

steps.title: Overlords, not bureaucrats: the mandala
steps.text: The dominant pattern was a rajamandala, where a king claimed overlordship (chakravartin) and collected tribute and homage while local chiefs kept their own armies, land and courts. In 1028 the map shows several peaks at once: Ghaznavids (2.994 Mkm² peak that year), Chola (0.522 Mkm², its peak), Pala (1.362 Mkm² in 825), Gurjara-Pratihara, Western Chalukya (0.754 Mkm² in 1000). Rajendra Chola marched to the Ganges and took its water home, a ritual victory rather than an annexation. Defeating a rival and receiving his submission conferred legitimacy, whereas absorbing him would have wrecked the very hierarchy that made you a great king. That is why empires like Pala or Rashtrakuta (1.144 Mkm² in 788) could be vast yet dissolve into their subordinates' kingdoms. Burton Stein's 'segmentary state' model for the Cholas is influential but contested. The Economic historian will show the regional surpluses that paid for each court; I add that the ideology of overlordship rewarded tribute over centralisation.

steps.title: Tughlaq's overreach and the Delhi–Vijayanagara split
steps.text: The Tughlaq Dynasty (1326 to 1414) hit 2.449 Mkm² in 1333, the closest India came to unity before the Mughals. Muhammad bin Tughluq tried direct control: he moved his capital to Daulatabad, about 1,100 km south of Delhi, and imposed token currency. By 1348, the year on your map, the south had slipped away, the Bahmani Sultanate was founded that year, and Vijayanagara (1344 to 1571, only 0.568 Mkm² at its 1450 peak) had arisen as a Hindu successor. Provincial governors and military commanders (amirs) built their own followings, so the centre's attempt to turn them into salaried officials caused revolt. Plague data from this window is thin for India, so I cannot link the Black Death to this; the Economic historian may add trade effects. Mughal success later came through the mansabdari ranking system and Akbar's abolishing of the jizya in 1564, which bought local-elite loyalty, while Aurangzeb's reimposition in 1679 coincided with a peak of 3.76 Mkm² in 1700 and rapid unravelling.

links.why: The separate river cores that geography lays out became separate self-financing granaries, so no single purse could pay for one state.
Because revenue could not cross the plateau, Tughlaq's salaried-official experiment at Daulatabad starved the centre and pushed governors toward revolt.
Northern cavalry needed imported horses, but sea trade paid for those horses in the south, so raids from Delhi met states that could buy their own armies.
The mandala habit of taking submission and ritual victory (Rajendra Chola's Ganges water) fit a Deccan wall that made annexation costly anyway.

whatifs.q: What if Muhammad bin Tughluq had held Daulatabad and kept the Deccan inside the Sultanate after 1347?
whatifs.a: He would have needed a southern revenue base that stayed loyal; the Bahmani revolt of 1347 shows the amirs could build their own followings, so he probably would have faced a permanent two-front state. A longer Delhi hold might have delayed Vijayanagara, but the grain-distance problem makes lasting unity unlikely.

q: Why did Rome fall but Constantinople last another thousand years?

answer.short: Rome's West fell because it had the worst combination: an open land frontier, a tax base that bled away province by province, and an emperor controlled by his generals. The East had a defensible capital on a strait, rich sea-linked provinces (Egypt, Syria, Anatolia), a stable gold coin, and a civil court that kept generals from owning the throne. So it could pay enemies off, wall them out, and rebuild after losses. It did not stay rich or safe, since plague, the Arab conquests, Manzikert and 1204 gutted it, but it stayed solvent and legitimate long enough to last to 1453.
answer.frame: Rome's western half collapsed by 476 while the eastern half survived to 1453; the question is what made the East structurally sturdier, and what it did differently.

plan.frame: Rome's western half collapsed by 476 while the eastern half survived to 1453; the question is what made the East structurally sturdier, and what it did differently.

steps.title: The strait that is a moat and a highway
steps.text: Constantinople sits on a triangular peninsula with water on three sides, at the Bosporus (41.1N, 29.1E) where Europe and Asia are about 700 m apart at the narrowest. Constantine refounded it in 330 on Byzantium's site (listed in the Atlas from 657 BCE). An attacker had to pass the Dardanelles (40.2N, 26.4E), then the Marmara, then face the Golden Horn and, from the 5th century, the Theodosian land wall across the one landward side (about 5.5 km). Rome by contrast is 20 km inland on the Tiber, the Alps (Brenner Pass at 47.0N, 11.5E) are a 1,000 km open flank, and the capital stayed in Italy only a few days' ride from any invader. The strait also worked as a highway: Black Sea grain and trade funnelled through here, and the capital sat on the junction of every major route between the Danube and Syria. The Military historian will show the walls and fleet; what geography adds is that those were cheap to build because the site did most of the work.

steps.title: Anatolia: a fortress plateau behind the Taurus
steps.text: After 395 the East kept Anatolia, a high plateau (around 1,000 m) ringed by the Taurus (Cilician Gates at 37.3N, 34.8E) and the Pontic coast, with a heartland the Persians (Sasanian polity, 224-651) could raid but rarely hold. Invaders crossing the lower Danube met the Balkan Mountains (43.0N, 24.9E) and then Constantinople's walls, so they tended to slide west toward Italy and Gaul or south into Greece. Hunnic pressure peaked 370-469 on the Danube plain, which is flat, open steppe-edge pasture, and it fell on whichever empire sat closest. The East was more compact, centred on a sea (Aegean and Marmara) with Ephesus, Antioch and Alexandria linked by water, while the West was a long arc from Britain to Carthage with the Alps, Rhine and Pyrenees to guard. The Economic historian will show the silver and gold; what the map shows is why that revenue stayed safe: Egypt's grain and Syria's cities sat behind the sea and the desert, not on the Rhine.

steps.title: 1348: the sea lanes that carried plague home
steps.text: At the map's current year, 1348, the city we are asking about still stands, and geography explains both its survival and its limits. The same sea lanes that fed Constantinople carried the Black Death: it reached the city in 1347 from Caffa on a Genoese route, killing perhaps a third or more of urban populations across the region (estimates vary and the Byzantine record is thin). Constantinople is now a shrunken city of perhaps 50,000, far below its probable 400,000-plus in the 6th century, and the Ottomans (from 1299) already hold Anatolia's plateau, the very fortress that once shielded it. Only walls and the strait remain, and these held until 1453, when Ottoman guns, not geography, broke the Theodosian wall. The Economic historian will show the silver; what the plague data adds is that connectivity cut both ways, and the site that protected a capital could not protect a population.

steps.title: The West's tax base bleeds out
steps.text: Rome's fiscal engine was a fragile loop: tax the provinces, pay the army, defend the provinces. After Alaric sacks Rome in 410, the West loses tax-paying land piece by piece: Britain, much of Gaul, Spain, and then North Africa to the Vandals (Carthage, 439). Africa was the West's richest remaining province and supplied the grain and oil that fed Rome. As revenue fell, the state paid armies with land grants to federate troops, which meant less tax, which meant fewer troops. Treat the numbers as reconstructions: late Roman budgets are scholarly estimates, not accounts. The Military historian will show the armies; what the ledger adds is that the West ran out of money before it ran out of soldiers.

steps.title: The solidus: a coin that did not slip
steps.text: Constantine introduced the gold solidus around 309 at 72 to the Roman pound (about 4.5 g), and for roughly 700 years it kept its weight, a monetary record almost nothing matches. The East could afford this because it kept its richest, most urbanised provinces: Egypt, Syria and Anatolia, with Alexandria and Antioch among the great cities and the sea lanes between them cheap to sail. Egyptian grain fed Constantinople, and taxes in gold came back out as pay and as subsidies to buy off enemies. The Geographer will show why those sea lanes were safe; the money lens adds that the East could rent peace with gold the West no longer had. Exact tax totals are debated, so treat any single figure with suspicion.

steps.title: Plague, loss of Egypt, and a hub that outlived its empire
steps.text: The East was not invulnerable: the plague of 541 and the loss of Egypt and Syria to the Arab conquests in the 630s-640s cut its revenue roughly in half by most estimates, and it shrank to an Anatolian-Balkan state that survived on a leaner tax system. The Atlas's trade hubs show Constantinople as the Western relay's centre from 400 to 1204, longer than any other, then Venice takes over after the Fourth Crusade. By 1348, on the map now, the empire is a rump poorer than the Italian merchants who trade through it, and the Black Death arrives in the Mediterranean on those same ships. So the economic answer is not that the East stayed rich, but that it stayed solvent longer, through 900 years of fiscal adaptation. I go beyond the Atlas data here, which gives no Byzantine GDP series.

steps.title: Adrianople: the army that could not be replaced
steps.text: At Adrianople in 378 Gothic cavalry killed the emperor Valens, and barbarian groups were now living inside the empire on their own terms. Here is the military point: this disaster happened in the East, yet the East survived it. The Danube and Thrace are a few days' march from Constantinople, but the Bosporus and Dardanelles (both held by the Roman Empire in 284, then Byzantium until 1453 in your chokepoint data) forced the Goths to roam the Balkans rather than cross into rich Anatolia. In 410 Rome itself was sacked by Visigoths, the first fall of the city in 800 years, because the West had no equivalent strait to shut. The Geographer will show why that terrain mattered; what the battle record adds is that the same enemy produced opposite outcomes. This is partly my inference from the pattern of events, not a figure on the map.

steps.title: Deflecting Attila: pay, redirect, wall
steps.text: The Huns (Hunnic Empire, 370 to 469 in your index) hit the East hard in the 440s, and Constantinople answered with tribute and with stone: the Theodosian Walls, a triple line over 5 km long, were rebuilt in 447 within about two months after an earthquake, with the city's circus factions turning out as labour. The East paid gold to Attila and thereby steered him elsewhere, and in 451 Rome and the Goths stopped him at the Catalaunian Plains in Gaul, then he turned on Italy in 452. The West had to fight the Huns with its field army, while the East could pay and sit behind walls. The Economic historian will show where the gold came from; I would only add that tribute is a military tool when it buys time for walls and for regrouping. The tribute figures (roughly 2,100 pounds of gold a year late in Attila's reign) come from my recollection of Priscus and are less certain than the dates.

steps.title: The thousand-year test: Greek fire, then 1204 and 1348
steps.text: The walls were the system, but the navy made them work. In 717 the Umayyad Caliphate besieged Constantinople and Greek fire plus the city walls held, so the caliphate stopped trying; the Arabs had already taken Syria at Yarmuk in 636, yet could not take the one city that sat on the straits. Because the sea lanes stayed open, the city could be resupplied by water when besieged by land. Walls fell only to treachery of a different kind: in 1204 the Fourth Crusade and Venice, who had the ships, sacked the city, and Byzantium never fully recovered. Manzikert (1071) cost Anatolia's recruiting ground, and by your current year of 1348 the empire is a rump facing the Ottomans, who later held the Bosporus in 1453. Ankara (1402) bought 50 more years, nothing more. The plague data may show how a shrunken city with few defenders was bled further; I cannot see that from battles alone.

steps.title: Diocletian builds a machine, then splits it
steps.text: Start with the Roman Empire on your map: 5.263 Mkm² at peak in 117 CE, flagged 'watch' at 18% fragility. Diocletian (r. 284-305) answered the third-century chaos, with some 20+ emperors in 50 years, by creating the Tetrarchy in 293: two senior Augusti, two junior Caesars, each with a court and army. He split provinces into roughly 100 smaller ones grouped in dioceses, separating civil governors from military commanders. This made usurpation harder and tax collection more regular, but it also meant two courts, and after 395 the split was permanent. Rome itself stopped being the seat: emperors lived at Milan, Trier, then Ravenna from 402, so the 'capital' West was a fortress-court, while the East inherited a city, Constantinople, that was the capital and nothing else.

sources.cite: Peter Brown, The World of Late Antiquity (1971)
Wikipedia: Tetrarchy

steps.title: Who holds the emperor? Generals in the West, officials in the East
steps.text: The Atlas marks the Theodosian Code (438) and Edict of Thessalonica (380), both products of the East: Theodosius II had 16 books of imperial law compiled and published in both halves, a sign that the eastern bureaucracy was the institutional memory of the whole empire. Your map lists the Western Roman Empire (395-475) at 23% fragility, 'fragile', and the Eastern Roman Empire at 15%. The difference was who controlled the emperor. In the West a child emperor, Honorius at 10 and Valentinian III at 6, was managed by a master-of-soldiers (Stilicho, Aetius, then Ricimer), who held the army and so the real power. In the East, the court kept the generals out of the palace: the civil offices (praetorian prefect, master of offices, eunuch chamberlains) controlled access and pay, and Germanic generals like Aspar were checked and finally killed in 471. The Military historian will show the walls; what the court adds is that the East never let a single general become the state, so a weak emperor could still be a legitimate one.

sources.cite: A.H.M. Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964)
Wikipedia: Theodosian Code

steps.title: Legitimacy that survives defeat, even the Black Death
steps.text: Justinian's Corpus Juris Civilis (529) fixed a theory: one emperor, one law, God's viceregent, and that idea outlived the territory. Your map shows the Byzantine Empire at 22% fragility ('fragile') even though it lasted to 1453, and by 1348 it is a rump, a few thousand square kilometers around Constantinople, Thessaloniki and the Morea, while the Ottoman Empire (1305 onward) grows. What kept it alive was institutional, not material: a ceremonial court, a trained civil service, and a dynastic custom (the Palaiologoi since 1261) that let rivals fight over the throne without destroying the throne. The plague reached Constantinople in 1347 from Caffa, and John VI Kantakouzenos's own son died of it; the Economic historian will show the silver and the plague data the people, but the political point is that the state was designed to absorb shocks to the person at the top. Whether that is strength or merely stubbornness is the part I can't settle: by 1348 it could outlast defeat but not recover from it.

links.why: The site's water on three sides made the Theodosian Walls cheap and quick to build, so the East could answer Attila with tribute and stone instead of a field army.
Anatolia, Egypt and Syria sat behind sea and desert rather than on the Rhine, so their revenue stayed safe and could back an unchanged gold solidus.
As the West's tax base shrank, it relied on generals paid in land, which handed real power to masters of soldiers like Stilicho, Aetius and Ricimer.
Solidus revenue funded the gold paid to Attila, so money bought the time that walls and regrouping needed.

views.name: Peter Heather
views.claim: The West fell chiefly because Hunnic and Gothic pressure stripped away its revenue and army, and the East was spared mostly by position and luck.
views.for: Vandal Carthage in 439 removed the West's richest province; Adrianople in 378 hit the East but its straits redirected the Goths west.
views.against: It underplays internal political and fiscal differences; the East also faced the same enemies and survived with them inside its borders.

views.name: Bryan Ward-Perkins
views.claim: The fall was a real violent collapse of Western economy and civilisation, not a smooth transformation.
views.for: Pottery, building quality and coin use drop sharply in the post-Roman West, and the East's richer economy persisted.
views.against: Some historians stress continuity in law, church and elites, and the evidence varies by region.

views.name: Edward Luttwak
views.claim: The Byzantines survived by using diplomacy, bribery and defensive depth rather than seeking decisive battle.
views.for: Tribute to Attila, Greek fire and walls, and a navy that kept supply lines open all fit this pattern.

whatifs.q: What if the Western court had been based on a defensible, sea-linked site, and had kept Africa after 439?
whatifs.a: The West would have kept its grain and a larger share of its revenue, and might have paid for armies without handing out land. It still faced a longer frontier and a general-dominated court, so I expect a longer decline rather than survival for a thousand years.

q: What did the end of the world look like in 1177 BCE?

answer.short: Around 1177 BCE the end of the world was a chain reaction, not a single blow: drought and hunger strained palace granaries, the tin-and-copper trade that armed the palaces broke, and centralised states that fused food, metal, and legitimacy in one building could not adapt when Sea Peoples, quakes, or revolt hit. Ugarit and Hattusa died by about 1185 and 1180 BCE and Mycenaean Greece by 1101 BCE, while Egypt won the battle at the Delta and still lost the Levant. What survived was smaller, more decentralised, or backed by a different water source: Phoenician ports, Assyria's river core, Egypt's Nile, and iron, the metal no palace could tax.
answer.frame: Around 1177 BCE the Late Bronze Age palace-and-trade world of the eastern Mediterranean collapsed within decades: why did so many interlocked states fail together, and what survived?

steps.title: The dry decades before the fall
steps.text: The Atlas logs a Late Bronze Age drought, 1250-1100 BCE, centred near Ugarit, read from pollen cores in Cyprus and Syria. Kaniewski and colleagues (2013) put the dry spell at roughly 1200-850 BCE, a bit later than our window start, so treat the exact onset as contested. The mechanism is simple: palace states stored grain and redistributed it, so a run of failed harvests hit their legitimacy as well as their stomachs. Hittite letters from the late 13th century, including requests to Egypt for grain shipments, hint at hunger in Anatolia. I'm going from memory of those texts, and the Atlas shows no famine record for them. Drought is a stressor here, not a killer on its own.

steps.title: Ugarit burns, the grain runs short
steps.text: Ugarit, in the Atlas from 6000 BCE to 1185 BCE, is the clearest case: its last letters beg for ships and troops while the city is already doomed. The Military historian will show the raiders and the burn layers; what the climate record adds is that the countryside feeding the city was probably already strained. Earthquakes are a rival suspect. Nur Sherif and Amiet-style storm-of-quakes ideas, such as Nur and Cline's 'earthquake storm' paper (2000), are debated, since fire and quakes leave similar ruins. I would give the earthquake storm a modest weight. The Atlas has no quake or plague record for this window, so there is no data on epidemic disease either way. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence here.

steps.title: Who the drought spared
steps.text: The Atlas's collapse record, 1200-1150 BCE, says palace states 'from Mycenae to Ugarit fell within a few decades', and it marks Hattusa ending about 1180 BCE. Egypt (New Kingdom, to 1070 BCE) bent but held. The Nile's flood is fed by distant monsoon rains rather than Mediterranean winter rain, so it buffered Egypt from the eastern Mediterranean drought, though Egypt had its own troubles, with grain price spikes and strikes in Ramesses III's reign. The Political scientist will explain why institutions mattered; the climate view adds that Egypt had a different water source, which is a physical difference, not just a political one. That is my inference, not a Atlas record, and it fits the pattern but doesn't prove it. Cline (2014) calls the collapse a systems failure with many strands, and drought is one.

sources.cite: Cline, 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed (2014)

steps.title: The tin road that held the palaces together
steps.text: Bronze is about 90% copper and 10% tin, and that 10% is the whole story: Cyprus had copper, but tin had to come from far away, probably Central Asia, and was chokepointed through a few ports. The Atlas tracks Ugarit as the western trade-hub relay from 1450 to 1185 BCE, and it is where the system's logic is clearest: a middleman city taxing tin, copper, oil, textiles and purple dye moving between Hittite Anatolia, Egypt and Mycenaean Greece. The Uluburun shipwreck (sank c. 1320 BCE) carried about 10 tonnes of copper in ~350 ox-hide ingots and roughly 1 tonne of tin, enough for ~11 tonnes of bronze: a single hull holding a kingdom's arsenal. The Atlas has no recorded routes for this window, so the lines above are schematic and my reconstruction, not mapped records. Palaces ran the demand side: Linear B tablets at Pylos and Knossos tally bronze issued to smiths by the gram.

steps.title: Iron: the poor man's metal gets its chance
steps.text: Here is the economic twist: when tin supply broke, bronze became unaffordable, and iron went from curiosity to default. Iron ore is everywhere, so no palace could tax it, and that is what matters. The Atlas dates iron smelting to Hattusa around 1400, Megiddo 1100 and Athens 1050 BCE, a sequence that follows the collapse rather than leading it. Iron was initially worse than good bronze (steel needs carburizing and quenching), so it did not cause the crash; it was the fallback that outlived the system it replaced. The Epidemiologist and climate historian will show the drought and famine that hit grain surpluses; what the metal data adds is that palaces lost their grip on both food redistribution and the metal that armed their men, leaving no income to rebuild. Whether tin routes failed first or demand collapsed first is genuinely unresolved.

steps.title: Ugarit's last ledger, 1185 BCE
steps.text: The Atlas ends Ugarit's hub run at 1185 BCE, and the tablets show a commercial city starving its own logic: the king is asked to send grain to Hatti, and the Hittite overlord demands ships and troops while Ugarit's fleet is far away. A famous letter from Ammurapi says the enemy ships have come and burned his cities. Ugarit's wealth rested on being a toll point; when sea trade stopped, taxes, wages and the craft workshops dependent on them vanished at once. Hattusa falls around 1180 on the Atlas, and the Military historian will cover who burned what; the economic point is that Ugarit was never rebuilt, while Tyre and Byblos, smaller traders, kept the sea routes alive and became the Phoenician cities. What survived was decentralized, merchant-run commerce rather than palace-administered flows.

steps.title: Fortresses on the chokepoints
steps.text: In 1250 BCE the system is held by gates and walls. The map shows the Hittites holding the Cilician Gates (37.3N, 34.8E), the one pass between Anatolia and Syria, while Mycenaean Greece holds Thermopylae and the Isthmus of Corinth. Mycenae's Cyclopean walls and its secret cistern are built for this world, and the Egyptian New Kingdom is the other great army. These were palace armies: chariot squads, conscript levies and royal stores, all fed through the palace. That made them strong in set-piece battles and brittle against raiders who came by sea and could not be met at one gate. Bosporus, Suez and Otranto show '?' in the data, so I will not claim who held them.

sources.cite: Eric H. Cline, 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed (2014)

steps.title: Djahy and the Delta: the sea battle
steps.text: The map has two battles for this year, both Egyptian Empire versus Sea Peoples: Djahy (32.8E, 35.3N as plotted, in reality the Levantine coast) and the Delta (30.9E, 31.1N). Ramesses III's Medinet Habu inscription says that no land could stand before them from Hatti, Kode, Carchemish, Arzawa and Alashiya, and the Sea Peoples came with families and ox-carts, so this was migration under arms and not a raid. Ramesses claims he lined the river mouths with ships and archers, caught the enemy in a harbor-like trap, and pulled them ashore to be slaughtered. Ugarit's last king sent a letter that his ships were away in Hatti while enemy ships had burned his cities. That is a fleet-readiness failure, and the Economic historian will show the grain and metal ties that pulled those ships away; what the Epidemiologist and climate historian's drought data adds is why whole families were on the move at all. Egypt won, but the Hittite capital Hattusa and Ugarit are both dead by 1180 and 1185 BCE.

steps.title: After the walls: who still held the gates
steps.text: By 1100 BCE the map shows the Cilician Gates passing from the Hittites to Assyria, and Thermopylae and the Isthmus passing from Mycenaean Greece to the Greek Dark Ages. The gates stayed, but the states that garrisoned them did not. Egypt held its core but lost the Levant, and the New Kingdom ends in 1070 BCE. The lesson I draw is that no one lost a single decisive battle: Egypt won the one we know best, and still the system failed. We do not actually know how many sites were sacked by Sea Peoples rather than by earthquakes, civil war or internal revolt, and archaeologists still argue over it. Lens limit: Troy and Mycenae show destruction layers, but destruction layers do not name the attacker.

steps.title: Palace states: one point of failure
steps.text: Around 1250 BCE the great powers were run as palace economies: Hattusa, Mycenae, Pylos and Ugarit each concentrated tax, rations, bronze and ritual authority in a scribal centre. The Linear B tablets at Pylos record rations, bronze allocations and coastal watchers, which shows how much of the state was an accounting system run from one building. The Atlas model rates Mycenaean Greece at only 8% fragility and the Hittites at 10% (base rate 14%), so by area and apparent stability they looked calm, and the model did not foresee the collapse. That is the political lesson: legitimacy and logistics were fused in the palace, so each state was efficient in good times and had no fallback in bad ones. The Economic historian will show the tin and silver flows; what my lens adds is that the same centralisation made each ruler the only buyer, sorter and redistributor.

steps.title: Hattusa and Ugarit go dark
steps.text: Hattusa is abandoned around 1180 BCE and the Hittite Empire ends by 1151 BCE in the Atlas data. Ugarit's last years (to about 1185 BCE) have a famous sign: letters in which the king is asked for troops and ships while the enemy is already in the land, and Hittite overlords demand grain in a famine. A vassal system works only while the centre can protect and feed its dependents; once Hatti asked its vassals for food rather than giving protection, the bargain behind the loyalty was void. The Military historian will cover the Sea Peoples and the fallen fortresses; the Epidemiologist and climate historian will show the drought that emptied the granaries. My claim is narrower: the empire's multi-level vassalage turned local shocks into a chain of defaults. Whether Hattusa fell to invaders, internal revolt or simple abandonment is still debated.

steps.title: Who endured, and why
steps.text: Egypt survived because it had a Nile that produced grain without needing imports and a state that bent: the New Kingdom lasted until 1070 BCE in our index, but Ramesses III won in 1177 BCE at great fiscal cost, and the first recorded strike by royal tomb-builders at Deir el-Medina came in his reign. Assyria (fragility 13%, peak 0.599 Mkm² in 1220 BCE) shrank but persisted as a river-valley core with a militarised king, and its empire revived after 900 BCE. Small city-states such as Tyre and Byblos, along with Phoenician coastal towns, were less dependent on a single palace and resumed trade with the Levant in the following centuries. Greece shows the opposite result: Mycenaean Greece ends in 1101 BCE and the Greek Dark Ages begin, peaking at only 0.061 Mkm². The pattern is that survivors had a fallback in agriculture, a smaller scale, or a ruler who could be replaced. Egypt endured but weakened, so it was not unharmed.

sources.cite: Eric H. Cline, 1177 B.C.: The Year Civilization Collapsed (2014)

links.why: Drought hit grain stores that palaces had made the basis of their authority, so a climate stress became a legitimacy crisis in states with no fallback.
The tin-and-copper trade that supplied palace bronze made the armies a function of a few ports, so when sea trade was disrupted the gate-and-chariot defences lost their supply.
Hatti demanding grain and ships from vassals like Ugarit voided the protection bargain, and Ugarit, a toll city, lost the trade that funded its defence.
Egypt's Nile flood, fed by monsoon rain far upstream, gave it a physical buffer that its bending, replaceable state could use to endure where Mediterranean-rain palaces failed.

views.against: The model is hard to falsify, and it may blur which factor mattered most at each site.

whatifs.q: What if the Nile flood had failed in the 1180s as the Mediterranean rains did?
whatifs.a: Egypt would have lost its one physical buffer, and Ramesses III's victory at the Delta might not have held. With grain shortages already causing strikes at Deir el-Medina, a failed flood could have collapsed the New Kingdom decades earlier than 1070 BCE. This is speculation about a system that was already under strain.

q: What happened to the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World?

answer.short: Six of the Seven did not die from one cause: faults and soft ground broke the Lighthouse, Colossus and Mausoleum, Christian-era law and belief stripped Ephesus and Olympia of protection and purpose, and the Hanging Gardens may never have stood at Babylon at all. Giza survived because it was solid stone on stable ground, a tomb no army needed and no state could cheaply quarry. The common thread is upkeep: a monument without a funder or a reason to visit became a quarry, and the stone usually lived on in forts, castles and churches.
answer.frame: Six of the Seven Wonders were destroyed by earthquakes, fire, and conquest between 226 BCE and 1500s CE; only Giza survives, and Rishi's 1348 map shows the Mediterranean world where their last traces stood or fell.

steps.title: The Nile Delta's soft ground
steps.text: Alexandria's Pharos (280 BCE-1323 on your map) stood on a limestone islet at the edge of the Nile delta, on the Africa-Eurasia-boundary-adjacent Hellenic arc's reach, where tsunami and quakes are real hazards. Medieval accounts record damaging earthquakes in 796, 951, 956, 1303 and 1323; the 1303 event (centered off Crete) badly damaged the tower and 1323 ended it, and in 1477 the Mamluk sultan Qaitbay used the fallen stone for a fort. Thonis-Heracleion (700 BCE-750 CE) shows the same ground failing: the delta's saturated sediment liquefied and the port slid under the sea. Giza, by contrast, sits on a stable limestone plateau above the floodplain, near Memphis, so it had no soft ground to lose. About 2.3 million blocks and a 146 m height were the plan; geology did the preserving.

sources.cite: Guidoboni et al., Catalogue of Ancient Earthquakes in the Mediterranean Area up to the 10th Century (1994)
Lighthouse of Alexandria

steps.title: The Aegean's shaking coast
steps.text: Three wonders sat in the Aegean's western Anatolian fault zone, plus Rhodes on the Hellenic arc. The Colossus (33 m bronze, 280-226 BCE on your map) lasted only about 54 years: an earthquake snapped it at the knees, and it lay in ruins for centuries rather than being rebuilt. The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus (350 BCE-1522) stood long enough that later earthquakes loosened its structure, and in 1522 the Knights of St John took its stone for Bodrum castle. The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus faced a different geographic problem: the Cayster river silted up the harbour, so the sea retreated from the city, and Ephesus lingers on your map until 1400 as a marsh-bound ghost. The Temple of Artemis ended in 401 CE by Christian-era dismantling rather than a quake; at Olympia, Zeus (435 BCE-475 CE) was moved to Constantinople per tradition, and the site was then buried by Kladeos river floods and landslides. The Military historian will cover who stripped the ruins; what the terrain adds is that rivers and faults prepared the ground.

steps.title: Babylon: a garden on a river that moved
steps.text: The Hanging Gardens (600-100 BCE on your map) are the odd one out: no earthquake, no fire, and no archaeology that proves they existed at Babylon at all. Babylon sat on the Euphrates floodplain, where brick (no stone) dissolves in rain, floods and rising salt, and where channels shift. Once the Seleucids shifted their capital to Antioch and canal maintenance lapsed, the city shrank toward your map's end date of 100 CE. That is what a river city looks like without upkeep: the geography does not destroy it, it simply stops forgiving neglect. The Political scientist will cover who stopped maintaining; the honest answer on the gardens is that we don't know their site, and some scholars (Stephanie Dalley) argue they were at Nineveh.

sources.cite: Stephanie Dalley, The Mystery of the Hanging Garden of Babylon (2013)

steps.title: Alexandria's harbour: raided, then stripped
steps.text: The Pharos was a harbour fortress as much as a beacon. It stood from about 280 BCE to 1323 (the atlas dates). Earthquakes in 956, 1303 and 1323 broke it, and by 1349 Ibn Battuta found it a ruin. The soldiers' part came last: in 1477 the Mamluk sultan Qaitbay built a coastal fort on the site and reused its fallen blocks. The Library was a military casualty of a different kind. Caesar's fire in 48 BCE (the atlas shows Pharsalus the same year) damaged part of it, and the Roman era after Actium in 31 BCE ended its royal patronage. Its decline was slow, and the atlas bounds it at 391. The Geographer will show the fault lines; what the war layer adds is that Egypt's rulers reused the stone for forts once the tower was no longer worth rebuilding.

steps.title: Halicarnassus: the Mausoleum quarried by Knights
steps.text: The Mausoleum's long life (about 350 BCE to 1522 on the atlas) ends with a garrison. Earthquakes had toppled its upper structure by roughly the 1400s. In 1406 the Knights of St John began building Bodrum Castle beside it and took the fallen marble and stone for the walls. In 1522 the Knights' final surrender at Rhodes ended their hold, and the site was left to be taken apart for building material. The Colossus (about 280 to 226 BCE) is the earlier case: the atlas shows the quake in 226 BCE, but a later tradition says Arab forces sold its bronze in the 600s. That tale is late and doubtful, and I treat it as unproven. The Political scientist will name who tolerated or ordered the quarrying; I add that a fortress at the sea-gate is what finally consumed the ruin.

steps.title: Giza survives: the plague map's 1348 view
steps.text: Giza lasted because it was a tomb, not a strategic asset. No siege ever needed it, and the Mamluk Sultanate (1250 to 1517) held Cairo nearby with a standing slave army. Its outer limestone casing was stripped for Cairo's building in the Middle Ages, though the exact dates are debated. The structure itself is 2,560 BCE, and the great chokepoint at the First Cataract (24.1,32.9) lay far to the south. The map is set to 1348, the plague year, and the Black Death hit Cairo hard. The disease layer will show a loss of labour rather than a loss of walls. The Mamluks had little reason to demolish a mass of stone that nobody could storm or garrison.

steps.title: A tourist list, not a sacred one
steps.text: The Seven were never a religious canon. They were a Greek sightseer's checklist (theamata, 'things to be seen'), shaped after Alexander when the Greek-speaking world suddenly stretched from Olympia to Babylon. Herodotus had already marvelled at Babylon and Egypt in the 400s BCE; the short list we know is usually traced to Hellenistic authors, and the 'Antipater of Sidon' epigram (c. 140 BCE) is the best-known early text naming them, though the earliest lists varied (Babylon's walls sometimes replaced the Lighthouse). Notice the bias: all seven sit inside the Greek, Egyptian and Persian horizon, with none from India or China. The number seven itself carried weight, being a perfect, cosmic number in Greek and Near Eastern thought. So the list is a map of what Hellenistic readers could reach, not of what was greatest. Exact origins of the canon are uncertain.

steps.title: Sacred ones died, useful ones were quarried
steps.text: Belief decided the fate of the cult wonders. The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus (data: 550 BCE to 401 CE) ends in the age of Christian emperors; tradition ties its end to a Goth raid in 262 and to John Chrysostom's campaign against it around 401, and its stones reportedly went into other buildings, with some reused in Hagia Sophia, a claim that is medieval tradition rather than firm proof. Zeus at Olympia (ends 475 in the data) was reportedly carried to Constantinople as a prized ornament and burned there. The Library of Alexandria (ends 391 in the data) belongs to the same story of pagan sites closing. Hypatia's killing in 415 shows how heated Alexandria's Neoplatonist world had become. The Geographer will show where earthquakes struck; what religion adds is that Christian Rome let the pagan shrines lose their protectors and their purpose.

steps.title: Spolia: the Mausoleum and Lighthouse become other people's stone
steps.text: By 1348 the list had become a legend about ruins. The Lighthouse (data: to 1323) had stood about a thousand years, reportedly 100 m or more tall, until earthquakes in the 900s to 1300s brought it down; the last damage came in 1303 and 1323 by common account, and in 1477 the Mamluk sultan Qaitbay built a fort on its site with its blocks. The Mausoleum (data: to 1522) stood into the Middle Ages, was shattered by earthquakes, and the Knights of St John took its stone for Bodrum Castle from 1402, while its sculpted slabs reached the British Museum in 1846. Giza survived partly because it was a tomb too huge to quarry cheaply, though its casing stones were taken to build medieval Cairo. Where the Military historian will show the sieges and the Political scientist the rulers who stripped ruins, what ideas add is that stone had its best afterlife in new sacred buildings: castles, mosques and churches, an act of reuse rather than only loss.

steps.title: Kings who paid for wonders, and kings who stopped
steps.text: Most wonders were dynastic or civic projects, so they lived and died with the regime that funded them. The Hanging Gardens (map span -600 to -100) sit in Babylon, which the Neo-Babylonian Empire (600-531 BCE, fragility 7%) lost to Cyrus; later Seleucid and Parthian rulers had no reason to maintain a rival capital's garden, and Babylon itself fades by about 100 CE. The Colossus of Rhodes (-280 to -226) stood only 54 years: the earthquake of 226 BCE broke it, and by Pliny's account the Rhodians declined Ptolemy III's offer of funds to rebuild, citing an oracle. That is a rare case of a polity choosing not to restore a wonder. The Mausoleum at Halicarnassus (-350 to 1522) was a satrap's tomb, Mausolus of Caria under Achaemenid overlordship, and it outlasted every empire on my list until the Knights Hospitaller quarried it for Bodrum castle in 1522.

steps.title: Christian law ends Olympia and Ephesus
steps.text: Law, not just stone, did the killing. The Edict of Milan (313) made Christianity lawful; the Edict of Thessalonica (380) made it the imperial faith; and Theodosius I's later decrees closed pagan cults, with the end of the Olympic Games traditionally put near 393. The Temple of Artemis (map span to 401) was wrecked by Goths in 262 and then abandoned, with John Chrysostom's campaign against it around 401 as the last blow. The Zeus statue at Olympia (to 475 on the map) is traditionally said to have been carried to Constantinople, where it burned in 475; this is a later tradition and the evidence is thin. The Historian of faith and ideas will explain the belief side; what my lens adds is that the state withdrew funding, legal protection and a reason for pilgrims to come, and a monument with no budget becomes a quarry.

steps.title: The Lighthouse: a state-run beacon that outlived dynasties
steps.text: The Lighthouse (-280 to 1323 on the map) lasted about 1,600 years because every regime that held Alexandria, Ptolemaic, Roman, Byzantine, then Arab dynasties, needed the port to work. Earthquakes in 956, 1303 and 1323 (the last by the usual account) wrecked it; Ibn Battuta saw the ruin around 1326 and again in 1349. By 1348 the Mamluk Sultanate (1250-1517, peak 1.854 Mkm² in 1516) held it, and the Black Death arrived in Egypt that year, shrinking the tax base that funded repairs. Sultan Qaitbay then recycled the fallen stone into his fort in 1477-79, a case of a regime reusing a wonder rather than rebuilding it. Giza is the opposite case: it needed no maintenance and had nothing worth looting. The Geographer will show the faults; the question I leave open is whether a stronger state could have rebuilt after 1323, and the plague years make that doubtful.

links.why: Earthquakes in 956, 1303 and 1323 brought the Pharos down, and that left fallen blocks which the Mamluk military then reused for Qaitbay's fort in 1477.
The loss of belief in pagan cults (religion) was turned into closed temples and withdrawn funding by imperial decrees (law), so Ephesus and Olympia lost both pilgrims and protection.
Rulers' choice not to rebuild or maintain (Rhodes declining funds, Bodrum's builders tolerated) opened the way for the Knights to quarry the Mausoleum's fallen marble.
Babylon's river-and-brick geography needed constant canal upkeep, so when later rulers shifted their attention elsewhere the city faded and any gardens with it.

whatifs.q: What if the Rhodians had accepted funds and rebuilt the Colossus after 226 BCE?
whatifs.a: It would likely have faced the same Aegean seismic risk and, as a bronze statue, would have been a tempting target for metal-hungry rulers, so a long survival is doubtful. Its best chance was as a harbour-city symbol maintained by Rhodes' wealthy trade economy, as the Pharos was by Alexandria's regimes. This is speculation, and the Pliny story of the oracle is itself uncertain.

q: Which cities lasted for thousands of years, which vanished, and why?

answer.short: Cities lasted when they combined a crossroads or chokepoint with a water or food source that did not depend on a single channel (Damascus, Istanbul, Aleppo), or when a sacred duty kept outsiders paying to maintain them (Jerusalem, Varanasi, Mecca). They vanished when they were tied to one river channel (Ur, Mohenjo-daro), one toll commodity (Petra), a maintenance-heavy water network (Angkor), or a patron-dependent institution (Nalanda, the House of Wisdom). Climate and disease were usually the trigger, but the site's fallback options decided whether the city recovered.
answer.frame: Cities like Damascus, Jericho, Varanasi and Athens persisted for millennia while Ur, Babylon, Carthage, Angkor and Pataliputra faded, so we must explain what sustained or broke each site: water, trade routes, conquest, sacred status, climate.

plan.frame: Cities like Damascus, Jericho, Varanasi and Athens persisted for millennia while Ur, Babylon, Carthage, Angkor and Pataliputra faded, so we must explain what sustained or broke each site: water, trade routes, conquest, sacred status, climate.

angles.geographer: Which sites had water, soil, harbours and crossroads that kept cities alive, and which lost them?
angles.epidemiologist: Which droughts, river shifts, salinization and plagues emptied cities, and which cities recovered?
