steps.title: Springs, fords and holy rivers: the sites that would not die
steps.text: Damascus sits where the Barada river leaves the Anti-Lebanon and spreads into the Ghouta oasis, a green island at the edge of the Syrian desert; the water is permanent and the roads from Egypt, Arabia and Mesopotamia all have to pass it. Aleppo (named in the Ebla tablets, c. 2400 BCE) and Byblos (a cedar port occupied since about 5000 BCE) win on a different formula: a rainfed grain plain or a sheltered harbour backed by forest. Notice the pattern in the list: all of these sit on a crossroads plus a reliable local water or food source, so when an empire falls the site is still the best place to put a city, and the next conqueror rebuilds it. Jerusalem is the odd one, a hill town with a modest spring (Gihon) and no great hinterland, which suggests its survival owes more to status than to soil; the Historian of faith and ideas will show why. I am inferring the 'best site wins again' rule from the Atlas list; it is a pattern, not a measured law.

steps.title: Rivers that walked away: Ur, Uruk, Babylon and the Indus
steps.text: Ur (3800-450 BCE) and Uruk (4000 BCE-640 CE) were river cities in a land with almost no rain: they lived on canals cut from the Euphrates, and when the main channel shifted away from them, or salt built up in the irrigated fields, the city had no fallback. Ur lasted about 3,350 years in the Atlas, but its final abandonment around 450 BCE came as the river moved and the head of the Persian Gulf coast changed. Babylon, 100 km north on the Euphrates at the point where it comes closest to the Tigris, sat on a more flexible plain and survived from 2300 BCE to 100 CE. Mohenjo-daro (2500-1900 BCE) and Harappa (to 1300 BCE) had the same weakness: monsoon-fed rivers like the Indus and the Ghaggar-Hakra shift course, and a city cannot walk after a river. The Epidemiologist and climate historian will show the drought and salinity records; what the map adds is that the cities that vanished were tied to one channel, not one valley.

steps.title: Harbours that silt up, crossroads that never close
steps.text: Ephesus (to 1400) and Miletus (to 1500) were harbour cities on river mouths: the Maeander and Cayster rivers carried silt that pushed the coast outward until the quays were stranded kilometres from the sea, and the cities shrank. Thonis-Heracleion (700 BCE-750 CE) is the extreme case, a Nile-delta port that sank into the soft sediment. Carthage was destroyed in 146 BCE yet rebuilt, because the Gulf of Tunis site, 140 km from Sicily across a narrow sea, is too good to leave empty, and it only fades in 698 CE when Tunis and Kairouan take over the same function. Istanbul controls the Bosporus and Dardanelles: every ship and grain cargo between the Black Sea and the Aegean passes its gate, which is why it is still a capital at 1348 after being the seat of a Roman, Byzantine and soon Ottoman state. The Economic historian will show the silver that paid for dredging and rebuilding; what only geography sees is that a chokepoint is the one asset a plague, a fire or a siege cannot move.

steps.title: The rains fail at Tell Leilan
steps.text: The 4.2-kiloyear drought (c. 2200-1900 BCE) ran from the Mediterranean to the Indus, and at Tell Leilan the rain-fed wheat plains failed: Weiss and colleagues found the city abandoned and wind-blown dust in the layers, tied to the end of the Akkadian Empire (2334-2154 BCE). Irrigated southern Mesopotamia, Ur, Uruk and later Babylon, survived by drawing on the rivers, but paid for it in salt. Evaporating irrigation water left salt in the fields, and wheat, which tolerates salt poorly, gave way to barley across the south. This is a slow killer: Ur is on the map to 450 BCE, Uruk to 640 CE, so these cities died over centuries of shifting channels and falling yields, not in a single year. Harappa (to 1300 BCE) and Mohenjo-daro (1900 BCE) sit in the same dry band, though the Indus case is argued, not settled.

steps.title: Plague cities that came back
steps.text: Shocks hit cities in very different ways. Athens lost perhaps a quarter of its people in 430-426 BCE (Thucydides), and was still a city a thousand years later. Pompeii was buried by Vesuvius in 79 CE and never rebuilt, because a volcano removes the site itself. The pandemic that mattered most for survival was the Plague of Justinian: it reached Constantinople in 542, then returned in waves until about 750, after the eruptions of 536 and 540 had chilled the Late Antique Little Ice Age. Constantinople kept its walls, its grain fleet and its status, and so refilled; Carthage, hit by the Plague of Cyprian (249-262 CE) then by conquest, ends on the map in 698. The Economic historian will show the silver that rebuilt capitals; what disease adds is that recovery needed a steady inflow of migrants, because pre-modern cities lost more people to death than they gained by births. Whether the Justinianic death toll was as high as the 25-50 million sometimes quoted is debated.

steps.title: 1348: the plague meets the survivors
steps.text: The map's own arrival dates show a shipping disease: Kaffa September 1346, Constantinople July 1347, Alexandria and Messina October 1347, Marseille November, Genoa and Venice January 1348, then Damascus in July. Hub cities were hit first and hardest because they were hubs. Yet most survived: Florence (March 1348) and Venice lost very roughly a third to a half of their people by common estimates, and refilled by pulling in villagers. Note the quiet cause underneath. The Great Famine of 1315-1317 left children who died at higher rates in 1348 (DeWitte and Slavin), so one cold shock set up the next. Far off, Angkor's megadroughts (1340-1420) broke its water works, with drought then flood, and it was abandoned as capital by 1431. The Geographer will say which sites had water to keep; the disease lens notes that a city survives plague if its land can resupply people, but not a failing water system.

steps.title: Petra: a city that lived on a toll
steps.text: Petra (-300..700) shows the pure tax-base city. The Incense Route (700 BCE-300 CE) carried South Arabian frankincense and myrrh north from Sana'a via Mecca and Medina, and Petra grew rich taxing the caravans rather than producing anything itself. Such a city lives exactly as long as its route does. When Rome took over the Red Sea sea-lanes and the monsoon route (100 BCE-1500) undercut the camels, the toll dried up, and by the data's own end date (700) Petra was gone as a city. Damascus, by contrast, sat where several routes crossed and fed on a farming oasis, so it never depended on one commodity. The Geographer will show the water and rock that made Petra defensible; what only the ledger shows is that a toll city has no fallback income. I am inferring the Roman reorientation of trade from general scholarship, not from the map's records.

steps.title: The relay: hubs are handed on, not kept
steps.text: The Atlas's western trade-hub relay reads like a baton pass: Tyre (1000-332 BCE), Carthage (550-146 BCE), Alexandria (300 BCE-400 CE), Constantinople (400-1204), Baghdad (800-1000), Venice (1204-1500). Each city held the hub for roughly 200 to 700 years, then lost it, yet the sites mostly survived: Tyre and Alexandria remain on the map, Istanbul has run since -657, Venice since 421. Carthage is the clearest casualty: Rome razed it in 146 BCE, and its place entry ends in 698. So commerce makes a city rich, but surviving the loss of the hub depends on a second income (grain land, a capital's court, a harbour). Baghdad (founded 762) boomed as the caliphs' tax base, then slid as the Abbasid Caliphate weakened. The Epidemiologist will show what the plague and river data add to its fall; I am only showing that its money came from taxing, not making.

steps.title: Angkor and Pataliputra: rich on rice, ruined by upkeep
steps.text: Angkor (802-1431) was a rice-and-water-engineering economy: the Khmer Empire taxed harvests from vast reservoirs rather than controlling a toll. Such a state is expensive to maintain, so when the monsoon trade shifted toward ports like Quanzhou (1000-1400) and Palembang, inland capitals lost relative weight. Patna, by contrast, has a continuous record from -490 to the present because it sits on the Ganges plain, one of the world's densest farming zones. The Climate historian will show how drought hit Angkor's water works; the economic point is that a city whose wealth is a maintenance-heavy network collapses when revenue dips even a little. Whether trade or climate mattered more at Angkor is genuinely debated, and the Atlas data cannot settle it.

steps.title: Sacred ground outlasts its empires
steps.text: Jerusalem was destroyed by Babylon in 586 BCE, yet the Atlas dates Judaism at Jerusalem from 1000 BCE and the Second Temple from 516 BCE: the exiles came home and rebuilt. Jerusalem has little water, no harbour and no trade crossroads, so the Geographer will not find a material reason for this; what rebuilt it was a text and a promise, since the Hebrew Bible was largely compiled during and after the exile. Babylon is the mirror case: it had everything a city needs, but its sacred role was tied to a king and a temple, and it was marked 'ends 100 CE' on the map. A holy site can be rebuilt by people who live elsewhere and carry its memory as scripture, which makes the city a portable obligation.

steps.title: Pilgrimage as a city's insurance policy
steps.text: Varanasi has been in the Atlas since 1200 BCE, and Mecca (a desert town in a place with no farmland) is listed from 400 CE and became the centre of Islam from 610 CE. Neither city has a farming hinterland that explains it. What they have is a duty: every Muslim who can must go to Mecca once, and Hindus come to Varanasi to die or to scatter ashes. Each pilgrim brings money, builds lodging and demands that the shrine be kept up, so destruction becomes a loss for thousands of people far away. The Economic historian will show the silver; what the ideas layer adds is the reason the silver kept coming even when the trade routes shifted. I cannot give you reliable pilgrim numbers for this period; I am describing the mechanism, not measuring it.

steps.title: Learning centres die with their patrons
steps.text: Institutions without a holy site do not get rebuilt. Plato's Academy ended in 86 BCE when Sulla besieged Athens; the House of Wisdom ended in 1258 when the Mongols took Baghdad; Nalanda was sacked around 1197 and never revived, though its monks survived in Tibet. Compare al-Azhar in Cairo, founded 970 and still working, and Bologna, begun in 1088 as a student guild. Both outlived their founders because they were embedded in a mosque or a guild that could move and renew itself. Aristotle's road shows the same thing: his books survived by moving from Athens to Baghdad to Córdoba and Paris, even as each host city lost its place. The Epidemiologist will show whether the plague of 1348 hit these institutions. I only see that the ones attached to worship or a guild lasted, and I cannot say how much that is cause rather than coincidence.

links.why: Ur and Uruk depended on a single shifting canal system, so the drought and salinity records show how that geographic fragility turned into a slow collapse.
Petra's toll income vanished when trade moved to sea lanes, while Istanbul's chokepoint position meant that trade shifts could not strand it.
Angkor's megadroughts broke the water works that its rice-tax economy needed, and falling revenue then made repairs harder, a feedback loop between climate and finance.
Jerusalem lacks the water and crossroads that explain Damascus, so the geographer's pattern fails there and sacred status has to carry the explanation.

whatifs.q: What if the Euphrates had stayed in its channel by Ur?
whatifs.a: Ur would probably have kept some role as a port and temple city for longer, since its collapse followed the loss of its water. It would still have faced the salinity and political pressures that hit the south, so it would likely have shrunk rather than thrived.

q: How did the Black Death spread across Eurasia, and what did it change?

answer.short: The Black Death woke in Central Asian steppe rodent reservoirs (Chu valley pestilence recorded 1338), rode the Golden Horde's grain and caravan traffic to Caffa by 1346, then went by galley to Constantinople, Alexandria, Messina and Marseille in 1347 and up rivers, passes and the North Sea to Hamburg and the Baltic by 1350. Because it moved along the richest, best-connected routes, trade was both asset and vector, and a generation weakened by the Great Famine of 1315-17 was waiting. Killing perhaps 30-50% of Europeans made labor scarce, so wages and per-capita income rose (England's rose about 37% in seven years, a reconstruction), lords tried and failed to freeze pay by law, and land use and labor-saving technology shifted; the long-run causal story, especially for serfdom and innovation, is debated.
answer.frame: How a plague from Central Asian steppe reservoirs rode trade routes and ships to reach Europe, the Middle East and beyond by 1353, and how the mass death reshaped labor, wealth, faith and state power.

steps.title: The reservoir: where the bacterium woke
steps.text: The map's earliest arrival is the Chu valley (Kara-Djigach) in June 1338, near Lake Issyk-Kul. Gravestones there record an unnamed 'pestilence' in 1338-39, and a 2022 ancient-DNA study of those burials found Yersinia pestis on the lineage that gave rise to the Black Death strains. Plague lives in wild rodents (marmots and gerbils) and their fleas on the Tian Shan steppe, so the first question is why it jumped out of that reservoir. We cannot say for certain; climate swings that shift rodent numbers are the leading suspect, but the 1330s trigger is not proven, and the Chu site's precise link to the western epidemic is still debated. The data here shows the arrival date, not the cause.

steps.title: Fleas on the grain ships: Sarai to Kaffa
steps.text: The arrival log reads like a fuse: Sarai in March 1346, Astrakhan in April, Tana in June, Kaffa in September, roughly six months from the Volga to the Crimean port. That pace fits a disease riding the Golden Horde's caravan and grain traffic, with rats and fleas hitching rides in sacks and carts. The Geographer will show the roads and ports, and the Demographer the body counts; what the plague data adds is that spring-to-autumn timing suggests flea-borne spread was seasonal and warm weather-dependent. The famous tale of Mongol catapults hurling corpses into Kaffa comes from one chronicler, Gabriele de' Mussis, who was not an eyewitness; treat it as a story and not a mechanism.

routes.label: Plague down the Volga and around the Azov coast

steps.title: A hungry continent meets a ship's cargo
steps.text: From Kaffa (September 1346) the log shows Constantinople in July 1347, then Alexandria, Messina, and Famagusta all in October, and Marseille by November: a ship-speed epidemic crossing the Mediterranean in about 14 months. Winter slowed it, yet Genoa, Venice, Pisa and Avignon all report it in January 1348, so ports seeded inland towns that flared in spring (Florence in March, Paris in June, Bristol in August). The climate angle is the Great Famine of 1315-17: DeWitte and Slavin (2013) found that people who were children then died at higher rates in 1348, so a malnourished generation was waiting. The Economic historian will show what the labor shortage did next; what only this lens adds is that the death toll was shaped by who had been starved before. Whether rats or human fleas and lice did most of the spreading is still argued.

steps.title: Caffa: the plague meets a seaport
steps.text: Look at what the map shows: the Pontic-Caspian steppe is a flat grass corridor running from the Golden Horde capital Sarai (46.9N, 47.4E) straight to the Black Sea, with no mountain between. Horse-borne traders and armies moved goods and fleas along it without friction. Caffa sat at the end, a Genoese walled port bought from the Horde, and the Italian chronicler Gabriele de' Mussi tells of Mongol besiegers under Janibeg catapulting corpses over the walls in 1346 (his account is second-hand and written later, so treat the siege detail cautiously). What geography adds is that the steppe road ends at a harbour: once plague reached the quay, it left on ships, which moved far faster than any caravan. The Epidemiologist and climate historian will say where the bacterium came from; I only claim the road it took to the water.

steps.title: Through the Bosporus and down the sea lanes
steps.text: From Caffa, galleys passed the Bosporus (41.1N, 29.1E) into Constantinople in 1347, then fanned out through the Aegean like water from a split pipe. One arm reached Alexandria (31.2N, 29.9E) the same year; the other crossed the Strait of Messina, where Genoese galleys landed sick crews in October 1347, then reached Genoa, Venice and Marseille by winter. A fast galley covers roughly 100 to 150 km a day with a fair wind, so the whole Mediterranean was within weeks of the Black Sea. Ports were infected in sequence, not in a wave: distance by sea mattered more than distance on land. Genoa, Venice and Marseille sit at the mouths of Alpine and Rhone corridors, which is exactly why the inland spread started there.

steps.title: Up the rivers, over the passes, across the Channel
steps.text: Inland, plague obeyed river valleys and passes. It went up the Rhone from Marseille to Paris by mid-1348, jumped the Strait of Dover (33 km) to the south-English coast by summer 1348, and crossed the Alps by the Brenner toward Vienna and the Danube. In the east, the Nile carried it from Alexandria to Cairo, and caravan roads took it on to Damascus, so desert routes mattered as much as sea ones. The Economic historian will show the silver and wages; what the route data adds is that the places hit hardest first were hubs, and Hamburg and the Baltic were reached last, by 1350, when the North Sea and Hanse ships delivered it. Some isolated or off-route districts, such as parts of Bohemia and Poland, were hit lightly, though how lightly is still debated. Even so, a plague that began on a steppe road had covered most of the window's map in about seven years.

steps.title: Caffa to Messina: the plague enters the ledger
steps.text: The Atlas's population series shows Istanbul sliding from 123,000 (1330) to 116,000 (1342) to 109,000 (1353), and Alexandria from 62,000 to 59,000. Those are smooth interpolations, so they hide the real event: a few terrible months. Plague reached Constantinople by 1347 and Alexandria that autumn, where chroniclers describe hundreds of deaths a day. Cairo is listed at 443,000 in 1330 and 437,000 in 1353, a gentle decline that cannot be right. Egyptian sources suggest a toll in the hundreds of thousands in 1347-49, so treat the curve as a placeholder rather than a measurement. The Economic historian will show what scarcity did to prices; what the headcount adds is that the biggest city on the map was probably the biggest single loss.

steps.title: Florence loses a third, Cologne gains a sixth
steps.text: Florence's series runs 67,000 (1330), 54,000 (1342), 46,000 (1353). Boccaccio's Decameron frames its stories as escape from this very plague, and the usual estimate is that Florence lost roughly half to three-fifths in 1348. So the 1353 figure is plausible, but the drop began before the plague, likely from famine and bank failures. London falls from 56,000 to 42,000, again a smoothed fall: plague arrived in autumn 1348, and the usual national estimate is 40-50% mortality. Paris barely moves (200,000 to 204,000), which is suspicious: it was hit in 1348-49 and was refilled by migrants. Cologne rising from 84,000 to 117,000 is the odd one out. Treat it as a regional-data artefact, though the Rhineland did suffer less than Italy and the plague's patchiness is real. Venice is flat at 111,000, which hides a huge loss (reported near 60%) that incoming migrants soon replaced.

steps.title: Cities refill, villages vanish
steps.text: By 1353 Europe had probably lost 30-50% of its people, perhaps 25-50 million across Europe, with Mediterranean and port regions worst hit. The map's cities hide the real demographic change: towns survived by absorbing rural migrants, while thousands of villages shrank or were abandoned, as at Wharram Percy in Yorkshire, whose desertion came later. Ravenser Odd, the Humber port, was already being eaten by the sea and was gone by 1362, a reminder that not every vanished place was a plague victim. Bruges at 46,000 to 47,000 stayed stable as a trade hub drawing labour. Fez rising from 198,000 to 234,000 and Samarkand from 133,000 to 138,000 look like the data's blind spots: North Africa was hit in 1348-49, and Central Asia's own plague history is badly documented. The Economic historian will explain why surviving workers gained leverage; I can only say the survivors had been moved, urban and rural, in numbers we still cannot count precisely.

sources.cite: Herlihy, The Black Death and the Transformation of the West (1997)
Benedictow, The Black Death 1346-1353: The Complete History (2004)

steps.title: Caffa to Venice: the plague rides the spice ledger
steps.text: The plague traveled on commercial infrastructure, which is why it was an economic event before it was a demographic one. The Silk Roads were chains of caravan towns, and in the 1340s the Black Sea end ran through Sarai and the Genoese port of Caffa, where ships loaded grain, furs and slaves for Constantinople, Sicily and Genoa. A galley is a fast, dense, rat-friendly container, so a trade route that normally moved silk in months moved a disease in weeks. The Geographer will trace the exact ports; what price data adds is that the hubs which were richest, like Venice (hub since 1204) and Genoa, were the first and hardest hit because they were the most connected. Connectivity was the asset and the vector at once.

steps.title: The scarcity premium: wages jump, lords legislate
steps.text: Remove roughly a third to a half of the workers in England and the land stays; labor becomes the scarce factor, and its price rises. The Atlas's UK GDP per capita series shows it: $1,155 in 1346, $1,314 in 1350, $1,579 by 1353, a jump of about 37% in seven years, though this is a reconstruction (Broadberry and colleagues) and not a measured census, so treat the exact figures with care. Per-capita income rose largely because there were fewer mouths sharing the same fields and capital, not because anyone invented anything. Lords fought back with the Ordinance of Labourers (1349) and Statute of Labourers (1351), which tried to freeze wages at pre-plague 1346 levels. It mostly failed, because peasants could simply walk to a manor that paid more, and employers broke the law to hire them.

steps.title: Fewer hands, more machines, cheaper land
steps.text: Dear labor and cheap land pushed Europe toward saving labor, a pattern economists call induced innovation, and it is a hypothesis, not a settled law. Gunpowder weapons were already appearing in the Atlas's technology layer (Oxford and Florence 1326, Paris 1346), paper mills like Fabriano (1276) were spreading, and windmills reached Amsterdam by 1400; the long run points toward Gutenberg's press at Mainz in 1450, usually linked to the cost of scribes. Land use shifted too: arable gave way to pasture, which needs fewer workers, and Hanseatic routes (1250-1600) carried wool, grain and cloth between towns whose wage-earners now had money to spend. The tenants-in-chief of manorialism lost bargaining power in the West, while in the East, with a smaller post-plague labor shock and stronger lords, serfdom tightened later; the causal story is debated. The Demographer's death tolls set the size of the shock; what my lens asks is how it was absorbed.

links.why: The steppe road ending at a Genoese harbour (geography) is the same commercial chain of Sarai, Caffa and Venice that the economist shows turning trade connectivity into the disease vector.
The Great Famine's malnourished child cohort (disease/climate) helps explain why Italian cities like Florence, already shrinking from famine and bank failures, lost so heavily in 1348.
Mass death and village abandonment (population) left land abundant and labor scarce, which drove wages up and provoked the Ordinance (1349) and Statute (1351) of Labourers.
Dear labor and cheap land (economy) is the proposed pressure behind labor-saving shifts such as pasture over arable and, in the long run, printing, though the link is a hypothesis.

whatifs.q: What if Caffa's Genoese ships had been quarantined or refused entry to Mediterranean ports in 1347?
whatifs.a: Ragusa's later 30-day trentino (1377) shows quarantine could work, but in 1347 no one understood contagion, and plague could still have come overland or via other ports. A delay of a year or two might have reduced the Mediterranean toll somewhat, but full escape for Europe is unlikely.

q: What did the Columbian Exchange do to the Americas and the rest of the world?

answer.short: The Columbian Exchange emptied the Americas of perhaps 80 to 90 percent of their people through repeated waves of smallpox, measles, typhus and cocoliztli, and that collapse let a few hundred Spaniards inherit tribute systems already hollowed by disease and succession crises. The labor gap was filled by about 12.5 million enslaved Africans, while Potosí and Mexican silver crossed the Atlantic and the Pacific to fund Spain and feed Ming China. American crops (maize, sweet potato, potato, cassava) went the other way and helped roughly double China's population and lift Europe's, so one hemisphere's death helped feed the other three. The scale of the loss is contested, and the climate effect is a contributing factor, not a settled cause.
answer.frame: After 1492 two long-isolated disease pools, crop systems and animal stocks collided, killing most Native Americans and remaking diets, silver flows, empires and populations on every continent.

steps.title: Smallpox walks into Tenochtitlan
steps.text: The Atlas records smallpox reaching Tenochtitlan in 1520 with Narváez's expedition, and killing the emperor Cuitlahuac among many others. Nobody in the Americas had immunity to variola, so it hit every age at once, and the sick could not nurse or plant for the rest. The Political scientist will show the conquest; what the disease record adds is that Cortés besieged a city already hollowed out, and that the Aztec polity (1428-1521 in our index) lost its ruler to a germ and not a spear. Estimates of the central Mexican population run from roughly 15-25 million in 1519 to about 1-2 million by 1620, and the Demographer should own that number; I only claim that disease was the main driver, with war and forced labor secondary.

steps.title: Cocoliztli: the second wave nobody planned for
steps.text: The Atlas lists the 1545-1548 cocoliztli epidemic, a haemorrhagic fever that perhaps killed 80 percent of the native population of central Mexico. That figure is contested: 2018 ancient-DNA work by Vågene and colleagues found Salmonella enterica Paratyphi C in victims of the 1545 outbreak at Teposcolula-Yucundaa, which fits an enteric fever, though the cause is not settled. The lesson is that the Great Dying was not one event but repeated waves of smallpox, measles (from 1531), typhus and cocoliztli, each hitting survivors and their children. A population cannot rebuild when each recovery is cut down within a generation. Our map shows Mexico; the Andes had their own waves after Pizarro, and our data here is thin, so I go beyond it.

sources.cite: Vågene et al., Salmonella enterica genomes from victims of a major sixteenth-century epidemic in Mexico, Nature Ecology & Evolution (2018)

steps.title: The empty continent that cooled the planet
steps.text: Here is what only this lens sees: the Atlas links smallpox in the Aztec Empire to the Little Ice Age via Koch et al. 2019. Their estimate is about 56 million deaths by 1600 across the Americas, leaving some 55 million hectares of farmland to regrow forest and pull down enough CO2 to dip the atmosphere around 1610. Treat it as a contributing factor, not the cause: the Little Ice Age (1300-1850 in our data) also had volcanoes, and Huaynaputina in Peru in 1600 chilled the globe and brought the Russian famine of 1601-1603. The Economic historian will show the silver and crops that moved the other way; the disease record says the Americas were being emptied while the Old World was being fed. Koch's death count rests on assumptions about pre-contact populations that many scholars dispute.

sources.cite: Koch, Brierley, Maslin and Lewis, Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492, Quaternary Science Reviews (2019)
Little Ice Age

steps.title: Two worlds, one headcount
steps.text: Before Columbus the Americas held perhaps 50 to 60 million people, with estimates running from about 8 million (Kroeber's old low count) to over 100 million (Dobyns). Nobody knows exactly, and that is the honest start. By 1650 most estimates put the hemisphere at roughly 5 to 6 million, a loss of 80 to 90 percent. Central Mexico alone is often reckoned at 15 to 25 million in 1519, falling to about 1.5 million by 1620 (Cook and Borah's work, still debated). The Epidemiologist will show the pathogens; what the headcount adds is that the Aztec and Inca capitals, Mexico City and Cusco in the map's index, sat among some of the densest populations on Earth, which is why the pathogens spread so fast. Note that our city table has no 1492 value for Cusco, so the Inca figures here are beyond the map's data.

steps.title: The largest forced migration
steps.text: The map's migration layer records the transatlantic slave trade, 1501 to 1866: about 12.5 million people forced onto ships and about 10.7 million surviving the crossing, the largest forced migration in history (Slave Voyages database). Its headline count is blank on the layer, so I quote the totals from its description. Roughly 4.8 million landed in Brazil, with Salvador (founded 1549) and Rio (1565) as major ports, and the rest mostly in the Caribbean. It was driven by the American labor collapse: where Native people had died, plantations imported Africans. The Economic historian will show the sugar and silver this labor made; what demography adds is that the Africa side lost young adults for centuries, and Africa's population stagnated at around 100 million across the 1700s while the rest of the world grew.

steps.title: Calories that fed a billion
steps.text: The Americas' gift was calories. Maize, sweet potato, potatoes and cassava grew on poor, steep or dry land that rice and wheat could not use. China's population rose from roughly 150 million around 1600 to around 300 million by 1800 or later, helped by sweet potato and maize in the hills. In the map's data Nanjing grows from 1.8 million (1492) to 4 million (1646) to 6.3 million (1800), and Xi'an from 6.3 to 10.2 million, though these city counts look far too large and should be read as regional or metropolitan figures, not true urban populations. Europe's potato effect shows too: London goes from 131,000 to 1 million, and Ireland rose from about 3 million in 1700 to over 8 million by 1840 (beyond the map's window). The Political scientist will show what armies this population fed; I'd say the exchange both killed one hemisphere and fed the other three.

steps.title: The mountain of silver at Potosí
steps.text: Our map's silver-peso record starts at the Mexico City mint in 1536, then Potosí in 1545, the year Spain found the Cerro Rico. Mercury amalgamation, introduced at Potosí in the 1570s, let the Spanish refine low-grade ore at scale, and the mountain became the engine of a money system. Americas silver is commonly estimated at around 80% of world output in this period, and it flowed through Portobelo to Seville (1585) and on to Genoa, Antwerp and the Army of Flanders. Here is the point only the money lens sees: Spain did not keep the wealth. Seville's silver paid its debts to bankers abroad and spread across Europe. The Epidemiologist will explain the labor shock. What I add is that the mita draft put the survivors to work in the mines, so the demographic collapse and the silver boom were linked. Silver output numbers are scholarly estimates, not precise counts.

steps.title: Silver crosses the Pacific to China
steps.text: Manila was founded as a Spanish hub in 1571, and our trade-hub relay lists it from 1571 to 1815. Our silver-peso record follows the coin from Acapulco (1565) to Manila (1571) to Yuegang, Fujian (1575) and Beijing (about 1581). Ming China was converting taxes to silver, so it absorbed the metal and sold silk and porcelain. Mexico City received porcelain by 1574. Flynn and Giráldez date the birth of true world trade to this link, though scholars debate how much silver reached China and by which route. Around the same time, Dennis Flynn's reading is that silver's price in China ran far above its price in Europe, so merchants made profit just by carrying it. The Political scientist will show how this funded Spanish power. What I add is that Ming fiscal reform made China the sink that kept the whole system turning.

steps.title: Sugar, slaves and the crops that fed them
steps.text: Our sugarcane record runs Madeira 1455, São Tomé 1500, Pernambuco 1535, Barbados 1643 and Saint-Domingue 1750, a plantation model moving west with the Atlantic. Sugar was an American crop only through Old World transfer, and it demanded labor the depopulated Americas could not supply, so Africans were shipped in. The Atlantic triangular trade (1640 to 1807 on our map) turned sugar and cotton into British capital. UK GDP per capita rose from 1,649 dollars in 1492 to 2,257 in 1712 and 3,343 in 1800, while India's fell from 1,264 in 1600 to 1,068 in 1750. I won't claim the Atlantic caused all of that gap, since historians argue about how much slavery profits fed British industry. Meanwhile new crops also moved: maize reached Elmina in 1550 and Beijing in 1555, cassava reached Mbanza Kongo in 1550, and the potato reached London in 1590. The Demographer will count what those calories did to populations.

steps.title: Cortés buys an empire from its resentful tributaries
steps.text: The Aztec Empire (1428-1521 on our map) was a hegemonic tribute network: the Triple Alliance ran it by extracting goods and sacrificial captives from subject cities, not by administering them. That was a political opening. Cortés landed in 1519 with roughly 500 Spaniards, and the force that besieged Tenochtitlan in 1521 was mostly Tlaxcalan, Texcocan and other indigenous allies, tens of thousands strong. The Cholula massacre (1519) shows the terror logic on the road in. Smallpox arrived in 1520 and killed the ruler Cuitláhuac within months, so the Mexica lost a king and a large share of their people at the moment of siege. The Epidemiologist will give the mortality; what my lens adds is that the epidemic hit a system where succession depended on a few individuals, so the shock became a legitimacy crisis. Spain did not conquer a state so much as inherit a tribute system, then keep its collection points.

steps.title: The Inca civil war meets the plague
steps.text: The Inca Empire peaked at 2.095 Mkm² in 1497, and the map flags it as fragile (31% collapse risk). Its real weakness was succession: Huayna Capac died around 1527, probably of an epidemic that outran the Spaniards by land, and his sons Huáscar and Atahualpa fought a civil war. Pizarro arrived in 1532 with under 200 men, seized Atahualpa at Cajamarca and ransomed him for a room of gold and two of silver. Because the Inca state was a centralized, personalized hierarchy, capturing the head paralysed much of it. Spain then built a viceroyalty at Lima (founded 1535), but held out-of-reach Vilcabamba until 1572, when the last Inca, Túpac Amaru, was executed. The Demographer will give the scale of the die-off; the political point is that disease and civil war together removed the people whose loyalty held the state up.

steps.title: Law tries to tame the conquerors, and silver pays for the empire
steps.text: The New Laws of the Indies (1542) tried to end new encomiendas and curb the conquistadors, whose private grants threatened to create a hereditary American aristocracy beyond the crown's reach. Peruvian settlers rebelled under Gonzalo Pizarro, and the crown backed down on key clauses; that is the pattern of an empire that governs at a distance. The fix was institutional: viceroys, audiencias, and the Casa de Contratación in Seville to tax and register every cargo. Potosí, founded 1545, then funded the system through silver and the mita labor draft. The Economic historian will show the silver flows; my lens says the Spanish Empire (peak 11.354 Mkm² in 1809, but 22% fragile by the model) lasted three centuries because bureaucracy, not conquest, kept the revenue flowing. Portugal ran a looser version with coastal captaincies and Salvador (1549).

links.why: Smallpox killed Cuitláhuac in 1520 and hollowed out Tenochtitlan, so the siege of 1521 met a polity with a succession crisis and a shrunken population, which let Spain inherit the tribute system.
The American population collapse removed the labor that plantations and mines needed, so Europeans shipped about 12.5 million Africans across the Atlantic to replace it.
Potosí silver, refined by mercury amalgamation and extracted through the mita, was carried via Acapulco and Manila to Ming China, which was converting taxes to silver and so absorbed it.
New crops like maize, cassava and the potato traveled alongside sugar and slaves, and their calories on marginal land helped swell populations in China, Africa and Europe.

whatifs.q: What if the Americas had not lost most of their people to Old World disease?
whatifs.a: Spain would have faced large, organized states with intact armies and tax bases, and conquest would likely have been slower, partial and more like later European footholds in Asia. Without a depopulated continent, there would be less land and labor for plantations, so the slave trade and the silver-driven world economy would probably look very different.

q: How did the 1918 influenza spread around the world so quickly?

answer.short: The 1918 flu spread fast because WWI had built a global system for moving dense, young, immune-naive people on fixed schedules: draft camps, crowded troopships, coaling ports, railways and imperial shipping lines. A mild spring wave went unnoticed, and wartime censorship hid the danger, so by late August 1918 a deadlier strain surfaced almost at once in Brest, Freetown and Boston. Its short infectious period (a few days) meant it outran any quarantine, and demobilization then re-seeded it worldwide. Where states quarantined (American Samoa) people lived; where states were thin or hungry (India, Western Samoa) the toll per head was highest.
answer.frame: The 1918 flu raced worldwide in about a year because WWI troop movements and steamship, rail and port networks carried a novel virus faster than any earlier pandemic.

steps.title: Haskell, Kansas: a virus in the barracks
steps.text: The Atlas marks the 1918 influenza pandemic (1918-1920) as an H1N1 virus that spread with troops and killed young adults unusually often. Where it began is not settled. Kansas is one candidate: Dr Loring Miner reported a severe flu in Haskell County in early 1918, and Camp Funston had hundreds of cases by March. Other candidates are the army camp at Etaples in France, where a respiratory illness was reported in 1916-17, and China. Michael Worobey's 2014 phylogenetic work points to a North American origin of the H1N1 lineage, but the dating is uncertain. The 'Spanish' label is a misnomer: neutral Spain simply reported freely. The Military historian will show the camps and troopships; what the virus data adds is that wave one, spring 1918, was mild and easy to overlook, which hid the danger.

steps.title: Autumn 1918: the same virus turns lethal in three ports
steps.text: Wave two struck within days in Brest, Freetown and Boston at the end of August 1918. This fits a mutated, more lethal strain seeded through Atlantic shipping hubs at almost the same moment. Freetown matters because it was a coaling station for convoys: the ship HMS Mantua brought sick sailors in, and thousands of Sierra Leoneans fell ill within weeks. Most of the pandemic's death toll fell between September and December 1918. The usual estimate is 50 million deaths, within a range of about 17 to 100 million. The Economic historian will show the ports and rails; the epidemiological point is a short generation time. A person was infectious for only a few days, so the virus raced ahead of any quarantine.

steps.title: Wave three and the long tail: the virus reaches everywhere
steps.text: India lost an estimated 12 to 17 million people, the highest toll of any country; the virus arrived in Bombay by ship in June 1918, then travelled with the monsoon-season harvest failure. Western Samoa, then under New Zealand, lost about a fifth of its people in weeks after the ship Talune landed in November 1918, while nearby American Samoa kept the virus out through quarantine. Remote groups with no earlier flu exposure suffered most, as at Brevig Mission, Alaska. A third, weaker wave in early 1919 and a fourth in some places show the virus fading as immunity built up. The Political scientist will show who failed to act; what the climate and disease data adds is that drought and hunger in India raised the death toll before the virus even arrived. I go beyond the Atlas record here, which gives only the headline entry for 1918-1920.

steps.title: Camp Funston: the army camp as incubator
steps.text: A mass army is a virus's dream: tens of thousands of men from every county, drafted, packed into wooden barracks, sharing mess halls and bunks, then shuffled between camps. The US built cantonments in months; Camp Funston in Kansas held about 56,000 men, and its early March 1918 flu outbreak is often cited as the first big military cluster, though whether it was the origin is disputed. Camp Devens near Boston saw roughly 14,000 cases within weeks in September 1918. Military logic then did the rest: the AEF shipped about two million men to France between 1917 and November 1918, usually in crowded troopships out of New York. The Economic historian will show the commercial steamship web; what the camps add is that the army manufactured the dense, young, constantly-moving population that turned a local outbreak into a seeding machine.

steps.title: The Western Front: a conveyor belt of bodies
steps.text: The front was a funnel: men came in by sea at Brest and Le Havre, moved by rail to the line near Verdun (49.2N, 5.4E) and the Somme (50.0N, 2.7E), rotated out to rest billets, and went home on leave or on hospital trains. Étaples, a British camp holding around 100,000 men, was already linked to a 1916-17 respiratory outbreak that some researchers (Oxford, Sherwood and Hammond) proposed as a precursor, though this is debated. In spring 1918 the first wave was mild; by August a deadlier strain surfaced at Brest, a port every American transport used. Crowded troopships were the worst vectors: some voyages lost dozens of men at sea. The Epidemiologist will track the three waves; the military point is that the Channel (Strait of Dover, held by France in the atlas) and the rail net behind the lines moved infected soldiers hundreds of miles in a day.

steps.title: Demobilization: armies carry it home
steps.text: Empires moved soldiers and labourers on a global scale: Indian divisions to France, around 100,000 Chinese and Vietnamese labourers to the Western Front, and African troops to and from Europe. Troopships touching Freetown in August 1918 are linked with the killer second wave's arrival in West Africa, where mortality was severe. The Cape of Good Hope and Suez, both British-held in the atlas for 1907 and 1919, were the pipes through which men and disease flowed east and south. After the Armistice of 11 November 1918, demobilization sent millions home in months, so a pandemic that might have burned out in the trenches was re-seeded into every garrison town and village. The Economic historian will show the trade routes to India and the Pacific; the military addition is that state-run troop movements, running on fixed schedules regardless of health, were a distinct and faster channel. How much was soldiers versus ordinary travellers? We do not know precisely.

steps.title: The steamship shrinks the ocean
steps.text: By 1918 the steamship (Atlas data: New York 1807, Glasgow 1812, Bristol 1838) had cut the Atlantic crossing to about a week, shorter than the flu's 2-day incubation plus 1 week of illness would need to outlast. A ship could leave port healthy, brew an outbreak at sea, and land hundreds of cases. That is exactly what happened at Freetown, Sierra Leone, in late August 1918, where the coal-bunkering station and its dockworkers took the virus from HMS Mantua; Patterson and Pyle estimate about 1,000 dead in Freetown alone within weeks. For comparison, the Atlas shows Atlantic news took 12 days in 1865 and 0 days after the 1866 cable. Words crossed instantly by 1918, but the virus still went at ship speed, and nobody could telegraph a quarantine fast enough to beat it. The Military historian will show who was on those decks; what the trade ledger adds is that coaling ports were the choke points of the whole system.

steps.title: Bombay, the railhead of death
steps.text: The Atlas dates the railway at Mumbai to 1853 and the telegraph at Kolkata to 1851; by 1918 British India had roughly 36,000 miles of track radiating from Bombay, built to haul cotton, wheat and troops. The virus came with returning soldiers and sailors to Bombay in late May and again in September 1918, then rode the trains to Delhi, Calcutta and the Punjab in weeks. The Atlas's Maddison series shows the toll: India's population stagnated at 304.8 million in 1917 and 305.6 million in 1920, when about 8 million a year of normal growth would have been expected, and GDP fell from 338.6 to 309.3 billion dollars (2011 prices). Per capita income dropped from 1,111 to 1,012, while Britain's fell from 8,665 to 7,017 as the war boom unwound. Estimates of Indian deaths run from 12 to 20 million (Chandra et al. propose about 18 million), the worst of any country, partly because colonial grain exports and a failed monsoon in 1918 left people undernourished. The Political scientist will address why the colonial health service was so thin; the economist's point is that the infrastructure of extraction became the infrastructure of contagion.

steps.title: Last islands: Samoa, Fiji, Tonga
steps.text: The Pacific shows how thin a trade line can be and still kill. The Talune, a small Union Steam Ship Company steamer running the copra and passenger route out of Auckland, carried sick passengers to Tonga, Fiji and Apia in November 1918, and the call at Apia on 7 November began an epidemic in which about 22% of Western Samoa's population, some 8,500 people, died within two months. Neighbouring American Samoa imposed a strict quarantine and recorded essentially no deaths, a rare natural experiment: the trade connection, not the island, decided the outcome. The Atlas has no map record for this route, so I go beyond its data here, but the pattern fits its trade layer: places at the end of the network, with no prior exposure and few doctors, paid the highest price per capita. The Epidemiologist will explain the immunology; what the shipping ledger adds is that the Pacific was reached last and hit hardest.

steps.title: Censored at the front, honest in Madrid
steps.text: The war turned bad news into a security matter. Britain's Defence of the Realm Act, the US Espionage and Sedition Acts (1917-18), and the French and German press controls kept morbidity and mortality figures out of newspapers, because they might hurt morale or help the enemy. Neutral Spain printed freely, including King Alfonso XIII's own illness in May 1918, so the world named the 'Spanish flu' after the one press that told the truth, not the place it began. The Epidemiologist will show where the virus came from; what this lens adds is that every belligerent government had an incentive to say it was nothing, and officials like Philadelphia's Wilmer Krusen let the September 1918 Liberty Loan parade go ahead with an estimated 200,000 people, after which deaths climbed into the thousands within weeks.

steps.title: States too thin to protect anyone
steps.text: Capacity mattered more than wealth. The British Raj (fragility 23%, 'fragile' in this atlas) had roughly one doctor per tens of thousands of villagers, and the 1918 monsoon failure had already weakened people. The usual estimate is 12 to 17 million deaths in India alone, perhaps 5% or more of the population, though the figures are uncertain. The Economic historian will show the rail and steamship lines; what this lens adds is that colonial states like British Africa (peak extent 10.64 Mkm² in 1919) and the Raj had almost no public-health apparatus beyond ports and garrisons, so the virus ran through the interior unrecorded. Contrast Samoa: New Zealand, then in control, let the ship Talune dock in November 1918 with no quarantine, and roughly 22% of Western Samoans died, while American Samoa quarantined and had essentially no deaths.

steps.title: Why no one coordinated a response
steps.text: The pandemic hit just as empires were breaking: Austria-Hungary and the German Empire ended in 1918, the Russian Empire in 1917, and the Ottoman Empire (fragility 32%, the highest in this window) was dying until 1922-23. The Military historian will show the troop camps; what this lens adds is that no international health body existed. The League of Nations Health Organisation only appeared in 1920-23, and the Office International d'Hygiène Publique in Paris, founded in 1907, had no power to compel anyone. Health was handled as a national matter, so quarantines depended on each government's will, and few governments in 1918 had the legitimacy or the money to impose them. Whether stronger states would have saved many lives is uncertain, since even capable ones like the US failed locally, but the pattern of Samoa versus American Samoa suggests that decisions mattered.

links.why: The mass-army camps (Funston, Devens) supplied the dense, young, constantly mixed population in which the mild spring virus could evolve and then turn lethal.
Wartime censorship hid the mild first wave and early autumn cases, so troop rotations and leave on the Western Front carried on unchecked.
Steamship speed and coaling stations like Freetown explain how wave two appeared in three Atlantic ports within days.
Railways built for extraction carried the virus inland in India, where a thin colonial health service and monsoon failure turned contagion into the world's highest death toll.
The Samoa contrast (Talune docking unquarantined versus American Samoa sealed off) shows that with no international health body, the choice of a single administrator decided who lived.

whatifs.q: What if the Allied governments had published honest flu figures and cancelled troop rotations and mass rallies in August-September 1918?

But events like Philadelphia's Liberty Loan parade might have been cancelled, and crowded troopships might have been delayed, which could have lowered peaks and saved many lives in the autumn wave. Samoa suggests such choices mattered, but a global fix is unlikely.

q: Why did the Silk Road matter, and was it really one road?

answer.short: The Silk Road mattered because it linked Eurasia's separate economies, faiths and technologies, and it was never one road: the Taklamakan forced a braid of oasis chains, steppe and sea routes competed with it, and goods moved in relays rather than end to end. Its biggest payloads were often know-how (paper, porcelain, printing) and religions, not luxuries. The Mongol-era steppe-and-sea system at its peak (1340s) also carried plague at the same speed, so connection and vulnerability were the same pipes.
answer.frame: The Silk Road was a shifting web of overland and sea routes, not one road, and its value lay in linking distant economies, ideas and diseases until the 1340s Mongol-era system began to fracture.

steps.title: The desert ring that forced the branches
steps.text: The first fact is a hole: the Taklamakan, roughly 1,000 km long, is a sand sea that no caravan crosses if it can walk around. So the route splits into a northern and a southern chain of oases, fed by snowmelt off the Tian Shan and the Kunlun, and the two rejoin near Kashgar before the Pamirs. Han China's Xi'an reaches this world through the Hexi Corridor, a thin strip of oases between the Tibetan Plateau and the Gobi (the Gobi is on your terrain list), which is why Dunhuang was a gate to be garrisoned. Zhang Qian's mission in 138-126 BCE found the Parthians and the Sogdian cities of Samarkand and Merv at the far end. So from the very start geography makes a braid rather than a line.

steps.title: Passes, steppe and the sea that competed
steps.text: West of the Pamirs the map opens into choices: the Hindu Kush passes (Khyber at 34.1,71.1; Bolan at 29.6,67.4) lead to the Indus, the Iranian plateau leads on through Merv, Nishapur and Rayy to Baghdad, and the steppe north of the Caspian offers a grass road with no oases but no mountains. Meanwhile the sea competed: monsoon winds carried ships from Guangzhou through the Strait of Malacca and across to the Gulf in a season's sailing, and Hormuz and Malacca are the two chokes that set its tolls. Tang-era shipwreck evidence, the Belitung wreck of about 830, shows Chinese ceramics going west by water in bulk. Sea carried the heavy and cheap (ceramics, grain, timber), while camels carried the light and costly (silk, jade, musk). That split, not a single road, is the real structure.

steps.title: 1348: the web at full stretch
steps.text: By 1348 the Mongol peace had stitched the steppe road to the Black Sea, with Sarai on the Volga as its hub and Caffa and Tana as the doors where Italian ships picked up the goods. The map's chokepoints show the last link: Kerch, then the Bosporus at 41.1,29.1, then the Mediterranean, a single funnel that any traveller, cargo or rat had to pass. The Epidemiologist will show how plague likely moved along this corridor; what geography adds is why it was fast: grassland needs no pass or oasis stop, so a steppe route is a continuous strip with no natural brake. The Economic historian will show the silver and the middlemen; the terrain explains why the Genoese and Venetians sat exactly at those ports. When Mongol order broke up in the 1340s-1360s, the overland link thinned and the sea lanes, plus the Mamluk Red Sea route via Cairo, gained ground.

steps.title: Relay trade: nobody walked the whole way
steps.text: The Atlas's own note on the Silk Roads says it best: 'few merchants went the whole way.' Goods moved in relays through caravan cities (Xi'an, Samarkand, Merv, Antioch), and every handoff added a markup, so Chinese silk reached Rome at many times its price in Luoyang. Middlemen got rich: Sogdians out of Samarkand, Parthian toll-takers, Kushan brokers, and Petra on the parallel Incense Route. The stakes were lopsided, though. Silk, horses and silver were high value per kilo; bulk goods never survived camel economics. And the Indian Ocean monsoon route (100 BCE-1500) was a rival, since ships rode the summer monsoon east and the winter one home, carrying pepper to Alexandria and Rome. Pepper reaches Berenike by 20 CE and Rome by 92 in the object records. So 'the road' was really a bundle of competing price arbitrages.

routes.label: silk, paper, horses and silver, passed hand to hand

Peter Frankopan, The Silk Roads (2015)

steps.title: Paper, porcelain and stirrups follow the money
steps.text: The Atlas's technology layer shows paper hopping Luoyang 105, Samarkand 751, Baghdad 794, Cairo 900, Xàtiva 1056, Fabriano 1276: about 1,150 years from China to Italy, and it moved at merchant and administrator speed, not armies'. Under the Abbasids, Baghdad became the Western trade hub (800-1000), and paper cut the cost of bureaucracy and bookkeeping, which is itself an economic technology. Porcelain tells the same story in reverse demand: Jingdezhen 1004, Quanzhou 1340, Fustat 1350, Kilwa 1400. The Economic historian's takeaway is that the Silk Road's biggest payload was often know-how, while the Historian of faith and ideas will cover how paper carried the texts themselves. Prices of the 'luxury' goods were a sideshow compared with this.

steps.title: 1348: a Eurasia-wide market at its peak
steps.text: By 1348 the Mongol peace had stitched together a real market: Quanzhou (Western relay hub 1000-1400) in the east, Calicut rising (1300-1500), Venice (1204-1500) and Bruges (1280-1490) in the west. Europe was the junior partner: Maddison's UK figure is about $1,159 per head in 1336, versus $1,531 by 1365, a rise driven by plague-thinned labour, not trade. The Economic historian will show the silver and spice flows; what the Epidemiologist and climate historian add is that the same caravans and Genoese ships from Caffa carried the pathogen. Trade profits and mortality used the same pipes, so the system's greatest efficiency was also its vulnerability. By 1368 Ming replaced the Mongols, and overland security faded while sea routes (Malacca from 1400) took over. I'm going beyond the data on the exact volume: nobody has reliable totals for medieval Silk Road trade.

steps.title: The Buddha walks east with the merchants
steps.text: The Atlas's 'Buddha goes east' chain runs Taxila 50 CE, Luoyang 68 CE, Kucha 350, Xi'an 401. It is carried mostly by monks and merchants, not armies. That is the point about 'one road': Buddhism hopped between oasis monasteries and Kushan-era Gandhara (Greco-Buddhist art, from about 50 BCE), so it followed the web of oases, not a line. Kumarajiva, born in Kucha-region Central Asia, produced the Chinese Lotus Sutra in Xi'an in 406. Faxian walked the other way, 399-412, to fetch monastic rules. The Economic historian will show the caravans' goods; what faith adds is that Buddhist monasteries were the inns, banks and storehouses that made the oases dependable.

steps.title: Paper, printing and the Light that vanished
steps.text: The Diamond Sutra printed at Dunhuang in 868 is the oldest dated printed book. Paper itself moved the other way across the same web: tradition links it to Samarkand after the Abbasid-Tang clash at Talas in 751, and Baghdad had paper by the 790s, which fed the House of Wisdom's translators from 830. Manichaeism shows the web's fragility: founded in Ctesiphon around 240, persecuted in Rome and Persia, adopted by the Uyghur court at Ordu-Baliq in 762, and still alive in Quanzhou in 1339 before it vanished. The Epidemiologist will cover movement of bodies; I add that texts and sects ride the same routes and die when their patrons do. The Talas story is partly legend, so treat the paper date as an approximation.

steps.title: 1348: the web carries faith, and fear, both ways
steps.text: By 1348 Islam had followed both a land and a sea branch: Baghdad to Bukhara and Delhi (1206), and the sea chain to Samudera Pasai (1297) and Malacca (1414). Mongol rule had briefly made Nestorian, Buddhist, Muslim and Catholic envoys neighbours at Karakorum, yet the khans of Sarai and Iran converted to Islam, and the Ming (1368) soon closed the East. The Epidemiologist will show how the plague data reaches Caffa and Europe by 1347-48; what faith adds is that the same sea and steppe ties that spread Sufi orders and Ibn Battuta's journeys also carried contagion. After 1368 the Atlas shows Hafez in Shiraz and Ibn Khaldun in 1377 theorising why dynasties decay, as if the age were explaining its own fracture.

steps.title: Steppe origin: Chu valley to the Volga
steps.text: The map records plague at the Chu valley in June 1338, and a cluster of tombstones there with Syriac inscriptions naming 'pestilence' is the classic clue. Eight years later it shows up at Sarai (March 1346), Astrakhan (April) and Tana (June), a hop of well over 2,000 km along the steppe corridor that Mongol peace had made fast and safe. Genetic work points to a Y. pestis lineage that radiated from the Tian Shan region (Spyrou et al. 2022), so the 'road' that mattered here was the northern steppe arm, not the oasis cities. I'm confident of the 1346 sequence in the data; the Chu link as the true origin is strong but debated, since the 1338 dead may have died of something else.

steps.title: Kaffa to Constantinople: plague boards the ships
steps.text: Sea lanes turned a steppe epizootic into a Mediterranean pandemic in about a year: Kaffa in September 1346, Constantinople in July 1347, then Rhodes, Alexandria and Messina all within October. The famous story of Mongol catapults hurling corpses at Kaffa is probably embellished, since rats, fleas and grain ships needed no help. What moves plague is cargo: grain from the Black Sea, with fleas in the sacks. The Economic historian will show the grain and slave trades that filled those holds; what the plague data adds is that the same merchants' schedules set the epidemic's timetable, with Alexandria and Messina hit in the same month. I'd put the arrival dates at high confidence; the exact ship-by-ship route is inference.

steps.title: 1348: the web closes on Europe and the Levant
steps.text: By January 1348 plague is in Genoa, Venice, Pisa and Avignon; Florence follows in March, Paris in June, Melcombe in June, Dublin in August. Land caravans carried it too: Alexandria in October 1347, Gaza in April, Damascus in July 1348. Wherever the web was densest, the timeline compresses to months. The wider damage was not even: DeWitte and Slavin (2013) find that those who had been children in the Great Famine of 1315-17 died at higher rates in 1348, so earlier cold and hunger had loaded the dice. The Historian of faith and ideas will trace pilgrims and preachers on these roads; the open question for the plague data is how many died, since estimates run from roughly a third to a half of Europe, and I would not claim more precision than that. Here the Silk Road's greatest gift, connection, becomes its worst export.

links.why: The Taklamakan forced routes into separate oasis chains, so goods had to change hands at caravan cities, which created the relay trade and its markups.
Sea carried the heavy and cheap while camels carried the light and costly, so the monsoon route competed with overland arbitrage and made the trade a bundle of price gaps rather than one road.
Buddhist monasteries acted as inns, banks and storehouses at the oases, which made the relay trade dependable and spread the faith along the same stops.
The steppe corridor had no passes or oasis stops to brake movement, so plague could cover over 2,000 km from the Chu valley to the Volga in about eight years.
Genoese grain and slave trade out of Caffa filled the ships whose schedules set the epidemic's timetable, so market efficiency became the pathogen's delivery system.

whatifs.q: What if the Mongol steppe route had stayed open and safe after the 1340s?
whatifs.a: Overland trade would probably have kept competing with the sea lanes and Italian ports like Caffa and Tana would have kept their role, but it would also have kept the plague corridor open, so recurrent waves could have reached Europe more often. The Ming closure and the rise of Malacca-centred sea trade make this unlikely, since the order that made the steppe safe was already fracturing.

q: How did the monsoon winds shape trade across the Indian Ocean?

answer.short: The monsoon turned the Indian Ocean into a twice-yearly one-way door, so a merchant got about one round trip a year and had to wait months at the turning points. That wait created the ports (Kilwa, Mombasa, Calicut, Quanzhou, the Malacca Strait), the credit and brokerage networks, the diaspora communities, and the tolls (Srivijaya, Mamluk Cairo) that states lived on. By 1348 the same seasonal clockwork linked the system's busiest nodes to the Black Death's arrival in Alexandria and Cairo, though the plague's reach down the monsoon lanes is not documented.
answer.frame: Seasonally reversing monsoon winds set the sailing calendar, ports, and merchant networks of the Indian Ocean, a system at its medieval peak just as the Black Death arrived in 1347-48.

steps.title: The Wind Gate: Two Seasons, One Ocean
steps.text: The Indian Ocean is a one-way door that swings twice a year. From roughly November to March the northeast monsoon blows from Arabia and India toward Africa. From April to August the southwest monsoon reverses it and drives ships back. A dhow leaving Hormuz or Sana'a in December could reach Mombasa (4°S) and Kilwa (9°S) in about 3-5 weeks, then had to wait for the reversal to sail home. That wait forced a year-long round trip and made the ports hold merchants and warehouses for months. The Swahili towns sit near the practical southern limit, because south of about 10-15°S the monsoon fades. The Mozambique Channel offered no reliable return wind, which helps explain why Kilwa, not Great Zimbabwe's coast, became the gold exit. In 1348 this clockwork was at its medieval peak. Dates are approximate and vary by year. Distances and timings are my estimates, not from the map data.

Southwest monsoon (Apr-Aug): East Africa back to India

steps.title: Gates of Grief and Hormuz: Ports Where Nature Pinched
steps.text: Two narrow gates funnel the western ocean's trade. The Strait of Hormuz is about 40 km wide at its narrowest and leads into the Persian Gulf and the Tigris-Euphrates corridor to Baghdad. Bab-el-Mandeb, the Gate of Grief, leads into the Red Sea, where reefs and contrary northerly winds make the upper sea dangerous. Cargo was often transshipped near the southern end, which favored a harbor like Aden (my addition, not in the index) and the Egypt road to Cairo and Alexandria. The Red Sea's reefs and northerly winds are why many deep-sea ships stopped short and smaller local craft carried goods north. The Economic historian will show the silver and pepper; what the map adds is that these ports exist because the wind and the coast gave a merchant no alternative.

steps.title: Malacca Strait: The Eastern Hinge
steps.text: At the eastern end the same winds meet the South China Sea's own monsoon, and ships from India rarely sailed straight through to China in one season. They waited around the Strait of Malacca (a long channel between Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula) for the next reversal, so entrepôts clustered there. Srivijaya, in the index until 1377, is the clearest example of a state living off this pause. By 1348 it was fading, and the Ayutthaya capital founded in 1351 shows power shifting toward the Gulf of Thailand. The Demographer will trace which communities settled at these hinges; the plague layer matters because a sailing system that moves every 6 months also moves a disease in weeks, so coastal hinge ports were exposed first. I am inferring that exposure from geography, not from a plague record in the map data.

steps.title: The wind is the calendar, and the calendar is the interest rate
steps.text: The Indian Ocean monsoon route in your data (100 BCE-1500) ran on a once-a-year clock: the summer southwest monsoon carried ships east to India from roughly April to August, and the winter northeast monsoon brought them home. A merchant therefore got about one round trip per year, or one turn of capital per 12 months, which is why cargoes had to be high value per ton: pepper, fine textiles, gold, ivory, and warhorses going the other way. Slow capital turnover made partnerships and credit the real technology, not the ship. Calicut (trade hub 1300-1500 in the Eastern relay) sat exactly where the winds delivered Arab, Gujarati and Chinese fleets. Pepper's own journey in the data (Malabar to Venice 1400) shows the endpoint, with each handoff adding margin. The exact monsoon dates and the sizes of those margins are my reconstruction beyond the map data; the Geographer will fix the wind windows, and I only ask what the delay cost.

steps.title: Two-year voyages: the China-to-Africa relay
steps.text: Because of the winds, no one sailed Quanzhou to Kilwa in one go; cargo moved in relays with a waiting season at each hinge. The Eastern hub chain in your data runs Palembang (680-1025), Quanzhou (1000-1400), Calicut (1300-1500), then Malacca (1400-1511), each one a place where a monsoon ended and goods changed hands. The porcelain journey shows the payoff: Jingdezhen 1330, Quanzhou 1340, Kilwa Kisiwani 1400, and Kashan cobalt 1320 shows the reverse flow of inputs. The magnetic compass (Hangzhou 1088, Guangzhou 1117, Isfahan 1232, Mocha 1282) moved along the same lane in about two centuries, which is a nice proxy for how fast information traveled with merchants. Pepper reached Northern Sumatra 1250 and Hangzhou 1290 in your data, showing Chinese demand for the spices the wind carried. The Political scientist will show who taxed this chain; my point is that waiting for the wind meant ports earned money on storage, brokerage and credit, not only on goods.

steps.title: 1348: the wind-borne fortune meets the plague
steps.text: Venice (trade hub 1204-1500) and Cairo's Mamluk Sultanate (1250-1517) were the western end of a wind-timed pipeline, and in 1347-48 plague rode the same ports. Honestly, the Atlas has no price series for pepper or spices, so I cannot show the shock in numbers. Its England series is a clue to the scale: UK GDP per capita rises from 1,159 in 1336 to 1,567 in 1357 (2011 dollars), a jump consistent with plague-driven labor scarcity, though that is Northwestern Europe, not the Indian Ocean. India's population is listed at 75 million for the year 1000, and nothing later in the window, so no check on the eastern side. The Demographer can say which ports were hit; I would ask whether the sailing calendar, a single yearly cycle, let disease travel in a predictable, seasonal pulse.

steps.title: Kilwa and Mombasa: the wind's southern edge
steps.text: The Atlas dates Kilwa Kisiwani and Mombasa from about 900 CE, and both sit near the southern limit where a dhow can ride the northeast monsoon down and still get home on the southwest one. That one-round-trip-a-year rhythm made seasonal merchants pause for months, and pausing is how towns form: Swahili stone towns grew from merchants who stayed to wait out the wind. I have no population figures for either city, and the Atlas has none, so treat sizes as unknown. Kilwa's later fame rests on gold from the Zimbabwe plateau (Great Zimbabwe, 1100-1450 in the index) reaching the coast via Sofala.

steps.title: The cities at the far ends of the wind
steps.text: Look at the terminals. By 1150 Cairo holds 293,000 (up from nothing at 969), Baghdad has shrunk from 669,000 at 900 to 341,000, and Xi'an's figure in the Atlas jumps to 2 million. Those are modelled estimates, so the exact values are soft, but the direction is firm: demand at the Chinese and Egyptian ends of the monsoon system was growing as Baghdad's fell. Between them, diaspora communities carried the trade. Arab and Persian merchants lived in Guangzhou, which suffered a massacre of foreigners in 878 by the rebel Huang Chao, and later in Quanzhou; Tamil guilds such as the Manigramam and Ayyavole operated under the Cholas and left inscriptions as far as Sumatra. I'm going beyond the Atlas for those communities, since it holds no records for them. The Political scientist will show how the Cholas and Srivijaya taxed this, and the Economic historian the cargoes. What I add is the people who settled at each stop.

steps.title: 1348: plague arrives at the system's busiest nodes
steps.text: The Atlas puts Cairo at 425,000 by 1400 and Alexandria at 54,000, down from 133,000 in 900. The Black Death reached Alexandria in late 1347 and Cairo in 1348, and chroniclers claim daily tolls in the thousands there. Those numbers are likely exaggerated, but Egypt probably lost a third or more of its people. Cairo was the western hub for Indian Ocean goods coming up the Red Sea, so its mortality hit the merchant networks directly. Whether the plague travelled on monsoon ships to India and East Africa is not well documented, and I would not claim it. The Geographer's sailing windows suggest it could have, but the record is thin. What does the Atlas's disease layer show for Aden or Calicut?

steps.title: Srivijaya: tolls on the strait
steps.text: The monsoon turned the Strait of Malacca into a toll gate. Ships from China waited for the northeast wind to go home and the southwest wind to return, so they had to winter in Southeast Asia. Srivijaya (674 to 1293 CE, only 0.538 Mkm² at peak in 718) made that wait a business: it required ships to call at its harbours, paid with loyalty and tribute, and punished those who bypassed it. The state was a thalassocracy, a state that governed sea lanes rather than land. The Chola Empire (peak 0.522 Mkm² in 1028) broke this in 1025 with Rajendra Chola's raid on Kedah and Palembang. Our model gives Srivijaya a 20% collapse risk and the Cholas 25%, but the model measures land area and cannot see tolls, which is the real asset here. Confidence is moderate: the raid is well attested in Chola inscriptions, but its motive (revenge for obstructed trade or a political show of power) is debated.

steps.title: Mamluk Cairo: the Red Sea toll
steps.text: At the western end of the monsoon system, the Mamluk Sultanate (1241 to 1518) did not run ships but ran the choke point. Cargo arrived on the southwest monsoon at Aden, went up the Red Sea, crossed to the Nile and reached Cairo and Alexandria, where Venetian and Genoese buyers waited. The Mamluks taxed it at every step: customs at the ports, transit duties, and, in later decades, state monopolies on pepper. That income paid the military slave-soldiers who sustained the regime, which is a political loop: wind, then spice, then tax, then army. Our data lists the Mamluk Sultanate with no fragility score, so that stability is the sultanate's own claim rather than a model finding. Beyond our data, I rely on scholarly accounts that the Karimi merchant guild, the Egyptian-based spice-trading community, was both an ally and a financial resource for the state. The Economic historian will show the cargo; the point from my lens is that Cairo's power rested on a place, not on a fleet.

steps.title: 1348: plague hits the tax base
steps.text: Now at 1348, the Black Death reached Cairo and Alexandria, and the Mamluk state lost a large share of its people and its tax revenue. Mamluk Egypt is often described as hit hard, with rulers after 1348 raising levies as a response. The Delhi Sultanate (Tughlaq, 1326 to 1414, peak 2.449 Mkm² in 1333) and the new Vijayanagara Empire (1344 to 1571) show a different pattern: states on the Indian side were strong on land but their ports in Gujarat and Malabar were run by merchant communities and local rulers. I should say plainly that the evidence for plague's effect in India and the Indian Ocean littoral is thin, and my claim here is a question rather than a result. The Demographer will show who lived in these ports; my lens asks who collected the tax when the merchants died. I do not have a specific 1348 revenue figure to give you.

links.why: The wind's southern limit and forced months-long wait on the East African coast is what turned seasonal merchants into permanent Swahili stone-town residents.
Ships from China had to winter around the Strait of Malacca for the next reversal, and Srivijaya converted that forced pause into mandatory harbour calls and tolls.
One capital turn per year favored high-value cargo like pepper, whose flow up the Red Sea gave the Mamluks a taxable choke point and funded their army.
The same narrow gates and Red Sea route that concentrated trade at Alexandria and Cairo also made them the first and hardest-hit nodes when plague arrived in 1347-48.

views.for: Predictable seasonal sailing windows, relay trade at hinge ports, and cargo concentrated in high-value goods fit the wind schedule closely.
views.against: Treating the ocean as one system can understate regional politics, coastal sailing outside the monsoon, and local trade.

views.name: Janet Abu-Lughod
views.claim: Around 1250-1350 a linked set of trade circuits from Europe through Cairo and the Indian Ocean to China formed a pre-modern world system, which declined partly because of the Black Death.
views.for: The chain Venice, Cairo, Aden, Calicut, Quanzhou fits the relay structure the panel traced, and the plague struck the western terminals in 1347-48.
views.against: Critics argue the system's decline had many causes (Mongol collapse, Ming policy, shifting politics), and plague effects on the Indian Ocean side are poorly evidenced.

sources.cite: Janet L. Abu-Lughod, Before European Hegemony: The World System A.D. 1250-1350, 1989

views.name: Oliver Wolters
views.claim: Srivijaya's power rested on controlling and benefiting from the maritime pause at the Strait of Malacca, rather than on territory.
views.for: Tribute, mandatory calls and the Chola raid of 1025 fit a state living off sea-lane tolls.
views.against: Evidence is thin and mostly from Chinese and Chola sources, and the Chola raid's motive is debated.

whatifs.q: What if the monsoon had been weak or unreliable, with no predictable seasonal reversal?
whatifs.a: Long-distance direct sailing would have been far riskier, and the relay ports, wait-based credit systems and diaspora communities would likely have been smaller or absent. Trade would probably have shifted toward overland routes through Persia and Central Asia, and Swahili stone towns might not have formed. This is speculation built on the panel's reading of the wind-calendar mechanism.

q: How did Mali become rich, and what did Mansa Musa's pilgrimage show the world?

answer.short: Mali got rich by sitting between the Sahara's salt and the Sahel-forest gold and taxing and rationing the exchange, with the Niger's flood-fed farming and cheap river transport supplying the surplus and the road system. Musa's 1324 hajj turned that hidden wealth into a public fact: it depressed gold's value in Cairo for years (per al-'Umari), won him recognition as a sovereign, and put a crowned African king holding gold on the Catalan Atlas of 1375. It showed that Africa was a central supplier of the Mediterranean's money metal, not a periphery, though the vivid numbers are second-hand and the long-run effect on Mali's income is unmeasured.
answer.frame: Mali's gold-and-salt wealth, the empire that Mansa Musa's 1324 hajj made visible to Cairo, Mecca and Europe, and what it revealed about Africa's place in world trade.

plan.frame: Mali's gold-and-salt wealth, the empire that Mansa Musa's 1324 hajj made visible to Cairo, Mecca and Europe, and what it revealed about Africa's place in world trade.
