steps.title: The Niger's flood and the gold forests
steps.text: Mali sits where three belts meet: the wet Guinean highlands in the south-west, the Niger's inland delta, and the Sahel grass belt just below the Sahara. Gold came from alluvial diggings in Bambuk and Bure, on Mali's southern and western margins, and Sundiata's heirs (after the 1235 founding) controlled the approaches. The Niger's annual flood is the quiet engine: it waters rice and millet around Jenné-jeno (on your map, 250 BCE to 1400) and gives canoe transport along hundreds of kilometres of flat river. A farming surplus plus cheap river haulage meant gold, grain and people could be gathered at a few market towns. The exact site of Niani and the scale of Bure output are debated, so treat those pins as approximate.

routes.label: Gold from Bambuk and Bure to the Niger

sources.cite: Nehemia Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali (1973)
Mali Empire

steps.title: Where the desert is a coast
steps.text: Geographically the Sahara works like a sea and the Sahel like its shore, with Timbuktu and Gao as ports and camels as ships. Salt slabs from Taghaza, in the desert, were worth carrying south because the humid Sahel has almost none; gold went north in return. Musa's 1324 hajj ran roughly 6,000 km or more each way (my estimate) from the Niger bend through the desert to Cairo and on to Mecca, only possible because Mali held the southern ports and the water-hole chain. Cairo is the key hinge: it lay beyond the Sahara and the Nile route, so Mali's gold appeared there as if from nowhere. The Economic historian will show what Musa's spending did to prices; what geography adds is that the road itself, with its wells and escorts, was the real asset.

steps.title: 1348: the edge of the map
steps.text: The Black Death reached Alexandria and Cairo in 1347 to 1348, and the map's disease layer shows how it hugged ports and river corridors. The Sahara was a firebreak: months of empty desert and few people per well made a poor path for a crowd disease, and whether plague reached Mali is simply not established, with no solid evidence either way. That is a geographic advantage and an evidence gap at once. The Economic historian will show the silver and gold flows; what the plague data adds is that the northern end of Mali's trade (Cairo, Tunis, Fez on your map) was shaken while the southern producers stayed largely out of reach.

routes.label: Western Saharan gold road to Morocco

sources.cite: Black Death in Africa (Wikipedia)

steps.title: Salt for gold at the Niger bend
steps.text: Mali's wealth was a toll-and-monopoly business sitting on the Trans-Saharan gold and salt route (700 CE-1600), where camels swapped Saharan salt and North African goods for West African gold. The forest and savanna south lacked salt, the desert lacked gold, so each side paid a steep premium; the empire taxed the crossing at Timbuktu, Gao and Jenné-jeno rather than mining everything itself. Arab writers such as al-'Umari (writing c. 1337-49) say the ruler kept gold nuggets for the crown while letting dust circulate, a deliberate supply control to protect the metal's value. I'd read that as early central banking by monopoly: Mali could not set a price in Cairo, but it could ration what reached it. Exact output is unknown; the Geographer will show where the goldfields lay, and what my lens adds is that rationing, not mining, made the money.

routes.label: Gold north, salt and goods south (Trans-Saharan route, 700-1600)

sources.cite: Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali (1973)
Hopkins, An Economic History of West Africa (1973)

steps.title: Musa floods Cairo with gold
steps.text: In 1324 Musa reached Mamluk Cairo and spent and gave gold so freely that, according to al-'Umari, who interviewed Cairo officials a dozen years later, the gold dinar lost value and took over a decade to recover. Contemporary sources give the caravan as tens of thousands of people with many camels carrying gold; the numbers (often 60,000 people, 80-100 camel loads of gold) are reported, not verified, so treat them as a sense of scale. The mechanism is plain economics: a sudden injection of gold into a market of fixed goods and a fixed money stock pushes prices up and the metal's value down, here in a single city. The shock was local and temporary, but it advertised that a Sahelian state sat on a supply bigger than the Mediterranean had assumed. The Political scientist will show how Mali financed the trip; I only see the price effect.

routes.label: Musa's hajj caravan: Niger to Cairo to Mecca

sources.cite: Levtzion & Hopkins (eds.), Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History (1981)
Mansa Musa

steps.title: After the glitter: a gold market goes global
steps.text: By 1348 the shock had faded, but the lasting effect was recognition: the Catalan Atlas of 1375 shows a crowned African ruler holding a gold nugget, meaning merchants in Mallorca now priced Mali into their plans. My data has Venice as a trade hub from 1204 and the Trans-Saharan route running throughout, so the Mediterranean demand for gold, to mint ducats and florins, kept pulling the caravans north. Be careful with causation, though: the Black Death reached the Mediterranean in 1347-48, and I have no gold-price series for the Sahel, so I cannot show Mali's income fell or rose. The Historian of faith and ideas covers the Atlas image; the question I pass on is how much of the 1350s monetary change came from plague rather than from Musa.

routes.label: Saharan gold to Mediterranean ports and Venice

sources.cite: Hopkins, An Economic History of West Africa (1973)

steps.title: Kouroukan Fouga: a charter spoken at Kurukan Fuga
steps.text: The Atlas lists the Kouroukan Fouga at 1236, the year Cliopatria starts the Mali Empire, and that is the political story: Sundiata's heirs inherited a constitution-like oral charter, not just a conquest. Tradition, preserved by griots and written down only in the 20th century, assigns clans their roles, protects the person, and sets rules for marriage and property. Treat it with caution: the text is oral, its date and wording are reconstructed, and some scholars doubt how early its contents are. What it shows is how a state of about 1.1 Mkm² (the Atlas's peak figure, reached in 1415) could be held together by negotiated clan roles and sworn alliance, rather than by a standing bureaucracy. The Geographer's goldfields and the Economic historian's trade are what gave the system something worth governing.

sources.cite: D. T. Niane, Soundjata ou l'épopée mandingue (1960)
Wikipedia: Kouroukan Fouga

steps.title: A king who could leave for two years
steps.text: Musa's hajj in 1324 is a governance test: a ruler left a realm bigger than anything in the Atlas's window except Mamluk Egypt and the Byzantines for roughly two years, and it did not unravel. That says the empire ran through provincial governors, tributary kings and a loyal military, with legitimacy resting on the dynasty and on Islam's prestige. The Atlas rates Mali at 16% fragility in 1318, just above the 14% base rate and flagged 'watch', so the pilgrimage was a calculated risk, not a safe bet. Cairo's Mamluks, rated calm at 13%, hosted him as an equal; al-Umari's later report on the visit is our best source, written some 12 years afterward, so the famous spending figures are hearsay. The Economic historian will show what that gold did to Cairo's prices; what only this lens sees is that the pilgrimage was also a diplomatic demand to be recognised as a sovereign.

routes.label: Musa's hajj caravan (approx. route via Walata/Tuat, Cairo, Mecca)

sources.cite: Nehemia Levtzion and J. F. P. Hopkins (eds.), Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History (1981)
Wikipedia: Mansa Musa

steps.title: Mali after Musa, in the plague year
steps.text: At the map's current year, 1348, the Black Death is devastating Cairo and the Mediterranean, yet we have no solid evidence that it reached Mali, and I will not guess. What the state record shows is a Mali that held together: Cliopatria has the empire lasting to 1611 and peaking at 1.114 Mkm² only in 1415, long after Musa died around 1337. Some tradition-based accounts, and Ibn Battuta's visit in 1352-53, describe a functioning court under Mansa Sulayman with order on the roads and strict justice, while also noting Sulayman's stinginess and palace intrigues. Rule rested on a ruler who could be Muslim for the Maghrebi trade and customary for his own subjects. The Economic historian's gold flows and the Geographer's routes are the engine; the open political question is whether Mali's later succession disputes were a weakness or just normal for a lineage-based monarchy.

sources.cite: Ibn Battuta, Rihla (c. 1355)
Wikipedia: Mali Empire

steps.title: A king who made Islam visible
steps.text: Mali's rulers were Muslim before Musa: the Sahel's merchants and clerics had carried Islam south along the trade roads for centuries. What the 1324 hajj did was make that faith a matter of state. Our data calls Musa the emperor whose 'gold-laden pilgrimage to Mecca put Timbuktu on the Islamic map', and the Atlas's Islam journey lists Timbuktu 1325 as a stop between Delhi 1206 and Malacca 1414. He is reported to have returned with scholars and an Andalusian architect, al-Sahili, though the sources (al-Umari, Ibn Khaldun) are Cairo-side accounts and details vary. I am going beyond the Atlas records here.

sources.cite: Levtzion, Ancient Ghana and Mali (1973)
Hunwick, Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire (1999)

steps.title: Mud-brick mosques and a school that outlived the empire
steps.text: The map's style record 'Sudano-Sahelian mud-brick' runs 1327 to now from Timbuktu, and the Sankore Madrasah is dated 1325 to today, with manuscript libraries that survive. That is a striking span: a 14th-century building tradition and a school still standing. Mud-brick is not 'poor' architecture; it is the answer to a land with little stone, rebuilt by communities each year. Timbuktu's scholarly fame peaks later, in the 15th and 16th centuries, so Musa's role was seeding, not creating, the scholarly city. The route line is schematic, not a documented itinerary.

steps.title: A continent on the map, and a theory of dynasties
steps.text: The Catalan Atlas of 1375, by Abraham Cresques's Majorcan workshop, shows a crowned, seated king holding a gold nugget, labelled Musa Mele, lord of the negroes of Guinea. It is a Latin Christian map imagining a Muslim African king as a sovereign of wealth, which is the hajj's lasting image abroad. In 1377 Ibn Khaldun wrote the Muqaddimah, and his history of Mali drew on Cairo informants who remembered Musa's visit. His thesis, that dynasties rise on group solidarity and decay in about three generations, fits Mali: Musa died c.1337, and by the 1360s succession struggles weakened it. The Economic historian will show the silver and gold flows; what the plague data adds is a question, since 1348 hit Cairo hard and I cannot say how far it touched the Sahel.

routes.label: News of Mali's gold to Europe (via Cairo, Maghreb, Majorca)

sources.cite: Ibn Khaldun, Muqaddimah (1377)

links.why: The Niger's flood-fed farming surplus and the gold of Bambuk and Bure gave Mali something to tax and ration, which is what the Economic historian calls the monopoly-and-toll engine.
Supply control over gold at home is what made a lavish spending spree in Cairo both possible and shocking, since Mali could release gold in one place at one moment.
Musa's demand to be received as a sovereign in Cairo fed the Cairo informants whose memories reached Ibn Khaldun and the Catalan Atlas image, so diplomacy became lasting global reputation.
Making Islam a matter of state through the hajj brought scholars and builders, seeding the mud-brick mosque and madrasah tradition at Timbuktu that outlasted the empire.

q: How big was the Atlantic slave trade, and where did the people go?

answer.short: About 12.5 million Africans were put on Atlantic slave ships between 1500 and 1866 and about 10.7 million landed alive, roughly one in seven dying at sea. Most went to Brazil (about 4.8 million) and the Caribbean (roughly 4 to 4.5 million), not North America (about 390,000 directly). Winds and currents set the routes, sugar and mining set the demand, and crown licenses, chartered companies and property law kept the system running until navies and abolition laws slowly choked the supply, long before slavery itself ended.
answer.frame: Roughly 12.5 million Africans were embarked on Atlantic slave ships between 1500 and 1866, about 10.7 million survived, and most went to Brazil and the Caribbean rather than North America.

plan.frame: Roughly 12.5 million Africans were embarked on Atlantic slave ships between 1500 and 1866, about 10.7 million survived, and most went to Brazil and the Caribbean rather than North America.

steps.title: The Wind Machine: Africa's Coasts and the Atlantic Gyres
steps.text: Start with the shape of the coast: a 6,000 km arc of West and West-Central Africa, from Senegambia to Angola, with few natural deepwater harbours and heavy surf, so ships anchored offshore and canoes did the loading. The trade clustered where rivers and lagoons gave access to the interior: Senegambia, the Bight of Benin (Benin City lies just inland of it), the Bight of Biafra's delta, and the Congo-Angola coast, which alone supplied roughly 5.7 million of the embarked, the largest single share in the Voyages database as I recall it. Winds set the first logic: the northeast trades and the Canary Current carry ships south from Lisbon, but the return needs the volta do mar, a wide loop out into the Atlantic to catch the westerlies. Portugal, the first to master that loop, is why 'Portuguese Empire' (from 1415) opens the story.

routes.label: Portuguese caravel track south along the African coast (volta do mar return arc)

sources.cite: Eltis & Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010)
Slave Voyages database (slavevoyages.org), Trans-Atlantic Slave Trade Database

steps.title: Two Conveyor Belts: Why Brazil and the Caribbean Won
steps.text: The Atlantic is two wheels, and the trade rode them. In the north, the trades and North Equatorial Current push ships from the Guinea coast to the Caribbean in roughly 5 to 8 weeks; in the south, the equatorial current and Brazil Current carry Angola's ships to Salvador and Rio in about 35 days or often fewer, the shortest voyage in the system, which as I recall is part of why Brazil alone took about 4.8 million survivors, the most of any destination. Distance matters: Angola to Brazil is about 6,000 km, against 8,000 or more to the Caribbean, and Brazilian-based traders could sail back directly. North America, by contrast, sits off the gyre's edge: the Gulf Stream pushes homeward-bound ships, and only roughly 390,000 landed there directly, which is why the US population was later fed mostly by natural increase. The Demographer will give exact landings; what geography adds is that the destination was largely settled by the wind before any contract was signed.

pins.name: Gulf of Guinea to Caribbean (Middle Passage, north gyre)

routes.label: North Atlantic route: Guinea coast to Caribbean on the trades and North Equatorial Current
South Atlantic route: Angola to Salvador and Rio on the South Equatorial Current
Ocean route into Rio de Janeiro

sources.cite: Eltis & Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010)

steps.title: The Other Door: Bab-el-Mandeb and the Cape Route
steps.text: By the 1800s the supply shifted around the continent: Southeast Africa (Mozambique Island) fed Brazilian demand by rounding the Cape of Good Hope, adding a 12,000 km-plus voyage with far higher mortality, though I'd treat exact rates as uncertain. Hmm, geography also makes this a reminder of what the Atlantic figures omit: Kilwa and Mombasa sat on the monsoon-driven Indian Ocean and Red Sea trade, which moved enslaved people toward Arabia and beyond along Bab-el-Mandeb on its own wind calendar. The Political scientist will show how British naval patrols after 1807 squeezed the Atlantic; geographically, the squeeze pushed traders to ever more remote, hard-to-patrol creeks and long routes. The Atlantic number, 12.5 million, is thus a measure of one wind system, not of all African bondage.

routes.label: Southeast Africa to Brazil, rounding the Cape of Good Hope (19th-century extension)

sources.cite: Eltis & Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010)
Lovejoy, Transformations in Slavery (2012)

steps.title: The ledger: 12.5 million embarked
steps.text: The Atlas's migration record 'Transatlantic slave trade 1501–1866' gives about 12.5 million people forced onto ships and about 10.7 million surviving, so roughly 1.8 million, one in seven, died at sea. Its headcount field is blank on the map (it reads NaN), so these totals come from the record's text and the Slave Voyages database, not from a plotted series. The voyage database is built from ship logs and insurance and customs records, so it is among the best-documented mass movements before 1900, though the numbers are estimates. Our map's 1348 clock predates the trade by 150 years, and the Portuguese Empire (from 1415) is the polity to watch. Salvador (founded 1549) and Rio (1565) are the Brazilian ports that received a large share. Lisbon and Seville are not in the 1500 city series, so I cannot say how much they drew from it.

routes.label: Embarked Africans to Brazil (largest single flow)
Embarked Africans to the Caribbean

steps.title: Where they landed: Brazil and the Caribbean, not Virginia
steps.text: Of the roughly 10.7 million who landed, Brazil took about 4.8 million and the Caribbean islands, British, French, Spanish and Dutch together, took roughly 4 to 4.5 million. British North America and the US received about 390,000, or under 4 percent. Yet the US reached about 4 million enslaved people by 1860 because that population grew by natural increase, an unusual result in the Americas, where sugar regimes consumed lives and needed constant fresh imports. The Atlas has Salvador, Rio, Havana, New York and Philadelphia as places, but its city series does not show the Brazilian ports' populations, so the scale of Black urban life there is beyond this data. The Economic historian will show the sugar and mining that set these destinations; the demographic fact underneath is that high mortality, not low demand, kept the inflow so large.

routes.label: Africans landed in Brazil (~4.8 million over the trade)
Africans landed in British North America/US (~390,000)

sources.cite: Eltis & Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010)
Mintz, Sweetness and Power (1985)

steps.title: The emptied coast and the missing millions
steps.text: Most captives came from West Central Africa (Kongo and Angola, perhaps 45 percent), then the Bight of Benin, Biafra and the Gold Coast. Patrick Manning estimated that Africa's population around 1850 was perhaps half what it might have been without the slave trades, counting those exported plus births lost, and that includes the Saharan and Indian Ocean trades. The Atlas holds Benin City and Kano, but no African population series for the window, so that gap is real and I would not claim a figure from the map. Our data is also silent on the many captives who died in the march or in coastal barracoons before embarkation, so 12.5 million is a floor on the human cost. The Political scientist will show how the states organized supply; what demography adds is the sex ratio, about two men for every woman and many children aboard, which cut fertility on both shores.

routes.label: Captives marched toward the coast

sources.cite: Manning, Slavery and African Life (1990)
Eltis & Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010)

steps.title: Sugar eats the Atlantic islands
steps.text: Follow the sugar. The Atlas tech layer dates sugarcane at Madeira in 1455 and São Tomé in 1500, and that sequence is the template: a luxury sweetener, a tropical island, and a labor force bought rather than hired. Cane is brutal to grow and crush, with boiling houses running day and night, and free Europeans would not do it for the wages planters could pay. Portugal had already bought gold, ivory and captives at Elmina, and the same ships now carried people to the cane. The point for an economist: the slave trade was invented to supply a crop, and the crop was invented to supply a European sweet tooth with a rising income.

routes.label: enslaved Africans to São Tomé sugar plantations
Madeira and São Tomé sugar to Lisbon

sources.cite: Stuart B. Schwartz (ed.), Tropical Babylons: Sugar and the Making of the Atlantic World, 1450-1680 (2004)

steps.title: Silver, gold and the Brazilian sugar boom
steps.text: The Atlas sugarcane layer shows Pernambuco in 1535 and Barbados in 1643, and the money followed: Brazil took by far the largest share of captives, because cane there was grown at scale and mortality was so high that planters kept buying rather than breeding. Spanish America ran on silver, with Potosí from 1545, and mines drew on a mix of forced Indigenous labor (the mita) and enslaved Africans, especially in Mexico, Colombia and Peru's lowlands. Brazilian gold, found in Minas Gerais in the 1690s, pulled in hundreds of thousands more. Profit was captured at several points: Portuguese and Dutch merchants, shipowners, planters and the Crown through taxes and monopolies. The Dutch seizure of Pernambuco in the 1630s and 1640s taught Barbados planters the sugar-and-slave package, which is why 1643 matters.

routes.label: enslaved Africans to Brazilian engenhos
Brazilian sugar to Lisbon and Amsterdam
Potosí silver, Spanish demand for labor

sources.cite: David Eltis and David Richardson, Atlas of the Transatlantic Slave Trade (2010)
Stuart B. Schwartz, Sugar Plantations in the Formation of Brazilian Society (1985)

steps.title: Triangle, cotton and the bill nobody paid
steps.text: The Atlas lists the Atlantic triangular trade for 1640 to 1807, carrying guns and textiles out, captives across, and sugar and cotton back. Saint-Domingue is on the sugarcane layer by 1750 and was the richest colony in the world, which shows what the system could yield per acre. The Atlas UK series has GDP per capita rising from 3011 in 1761 to 5451 in 1866 (2011 dollars), while India falls from 1068 in 1750 to 896 in 1861. Economists still argue over how much slavery caused British growth: Eric Williams said a great deal, while Stanley Engerman and Patrick O'Brien give it a smaller share of total investment. What is not disputed is that Britain banned the trade in 1807 yet slave-grown cotton fed Lancashire mills for decades, and Cuba and Brazil kept importing until the 1850s and 1860s. The Political scientist will show how states ended it; the economic fact is that abolition cost planters little until the supply of new captives actually stopped.

enslaved Africans to the Caribbean
sugar and cotton back to Britain

steps.title: Crowns license the trade
steps.text: The trade began as a state-licensed monopoly, not private smuggling. Portugal held the African coast (Elmina from 1482, Luanda founded 1576), while Spain, having no African bases, bought the right to import enslaved people through the asiento, a contract with the Crown. A royal license for direct shipment to the Caribbean appeared in 1518. The Atlas shows the Portuguese Empire (1502-1823) at a 15% collapse-risk 'watch' and the Spanish Empire (1516-1879) at 23% 'fragile', yet both lasted centuries. The slave trade was one of the institutions that held them up. The Demographer will count the people; what the law lens sees is that every embarkation began as a paper right sold by a sovereign.

steps.title: Code Noir: property in people
steps.text: By the late 1600s northern Europeans broke the Iberian monopoly through chartered companies: the Dutch West India Company (1621), the Royal African Company (1672), and French companies. The Code Noir (1685) shows how law made it durable. It defined enslaved people as movable property, regulated punishment and baptism, and gave planters a legal frame that kept the system predictable for investors. Britain and France came to dominate: Britain alone carried perhaps 3 million people, a bit over a quarter of all embarked, in my rough reading of Eltis and Richardson. The Economic historian will show who profited; the point for law is that credit, insurance and courts all treated humans as collateral.

steps.title: Ending it: law, navy, and the long tail
steps.text: Abolition came in steps. Denmark banned the trade in 1792 (effective 1803), Britain's Slave Trade Act and the US act both took effect in 1807-08, and Britain then used the Royal Navy and treaties to pressure others. Yet the trade did not stop: Brazil and Cuba, with Spain only 'fragile' on the map and the new Empire of Brazil (1822-1889) dependent on planter support, kept importing for decades. Brazil's Eusebio de Queiros Law (1850) finally ended its legal imports after heavy British pressure, and the last known transatlantic voyages, to Cuba, came around 1866, the end of the window. Slavery itself lasted longer: the US Thirteenth Amendment (1865), Cuba (1886), Brazil's Golden Law (1888). Abolishing the trade was easier than abolishing the system, because slaveholders were the state's own constituents. I go beyond the Atlas data on the naval patrol numbers; the Geographer can say which coasts were hardest to police.

The sugar template from Madeira and São Tomé needed brutal labor, and the high mortality on cane estates forced constant fresh imports, which is why Brazil and the Caribbean dwarf North America in landings.
Crown licenses and asientos turned embarkation into a state-sold right, which is part of why ship logs, customs and insurance records exist to document the 12.5 million.

q: Why was Song China so advanced, and why didn't it industrialise?

answer.short: Song China surged because coal, iron, canals and a million-person market sat close together in the Kaifeng core, and a bureaucratic, money-literate state bought iron for war and taxed trade (steps 1, 4, 5, 10). It stalled because the 1127 loss of the northern coal-iron belt, permanent defence and tribute spending, cheap water transport and labour, and then Mongol conquest all removed the pressure and the capital for mechanisation (steps 2, 6, 7, 11, 12). No single cause is proven; the best-supported pair is the geographic split between fuel and markets plus a state that was the main customer and chose security over risk.
answer.frame: Song China (960-1279) reached near-industrial iron, coal, printing, paper money and urban scale, yet never made the leap to sustained mechanised industry, so we must explain both the surge and the stall.

plan.frame: Song China (960-1279) reached near-industrial iron, coal, printing, paper money and urban scale, yet never made the leap to sustained mechanised industry, so we must explain both the surge and the stall.

steps.title: Coal and iron on the Kaifeng doorstep
steps.text: The Song core sat on the North China Plain, which the terrain index lists at 34.8,116.6, with Kaifeng (34.8,114.3) on the Yellow River's flat floodplain. Within a few days' haul lay the coal and iron of Henan, Hebei and Shanxi. Kaifeng was ringed by canals (the Bian and others), so bulky fuel and ore could be barged to a city of roughly a million people. Estimates (Robert Hartwell, 1962) put Northern Song iron near 125,000 tonnes by 1078, and coal replaced charcoal around the capital as forests thinned. That is the geographic surge: heavy resources, flat ground, water transport, all within one tight cluster. The Economic historian will show how big the output really was; what the map adds is that no other pre-modern state had its fuel, ore and market this close together.

steps.title: The northern loss: coal and iron on the wrong side
steps.text: In 1127 the Jurchen took Kaifeng, and by the 1142 treaty the border ran roughly along the Huai River. The Song kept the south: rice, rivers and ports, with Hangzhou (30.3,120.2) at the end of the Grand Canal. But it lost the Henan, Hebei and Shanxi coal-and-iron zone, the one place where the fuel and the ore sat together. Historians such as Elvin argue that southern China had iron and coal, but scattered and far from the big cities, so the cheap bulk-fuel advantage of Kaifeng was never rebuilt. The Military historian will cover the Jurchen armies; what the terrain shows is that the Yangtze delta is superb for boats and rice but offered no equivalent coal-iron cluster beside its markets. Whether this alone caused the stall is debated, and I would not claim more than a strong contributing factor.

steps.title: Water was too good, then the Mongols and the plague
steps.text: The Yangtze and its canals let rice, tea, silk and porcelain move cheaply across the south, so water, not steam, solved transport; there was little pressure for a new power source. Under the Mongols, the canal was re-cut in the 1280s-90s to feed Dadu (Beijing, 39.9,116.4), tying the centre of gravity back to the north without bringing the coalfields into the economy's engine. By 1348 the map shows plague and war layers on, and the date matters: the Yellow River flooded and shifted course in the 1340s, and rebellion followed, so Yuan China was fraying, not building factories. The Political scientist will explain the taxation and Mongol rule; what the geography adds is that the surge stalled where cheap water carriage, a lost northern fuel base and river hazards all pulled the same way. Plague in 14th-century China is real but its scale is uncertain, so I treat it as a possible additional shock rather than proven.

steps.title: Kaifeng: the iron and print boom
steps.text: The map's tech layer dates printing at Kaifeng to 1040 (movable type is traditionally credited to Bi Sheng in the 1040s), gunpowder at Kaifeng in 1044, and the compass at Hangzhou in 1088. Robert Hartwell's much-cited estimate puts Song iron output near 125,000 tonnes around 1078, roughly 1 kg per person. That is a figure of the same order as Europe's total output many centuries later, but it is a contested reconstruction, not a census, so treat it as an order of magnitude. Much of it went to the state: arms for armies facing Liao and the Western Xia, which means demand was fiscal and military rather than a mass market for machines. The Geographer will place the coal and iron; what my lens adds is that the buyer was the state.

steps.title: Paper promises and monsoon silver
steps.text: Sichuan merchants' private notes (jiaozi) became a state issue around 1024, among the first government paper money anywhere, because iron coin was too heavy to carry. Song also minted copper cash at a scale unmatched in its day, and the Atlas's Eastern trade-hub relay hands the crown from Palembang (to 1025) to Quanzhou (1000-1400) as the southern ports boomed. The object journeys show porcelain leaving Jingdezhen (1004) and pepper reaching Hangzhou by about 1290, so the market economy was oceanic as well as continental. This was commercialisation without mechanisation: money, credit and specialised regions raised output per acre, while rice paddies, not factories, took the capital. The Political scientist will show how taxes and the scholar-official state fed this; I add that the notes were also how the state paid for war.

steps.title: Why not the factory? Cheap hands, lost north
steps.text: By 1348 the Song are gone (1279) and the Mongol Yuan rules; the iron belt lay in the north, which was devastated by Jurchen and then Mongol conquest, so the coal-and-iron cluster was cut off from the rich Yangzi south where the people and markets were. Elvin's high-level equilibrium trap argues that with abundant cheap labour and falling returns to land, saving labour was never the profitable move; improving water control and rice yields was. Robert Allen's wage-price comparison is the modern version of this logic for Britain, where high wages and cheap coal made machines pay, a condition Song never had at the same time and place. Note the data: the Atlas shows UK GDP per capita near 1,100 to 1,500 dollars across 1268-1368, so the later divergence was not obviously foreordained by income alone, and I cannot say from this data that China was richer. This is a contested thesis, not settled fact; the Mongol break and a lack of coal next to the markets are my best two candidates.

steps.title: The northern gate falls: Kaifeng 1127
steps.text: Song never held the Great Wall line. The 979 Battle of Gaoliang River (near today's Beijing) failed to retake the Sixteen Prefectures, and Shanhai Pass sat with Liao, then Jin, then Yuan on the chokepoint table. So the capital Kaifeng sat on an open plain with no natural barrier, and Song bought safety with silver: the 1005 Chanyuan treaty paid Liao roughly 100,000 taels of silver and 200,000 bolts of silk a year (figures from memory, treat as approximate). In 1126-27 the Jurchen Jin, who had been Song allies against Liao, took Kaifeng and captured two emperors. The point for your question: a state whose richest city is indefensible spends on armies and tribute first, and civil innovation second.

steps.title: A navy behind the Yangtze: Caishi 1161
steps.text: After 1127 the court settled at Hangzhou and the Yangtze and Huai became the frontier. At Caishi in 1161, Yu Yunwen's Song fleet, with treadle paddle-wheel ships and gunpowder weapons, beat the Jin army of Wanyan Liang, who was then killed by his own officers. The map also logs Tangdao the same year, a Song naval win off Shandong. Jin had cavalry but no river fleet, so water became the Song equaliser. The cost was a permanent standing navy and a huge army: the Southern Song budget was dominated by military outlays, which the Economic historian and Political scientist can price. My lens adds that this security spending was fixed by geography, not choice.

steps.title: Xiangyang: six years, then counterweights
steps.text: The Mongols attacked Jin first, with the 1232 Kaifeng and 1233 Caizhou sieges ending that dynasty, then spent decades on the Song. The decisive fortress was Xiangyang, besieged about six years until 1273, when Persian counterweight trebuchets broke it and opened the Yangtze. Hangzhou fell in 1276 and the Song ended at Yamen in 1279, with all China under Mongol rule. The Mongols won by absorbing Song and Persian engineers and a river fleet, not by cavalry alone. The Song had the technology; they lacked a unified, affordable system to field it. Whether a richer fiscal-military base could have held is the counterfactual; I would not claim it.

steps.title: The exam state: Kaifeng's civil bureaucracy
steps.text: Northern Song (peak 2.8 Mkm² in 1056, fragility 14%, 'watch') was ruled from Kaifeng by civil officials, not generals. After Zhao Kuangyin took power in 960, the court subordinated the military to civil bureaucrats and recruited through the palace-supervised jinshi examination, which grew to several hundred degrees per sitting by the 11th century. That meant a talent pool drawn well beyond aristocratic families, and a state that could fund canals, granaries and tax collection. The same design capped growth: the court feared warlords more than stagnation, kept a very large standing army (over a million men by the 1040s), and ate much of its revenue in defence and payments to Liao and Xia. Compare Korea's Gwageo exams (958) in the law layer, a sign this exam-state model was spreading. I am confident about the structure; exact exam quotas and army figures vary by source.

steps.title: A state that taxed trade, not just land
steps.text: Southern Song (1139, 2.057 Mkm², fragility 14%) lost the northern heartland to Great Jin but not its fiscal appetite. From Hangzhou it leaned on commercial taxes, monopolies on salt, tea and wine, and paper money, so tax came from markets rather than only from farmland. The Economic historian will show the iron and notes; what my lens adds is that the state was the chief customer and regulator, which rewarded security and revenue over risky private machinery. The 1142 treaty with Jin made the state a permanent tribute payer while still defending the Huai line, so spending was locked in. A state this fiscal and this bureaucratic could promote markets, yet it had no patent-style protection or independent corporate form for private innovators, and I am inferring that gap from institutional history rather than from the map data.

steps.title: Mongol conquest and the reset
steps.text: The Mongol Empire peaked at 27.4 Mkm² in 1279, the year the last Song forces ended at Yamen; Hangzhou had already surrendered in 1276. The Yuan (1294 onward, 14.25 Mkm² peak in 1352) inherited Song cities and canals but put a foreign military elite above the exam class, and examinations were suspended for decades, resuming only in 1315. By 1348 the map shows disease and war on the same layers: the Yuan state was fiscally strained, over-issuing paper money, with unrest soon to topple it by 1368. The Military historian will cover the campaigns; what the institutions show is that the first industrial-scale economy lost its administrative mind, not its technology. Whether Song would have industrialised without the Mongols is a counterfactual we cannot know, and I would put it at unlikely, since the incentive problems were already there. Plague data for China in 1348 is uncertain.

links.why: The coal-iron-market cluster at Kaifeng made Song rich, but the same open North China Plain had no natural barrier, so the wealth was exposed to Liao and Jin.
The military collapse of 1126-27 is what physically severed the Song from the Henan-Hebei-Shanxi coal and iron, turning a geographic advantage into a loss.
Iron output was driven by state arms demand, and a state that was both chief buyer and regulator rewarded revenue and security over private machine-building.
Fixed naval and army spending on the Yangtze frontier absorbed capital that a labour-saving factory economy would have needed, reinforcing the cheap-labour, water-transport equilibrium.

whatifs.q: What if the Jurchen had never taken Kaifeng in 1127 and the Song kept the northern coal and iron?

q: How did the Mongols build the largest contiguous land empire in history?

answer.short: The Mongols turned a pasture-rich corridor into an empire by pairing it with institutions that steppe raiders usually lack. Grass fed the remounts along some 8,000 km of unbroken steppe, Genghis's 1206 decimal army and keshig bound loyalty to the center rather than the clan, and conquered engineers and merchants supplied siege skill and cash. The yam relay and the Yasa's price list of surrender versus terror made the pieces act as one state, but succession crises (1241, 1251, 1260) and the edge of the grass (Hungary, Syria) set its limits.
answer.frame: How a steppe confederation of perhaps a million people conquered Eurasia from China to Hungary in about 60 years, and what made it hold together as one contiguous empire.

steps.title: The Steppe Highway Begins at the Onon
steps.text: The Mongol homeland is a grassland of about 1.5 million km² between the Altai, the Gobi (south of it) and the Siberian forest. Grass there feeds horses without farmers, so a family of herders could field a mounted warrior with 4-5 remounts each. Karakorum (founded 1220) sits on the Orkhon, in the best pasture of the heartland. From here the Eurasian steppe runs west almost unbroken for about 8,000 km to Hungary, and the Mongols did not conquer a barrier so much as ride down a corridor. The Atlas's terrain shows the first great gates: the Altai, then the Dzungarian Gate (45.3N, 82.5E), which opens onto the Kazakh Steppe. The Military historian will show how the tactics worked; what geography adds is that fodder, not food, set the pace.

routes.label: Steppe belt: Mongolia west to the Kazakh Steppe

steps.title: Oases as Stepping Stones: Merv, Bukhara, Samarkand
steps.text: South of the steppe lie river oases fed by the Amu and Syr Darya: Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv, Herat, Nishapur. Each is a farming island in desert, and each fell in 1220-21; Merv, in the Atlas, ends in 1221. Geography made them easy to isolate: a Mongol army crossing the Kyzylkum came out behind the defenders at Bukhara, who expected an attack on the road from the east. The same oases stored grain and held irrigated meadows, which is why the army wintered in places like the Murghab and Balkh valleys rather than dying in the desert. The Economic historian will show the silver and caravans these cities produced; what the map adds is that conquering the oases cost almost nothing in distance, since each lay within ~300-400 km of the next. Population figures for the sack of Merv (often 700,000+) are doubtful; I would not trust them.

steps.title: Where the Grass Ends: Hungary, Syria and the Limit
steps.text: The Pontic-Caspian steppe carried Batu's army from the Volga to the Carpathians; the Hungarian Plain is its last western outlier, about 100,000 km² of grass, and a debated argument holds that Hungary's pasture could support only some 30,000 horses at a time, which may help explain why the army withdrew in 1242 (the death of Ögedei is the other cause; I think both mattered). Hülegü's push into Iran ended differently: Baghdad fell in 1258, but Syria's grass is thin, and at Ain Jalut in 1260 the Mamluks fought at the edge of what the horse armies could feed. Sarai (founded 1250) on the lower Volga marks the western pasture base. What the Disease layer adds for 1348, when the map is open: the same steppe corridor that moved armies is a leading candidate for the route by which plague later reached the Black Sea ports, though that's contested. The Political scientist will show how the khan's institutions held these zones together; geography shows that the empire's reach stopped roughly where pasture did.

steps.title: Hunting the Jin: Yehuling and Zhongdu
steps.text: The map lists the Battle of Yehuling (1211) and the Siege of Zhongdu (1215), and the Shanhai Pass and Hexi Corridor switch to Mongol hands by 1233. The pattern is a field battle first, then a long strangling of the cities. Each Mongol trooper rode with several remounts and lived on mare's milk and hunting, so the army could cross the Gobi without a supply train. Jin fielded far larger infantry armies (contemporary figures run to hundreds of thousands, which I treat as unreliable), but they could not catch riders who refused to stand and fight. At Zhongdu the Mongols learned sieges the hard way, and they recruited Chinese and Khitan engineers who became the core of their artillery. The Economic historian will show the silver and tribute that paid for this; what the siege record adds is that conquered specialists, not steppe tradition, supplied the walls-breaking skill.

steps.title: Khwarezm: a chain of cities falls in 1220-21
steps.text: The map records the Otrar Catastrophe (1219), then Khujand, Bukhara, Samarkand and Gurganj in 1220, and Merv, Herat, Taliqan, Bamyan and the Indus in 1221. Genghis split his force into columns that converged, and the Khwarezmshah, who had garrisoned his cities rather than massed a field army, never faced the whole thing at once. Cities were taken in days or weeks using local prisoners as forced labor and shields, an economy of terror that also bought later surrenders. The Atlas border layer shows the payoff: the Mongol Empire gains 4.5 million km² in 1220 and 5.5 million km² by 1227. Casualty counts for Merv and Herat (hundreds of thousands in the chronicles) are almost certainly inflated; the destruction was real, the arithmetic is not. The Geographer will show the grass and corridors; what I add is that the columns were timed to meet, which takes a courier network and discipline, not just good pasture.

steps.title: The limits: Mohi, Baghdad, Ain Jalut
steps.text: Kiev fell in 1240, the Mongols crushed Hungary at Mohi in 1241, and Baghdad was taken in 1258, ending the Abbasid caliphate. Then comes the limit: at Ain Jalut in 1260 the Mamluks beat a Mongol force, the first lasting defeat. The likely reasons are military and logistical. Syria's pasture could not sustain a huge horse herd, and much of Hulagu's army had withdrawn after Mongke's death in 1259 (historians debate how small the remaining force was). The Mamluks were also a horse-archer army of their own, so the Mongol edge was gone. The Atlas lists Mohi's Hungarian withdrawal as tied to the Great Khan's death, which fits a pattern: succession politics, not defeat in the field, stopped the westward tide. The Political scientist will explain why a death could halt armies; the war data says it did, twice.

steps.title: 1206: A khuriltai turns a war band into a state
steps.text: In 1206 a khuriltai proclaimed Temujin 'Chinggis Khan', and the Atlas starts the Mongol Empire that year, with a fragility of only 7% (calm) against a 14% base rate. The key move was institutional: he broke up the old tribal and clan units and reorganized people into decimal units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000 under commanders he chose by loyalty and merit rather than by birth. A tribe that once fought for its own chief now belonged to a thousand whose captain owed his rank to the Khan. He also built a personal guard (the keshig, expanded to roughly 10,000) that doubled as a training school for future officers and a hostage pool of elite sons. This is the political answer to 'raiding versus empire': raiding rewards loot for your kin, while the decimal army and keshig rewarded service to the center. Exact unit numbers come from the Secret History and later sources, so treat them as approximate.

steps.title: The Yasa: one law for a steppe and its conquests
steps.text: Law was how a conqueror's word became a norm. The Yasa, the Khan's body of decrees, bound his people on matters like hunting rights, the treatment of envoys, and religious tolerance, and Mongol sources treat the protection of envoys as near-sacred. That is why the killing of a Mongol trade mission at Otrar (c. 1218) was a casus belli the Mongols saw as legal, not merely opportunistic. The Atlas shows the cost of defiance: Merv, a city on the map from -500, ends in 1221, and Bukhara and Samarkand fell the same campaign. Cities that submitted were taxed and spared, and those that resisted were made examples, so terror worked as a published price list. Compare the Atlas's law layer: Magna Carta (1215) and the Golden Bull of 1222 limited kings through nobles, while the Yasa made the Khan himself the source of law, so I'd flag that the Yasa's exact text is lost and much of what we call it is reconstruction from later Persian and Mamluk writers. The Military historian will show how the sieges were won; I add why surrender was made rational.

steps.title: 1227-1260: Succession, the empire's real stress test
steps.text: Genghis died in 1227, and his empire survived the part that kills most conquest states: transition. Ogedei was elected at a khuriltai in 1229, built Karakorum (on the map from 1220), and extended the empire to Jin's fall in 1234 (Great Jin ends 1235 in the Atlas, fragility 28%). When Ogedei died in December 1241, the army in Hungary reportedly withdrew, and many historians link this to princes returning for the succession vote, though that causal claim is debated. Then came the fault line: the Toluid coup of 1251 put Mongke on the throne, and by 1260 civil war between Khubilai and Ariq Boke split the unity, even as Hulagu destroyed the Abbasid Caliphate in 1258 (listed as ending 1258/1259). The Atlas's model gave the empire just 7% fragility in 1233, which looks right for external shock but blind to internal succession risk. That is the lesson: the empire was calm to outsiders and brittle inside. The Economic historian will show the silver and yam that bound it; what the plague data adds is the 1340s tail, since the Atlas map is set to 1348 when Mongol-linked routes carried disease. My caveat: the Hungary link is a hypothesis, not a settled fact.

steps.title: A poor steppe, a rich neighbour
steps.text: Steppe herders produced meat, horses and felt but no silk, grain or silver, so the nomad economy depended on getting those from settled neighbours by trade, tribute or raid. Temujin's 1206 proclamation as Genghis Khan came just as the Silk Roads, which our map shows as chains of caravan cities where few merchants went the whole way, were the only large source of cash around him. Muslim merchants such as the Khwarazmian caravan-men he used as agents were his first financiers: they advanced goods and silver and got protection and tax breaks in return. Karakorum (founded about 1220, Ögedei walled it in the 1230s) is the map's marker of where that income was parked. I'd say the empire began as a protection racket over trade, and conquest was the upgrade.

steps.title: Otrar to Merv: the caravan that started a war
steps.text: The trigger was commercial: around 1218 the governor of Otrar seized a Mongol-backed caravan of roughly 450 merchants, a violation of the deal that made the trade pay. The reply was Bukhara, Samarkand, Merv (the map shows Merv ending in 1221), Nishapur and Herat, the richest caravan cities on the Silk Road. Conquest paid twice: coin and goods were seized, and skilled artisans were deported east, which is how weavers, engineers and clerks reached Mongolia. Much of the old trade network survived because the Mongols wanted its tolls and its merchants; even so, Merv and Nishapur show how the cost fell on the cities themselves, and casualty figures in the chronicles are widely thought inflated. The Military historian will explain how the cities fell; what the ledger adds is that they were worth taking.

steps.title: The yam: a relay that made one market
steps.text: Ögedei (r. 1229-41) formalised the yam, a post-station relay with horses at stops roughly a day's ride apart, paid for by local households as a labour tax. Officials with a paiza (tablet) could demand mounts and food, so messages could cover several hundred km a day at the extreme, which compares to Rome's 7 days for Nero's death to reach Galba in the map's data. Ögedei's court also paid merchants more than goods were worth, in silver ingots and paper-backed notes, so that tribute became a flow back into trade. The map's tech layer shows what rode these roads: gunpowder appears at Heilongjiang in 1288 then Oxford 1326, Florence 1326 and Paris 1346, and paper reaches Fabriano by 1276. By 1260 the same roads had carried Hülegü to Baghdad (1258), but the chain's success was also its risk: our 1348 map shows the disease layer, and I'd bet the same relay network is part of how plague later moved. The Geographer should say whether the grass corridors or the stations did more of the work.

links.why: Steppe grass fed several remounts per rider, which let Mongol armies cross the Gobi without a supply train and made the strangling of Jin cities possible.
The decimal units and keshig created the discipline needed to time separate columns to converge on Khwarezm's cities in 1220-21.
The Otrar seizure of a Mongol-backed caravan was the commercial trigger that the Yasa's envoy and merchant protection norms recast as a legal casus belli, making terror a published price.
Ögedei's death in 1241 and the limit of Hungarian pasture are competing and probably combined explanations for the westward halt, so politics and geography reinforce each other.

whatifs.q: What if Ögedei had not died in December 1241?
whatifs.a: The Mongol army in Hungary might have pushed on into Austria and Italy, but pasture limits and the strain of campaigning far from the base would probably have slowed it within a few years. Ecology and logistics argue for a limited stay, though Mongol commanders did take winter-frozen rivers and Danube crossings in their stride.

whatifs.q: What if the Otrar governor had not seized the Mongol-backed caravan in 1218?
whatifs.a: Genghis might have turned first to completing the Jin conquest, delaying or avoiding the Khwarezm campaign, though the Khwarezm shah was a large rival on the Silk Road. The empire would likely have reached Central Asia anyway, but perhaps later and with less devastation of Merv, Nishapur and Herat.

q: Why did Constantinople fall in 1453, and what changed afterwards?

answer.short: Constantinople fell because the walls outlived the state behind them: by 1453 the Ottomans held Thrace, Anatolia and both straits, so the city was an island with about 7,000 defenders on a long wall, no hinterland, no field army and a tax base smaller than Genoese Galata's. Mehmed II, with one chain of command and the fiscal reach to buy Orban's bombards, concentrated fire on the Lycus valley and forced the thin garrison to cover the sea walls too. Afterwards the city became an imperial capital holding both straits, with the millet and devshirme systems; trade shifted from Italian privileges to Ottoman tolls, though the Portuguese route round Africa (1498) mattered more to spices than 1453 itself.
answer.frame: A rich, ancient city shrunk to a besieged rump by 1453: why could Mehmed II take walls that held for a thousand years, and how did the Ottoman capture reshape trade, power and ideas?

steps.title: A city built on a triangle of water
steps.text: Istanbul (41.0N, 29.0E) sits on a triangular peninsula with water on two sides: the Sea of Marmara to the south and the Golden Horn inlet to the north. That leaves only about 6.5 km of land front, and the Theodosian Walls (built 413, doubled after the earthquake of 447) filled it with a moat, an outer wall and a taller inner wall, roughly three lines of defence. The Bosporus (41.1N, 29.1E) feeds a current that runs south through the strait, and the Golden Horn could be sealed with a chain boom. In 1348 the city was still a prize, but even then the data shows a polity, the Byzantine Empire (395 to 1453), whose main asset was one superb piece of terrain. Terrain can hold a line; it cannot create people to stand on it.

steps.title: The strait was already surrounded
steps.text: Geography's key fact is that by 1400 the walls no longer sat in a region the Byzantines controlled. The Ottomans crossed the Dardanelles (40.2N, 26.4E) into Thrace, took Plovdiv and the Balkan routes, and held Anatolia on the other bank, while Ephesus (listed ending 1400 in the Atlas) and Sardis (to 1402) had already slipped out of Greek hands. Thessaloniki, the empire's second city, was also lost to Ottoman rule in this period. Anadolu Hisari (1394) and Rumeli Hisari (1452), two forts facing each other across the narrowest point of the Bosporus, let Mehmed II cut the Black Sea grain and supply line. The Economic historian will show the silver; what the map adds is that Constantinople had become a city with no hinterland, an island of 5 or 6 km of wall inside Ottoman land.

steps.title: Walls that outlived their geometry
steps.text: The walls stood about 1,000 years, but they only worked if enough defenders manned all 6.5 km; the Greeks had perhaps 7,000 men, so the garrison was thin and the dip around the Lycus valley (the Mesoteichion) became the weak spot where the cannon concentrated. The terrain gave one more twist: Ottoman ships hauled over the ridge behind Galata on 22 April 1453 bypassed the chain across the Golden Horn and forced the defenders to cover the sea walls as well. The Military historian will cover the guns and the 53-day siege in detail; geography's point is that a fixed line is only as strong as the number of people available to stand on it, and the city's wall length stayed constant while its population fell to a fraction of its former size. Afterward, Istanbul (about 81,000 in the Atlas) became an imperial capital again, holding the Bosporus and Dardanelles together under one ruler, with Hagia Sophia turned into a mosque.

steps.title: Venice's Black Sea toll booth, Constantinople's empty till
steps.text: Venice appears in the trade-hub relay from 1204, the year the Fourth Crusade sacked Constantinople. From then on the Italians, not the Greeks, ran the merchant fleets of the eastern Mediterranean. In 1348 the Genoese across the Golden Horn at Galata collected so much customs revenue that, by Nicephorus Gregoras' famous complaint, it dwarfed what the emperor took at his own port: roughly 200,000 hyperpyra against 30,000. The Byzantine state had the world's most valuable crossroads and a tax base the size of a market town's. My lens sees a landlord who had leased out his own doorway.

steps.title: Cannon money: who could afford the new artillery
steps.text: The tech layer dates gunpowder in Istanbul to 1453, but the cost curve matters more than the date. Mehmed's great bombards, cast by the Hungarian founder Orban (who first offered his services to Constantine XI, who could not pay him), cost a fortune in bronze and took teams of oxen to haul. Only a state with a large, centralised tax base could field them, and Byzantium by then held little beyond the city, a few Aegean islands and the Morea. Walls that had cost the attacker nothing to respect for a thousand years met the first artillery whose price only an empire could pay. The Military historian will show the siege itself; what money adds is that the guns were a fiscal weapon before they were a military one.

steps.title: The toll moves, the spice road goes around
steps.text: After 1453 the Ottomans did not close the road, but they taxed it, and Italian merchants lost the privileged footing they had held under the Greeks. Venice made a treaty with Mehmed in 1454 and mostly kept trading, since the spice trade ran through Mamluk Cairo and Alexandria rather than through Constantinople. The real shock came when Da Gama reached Calicut in 1498: the data shows pepper at Lisbon in 1499 and Antwerp in 1508, and the Carreira da India took spices off the Venice monopoly. Historians still argue over how much 1453 pushed the Portuguese; Portuguese Atlantic expansion began in 1415, decades earlier, so I would call 1453 an accelerant, not the cause. The Political scientist will explain how the Ottomans organised the new empire; what I add is that the hub of Mediterranean trade ended up with a sultan as its landlord.

steps.title: The straits fall before the city does
steps.text: The map's chokepoint table tells the story: in 1300 the Byzantine Empire held both the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, and by 1400 the Ottomans held both. The Fall of Gallipoli in 1354 gave them a permanent bridgehead in Europe, and Maritsa in 1371 broke the Balkan armies that might have relieved the city. Constantinople was cut off from its hinterland long before Mehmed arrived: Thrace, the grain and manpower base, was Ottoman. The Geographer will show why the walls were strong; what the war layer adds is that walls only matter if a field army can reach them, and after 1371 none could. I am going beyond the map's records in the detail of how the crossings worked, which is from general histories.

steps.title: The fifty-year reprieve and the 1402 gamble
steps.text: The map records the Battle of Ankara in 1402: Timur captured Sultan Bayezid, and Ottoman expansion paused for a generation, giving Byzantium roughly 50 more years. Bayezid had been blockading Constantinople for years, and his defeat removed that pressure overnight. But it bought time, not a solution: the Ottoman state reunified under Mehmed I and Murad II, and the Byzantines never rebuilt an army to use the time. Defence rested on a few thousand men, with the city's garrison in 1453 usually estimated at only about 7,000 including foreigners, holding some 20 km of walls against a force of perhaps 50,000 to 80,000 (estimates vary widely). A reprieve is only useful if you convert it into strength, and the Empire could not.

steps.title: 53 days: guns, ships over the hill, and the last assault
steps.text: The map's entry for 1453 reads: the Ottoman Empire beat the Byzantine Empire, ending the Roman Empire in the east, and the Ottomans now held the Bosporus. The siege ran from early April to 29 May. Mehmed's large bombards, cast by the Hungarian engineer Orban, were slow (a handful of shots a day), but sustained fire opened breaches in the Lycus valley, and the defenders repaired them by night. The turning point was at sea: a chain boom closed the Golden Horn, so around 22 April the Ottomans hauled ships overland to bypass it, forcing the thin garrison to defend the sea walls too. The Economic historian will show the silver that left Byzantium starving; what the siege adds is that the final assault on 29 May hit a line stretched past breaking. Many details, including the ship count and the Kerkoporta gate story, are disputed in the sources.

steps.title: A empire with a 44% collapse score
steps.text: At 1400 the Atlas model gives the Byzantine Empire a 44% chance of collapse within 50 years, against a 14% base rate: the highest 'critical' reading in the window. The peak of 2.338 Mkm² in 633 CE had shrunk to a city, Thessaloniki and the Morea, ruled by rival Palaiologan branches who fought civil wars (1341-47, 1373, 1390, 1421-22) and often asked Ottoman or Genoese help against each other. Around them the Serbian Empire (1352-1458, 27% fragile) and Second Bulgarian Empire (33%, ended 1394) were also brittle, so no buffer state remained. The Economic historian will show the silver that left; what my lens adds is that an emperor who cannot tax, command his own family or hold allies has walls but no state behind them.

steps.title: One sultan, one will, one siege
steps.text: Mehmed II, aged 21, could command roughly 50,000-80,000 men (estimates vary widely) with one chain of command, funded by a state that had already tamed its rivals: the Beylik of Karaman (1305-1467) was pressed hard and the Germiyanids had ended in 1439. Constantine XI had perhaps 7,000 defenders, about 2,000 of them foreign, including Giovanni Giustiniani's Genoese, and could not stop Venetian and Genoese captains from acting on their own interests. The Military historian will cover the cannon and the 53 days; the political point is that Mehmed built Rumeli Hisarı in 1452, which cut the strait, and could afford a bronze-founder like Orban because he alone decided. The Latin West had promised crusade at the 1439 Union of Florence, but the Orthodox clergy rejected it, so the legitimacy cost was paid and no help came.

steps.title: The conqueror's empire: kanun, millets, devshirme
steps.text: Mehmed made Constantinople his capital and absorbed the rump: Serbia fell in 1459 (the Serbian Empire entry ends 1458), the Despotate of Epirus in 1481, Bosnia in 1463 and Karaman in 1467. He recognised Gennadios Scholarios as Orthodox patriarch in 1454, a bargain that later grew into the millet system, letting Christians run their own courts and taxes under the sultan. His kanun (secular decrees) sat beside sharia, and his devshirme-recruited slave-soldiers and officials, loyal to him not to noble families, replaced Byzantium's quarrelling aristocracy. Hagia Sophia became a mosque, a signal of legitimacy as heir to Rome; the Atlas Rule & law layer holds no Ottoman code in this window, so this is from outside our data, and details of Mehmed's own law codes are debated.

links.why: Ottoman control of Gallipoli (1354) and Thrace after Maritsa (1371) meant no relief army could reach the walls, so the fixed 6.5 km line had to be held by the garrison alone.
A Byzantine state that had leased its customs to Genoa and Venice could not even pay Orban, so the gun founder went to the one ruler whose tax base could afford bronze bombards.
The 50-year reprieve after Ankara (1402) was wasted because civil wars and a 44% collapse score meant no institution could turn time into an army.
Once Constantinople became the Ottoman capital, a centralised sultan taxed the Mediterranean hub directly, pushing Europeans toward the Atlantic route that Da Gama completed in 1498.

whatifs.q: What if the Byzantines had used the 50-year reprieve after 1402 to rebuild a standing army and fiscal base?
whatifs.a: The walls plus a few more thousand paid troops might have survived the 1453 attempt, since the defence was stretched rather than outclassed on terrain. But with Thrace and the Balkans lost, the city would likely have stayed a besieged enclave and fallen to a later assault or been reduced by economic strangulation. The Ottomans' fiscal edge would have grown anyway.

whatifs.q: What if Western Europe had sent a real crusading relief force after the 1439 Union of Florence?
whatifs.a: A strong field army landing in Thrace could have forced Mehmed to fight outside the walls and broken the sea blockade. However, the Crusade of Varna in 1444 was crushed by the Ottomans, which suggests that Western coordination was weak and a relief might have failed too.

q: How did a few hundred Spaniards bring down the Aztec Empire?

answer.short: About 500 Spaniards did not topple the Aztecs; they detonated a fault line. Tribute-based hegemony had made Tlaxcala and other subject states eager to defect (government), their tens of thousands of warriors did most of the fighting and razing (military), Malinche's Nahuatl diplomacy and Cortés's gambles turned a battered column into a coalition (people), and smallpox in 1520 killed Cuitlahuac and hollowed out the city just before the siege (disease). Steel, horses and thirteen brigantines mattered, but only on open ground and the lake, as the keystone rather than the arch.
answer.frame: Cortés's roughly 500 Spaniards did not conquer alone: Mesoamerican allies, smallpox, and the Aztec tribute system's fragility decided 1519-1521.

steps.title: A virus lands on the Gulf coast
steps.text: The Atlas's shock record reads: smallpox reached Tenochtitlan in 1520 with Narváez's expedition. Narváez came from Cuba to arrest Cortés, and the virus rode in with his men (and reportedly an enslaved African with the fever, per Sahagún's Florentine Codex tradition). Variola had never touched the Americas, so no one had immunity, and it spread along the same roads the allied armies used. Cortés had left Tenochtitlan in the Noche Triste retreat of 30 June 1520, and the virus stayed behind in a city of perhaps 200,000 or more people. We lack firm counts for the epidemic's start date and spread, and the sources are Spanish and later Nahua accounts.

routes.label: Smallpox from Narváez's force toward the Valley of Mexico

sources.cite: Alfred Crosby, The Columbian Exchange (1972)
Bernardino de Sahagún, Florentine Codex (c. 1577)

steps.title: The emperor dies of the fever
steps.text: The Atlas records that smallpox killed the emperor Cuitlahuac, linked to the Aztec polity by Crosby (1972). He had ruled for about 80 days after Moctezuma II's death, in late 1520. His loss meant a second succession crisis in months, and Cuauhtemoc, a young war leader, took over. Nahua accounts describe people too sick to move, to fetch water or to bury the dead, and the disease hit just when the city needed to mobilize. The Biographer will show what Moctezuma's and Cortés's choices did; what the plague data adds is that the empire's decision-making was decapitated twice in a year, and the death of nobles and priests removed experienced commanders. Mortality estimates for Tenochtitlan are guesses, with figures from a fifth to a half cited, and I'd treat any single number cautiously.

sources.cite: Alfred Crosby, The Columbian Exchange (1972)
Miguel León-Portilla, The Broken Spears (1962)

steps.title: Besieged by sickness and thirst
steps.text: When Cortés returned in May 1521 with brigantines and allied armies, the siege fell on a city weakened by an epidemic that had run through the winter and spring. The Military historian will cover the ships and causeways; what the disease lens adds is the other side of the lines: defenders who had survived smallpox were often scarred, weak and short of kin, while crowded refugees, cut-off water and little food worsened outbreaks. The Atlas notes the epidemic killed much of Tenochtitlan during the siege, which ended on 13 August 1521. The Spanish and their allies were largely not hit as hard in this wave: some Spaniards had immunity from childhood exposure and the Tlaxcalans were presumably also struck, though the Political scientist's allies show the disease did not decide things alone. Longer term, the Atlas links the Great Dying to carbon drawdown from regrowing forests (Koch et al. 2019), a side effect that outlasted the empire.

sources.cite: Alfred Crosby, The Columbian Exchange (1972)
Koch et al., Earth system impacts of the European arrival and Great Dying in the Americas after 1492 (2019)

steps.title: An empire built on tribute, not integration
steps.text: The Atlas shows the Aztec Triple Alliance (Tenochtitlan, Texcoco, Tlacopan) at its 1502 peak of 0.212 Mkm², yet its model rates fragility at only 11%, below the 14% base rate. That calm reading is the puzzle: the model sees size and duration, not how the empire ruled. It was hegemonic, not bureaucratic. Conquered city-states kept their own rulers and paid tribute in cloth, maize, feathers and labor, enforced by garrisons, tribute collectors (calpixque) and the threat of the next campaign. Subjects were bound to the center by fear and payment, not by shared law or identity, so every provincial ruler had a standing reason to defect if a credible alternative appeared. I am inferring that from the political structure; the fragility score itself does not capture it.

sources.cite: Hassig, Aztec Warfare: Imperial Expansion and Political Control (1988)
Smith, The Aztecs (1996)

steps.title: Tlaxcala: the enemy the empire could not swallow
steps.text: Tlaxcala was a confederation of several city-states, roughly encircled by Aztec-controlled territory and cut off from salt and cotton, so it had every reason to hate Tenochtitlan. After fighting the Spaniards hard in September 1519, its leaders judged that an alliance with the newcomers beat a lifetime of siege. It is the strongest case for a hegemon's weakness: it never absorbed a rival 40 km-odd away, and that rival became the anvil. Cholula, a Tlaxcalan-adjacent holy city on our map, was then massacred in October 1519, which both terrorized waverers and showed the Spaniards could break an Aztec-linked center. The Military historian will show how allied tens of thousands changed the siege; what my lens adds is why those men volunteered: they were buying an end to tribute and a share of the spoils.

routes.label: Cortés and allies march inland

sources.cite: Gibson, Tlaxcala in the Sixteenth Century (1952)
Restall, Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest (2003)

steps.title: Collapse of the tribute web, then the new tribute
steps.text: When Moctezuma II died in 1520 and his successor Cuitláhuac died of smallpox within months, the empire's central node lost leadership just as its periphery was defecting; Texcoco, a Triple Alliance partner, came over to Cortés by 1521. The Epidemiologist will show the plague's toll; what governance adds is that a hegemony has no institutional depth to absorb a decapitation, so the shock cascaded. Tenochtitlan fell on 13 August 1521 under Cuauhtémoc. Then the Spaniards did what many conquerors do: they kept the tribute machinery, reusing the old obligations and often the old indigenous elites, which made the allies' reward smaller than they hoped. Our law layer only starts later, with the New Laws of the Indies (1542), a reminder that formal rules arrived after the conquest, to restrain what it had unleashed.

routes.label: Allied forces converge on Tenochtitlan

sources.cite: Gibson, The Aztecs under Spanish Rule (1964)
Restall, Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest (2003)

steps.title: La Noche Triste: the causeways kill an army
steps.text: Tenochtitlan was an island city reached by three causeways with removable bridges, so the Aztecs could turn every road into a kill zone. On the night of 30 June 1520 the Spaniards fled along the Tlacopan causeway, found the bridge gaps held by canoe-borne warriors, and lost perhaps 600 Spaniards and a far larger number of Tlaxcalan allies (estimates vary widely; I'd trust the order of magnitude, not the figure). Horses and steel were nearly useless here: cavalry cannot charge on a narrow, breached causeway. This is the lesson of the whole war: the Spaniards' technological edge worked only on open ground, so Cortés had to change the terrain.

routes.label: Spanish retreat west along the Tlacopan causeway, 30 June-1 July 1520

sources.cite: Hugh Thomas, Conquest: Montezuma, Cortés, and the Fall of Old Mexico (1993)
Ross Hassig, Aztec Warfare: Imperial Expansion and Political Control (1988)

steps.title: Otumba: cavalry on open ground
steps.text: The Battle of Otumba (July 1520), on the Atlas's war layer at 19.7, -98.8, is the counter-example: on the open plain, a few dozen horsemen and the Spaniards' close-order sword-and-shield work broke a much larger Aztec force after Cortés reportedly killed a commander and seized his standard. That is why steel and horses mattered: they won pitched battles in the open, and let the survivors reach Tlaxcala. The Political scientist will show why Tlaxcala took the battered force in, and the Epidemiologist what smallpox did to the Aztec side that same year; what my lens adds is that the retreat was saved by terrain choice, not by superior numbers.

routes.label: Retreat from Tenochtitlan around the lake to Tlaxcala, July 1520

sources.cite: Hugh Thomas, Conquest: Montezuma, Cortés, and the Fall of Old Mexico (1993)

steps.title: Thirteen brigantines and a lake siege
steps.text: Cortés had thirteen brigantines built in pieces at Tlaxcala, carried on porters' backs to Texcoco and launched in April 1521. They swept the canoes from Lake Texcoco, cut off food and water (the Chapultepec aqueduct was broken), and let his forces advance down all three causeways at once. The siege ran roughly 75 days to 13 August 1521 (the Atlas's Fall of Tenochtitlan record, with Colhuacatonco as a street-fight in it). Spaniards numbered under 1,000; the allied host is commonly put in the tens of thousands, and the sources disagree wildly on how many (figures of 100,000+ appear in conquistador accounts, which I treat as inflated). Allies did most of the killing and the building demolition, filling canals with rubble from every house they razed. Spanish steel and guns were the keystone, not the arch: the Aztecs were beaten by a lake navy, a starved city and an alliance of Aztec enemies, and I go beyond the Atlas's data on all the numbers here.

steps.title: Malinche: the mouth that made allies
steps.text: Cortés landed in 1519 with about 500 men, but he could not speak to anyone. Malinche (Malintzin, born c.1500, enslaved and given to him at Potonchán with 19 other women) spoke Nahuatl and Maya, and with Gerónimo de Aguilar formed a relay: Nahuatl to Maya to Spanish. Her role was more than translation: she read tone and politics, and Cortés's later claim of the Cholula massacre (c.October 1519, thousands killed) rests partly on her warning of an ambush. The Political scientist will show why Tlaxcala was ready to ally; what only the biographer sees is that without a voice to negotiate in Nahuatl, the alliance might have been a battle. Her exact words are lost, since nearly all accounts are Spanish or later indigenous retellings.

routes.label: Cortés and Malinche, Veracruz to Tlaxcala to Cholula to Tenochtitlan

sources.cite: Matthew Restall, Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest (2003)
Camilla Townsend, Malintzin's Choices (2006)

steps.title: Moctezuma II: the ruler who let them in
steps.text: Moctezuma II (1466–1520, born Tenochtitlan) ruled since 1502 and was a hard-nosed expansionist, not a man paralyzed by prophecy; the 'Cortés as returning god' story is largely a later construction, Restall argues. His real choice on 8 November 1519 was to admit the column into his island capital rather than fight it on the causeways. Within weeks Cortés seized him and held him as a hostage-ruler, which froze the empire's chain of command: nobles waited on a captive king. When Cortés left in 1520 to fight Narváez, Pedro de Alvarado's massacre at the Toxcatl festival turned the city against the Spaniards, and Moctezuma died around 29 June 1520. Whether spears, stones or Spanish hands killed him is disputed, and we do not know.

routes.label: Spanish and allied column enters Tenochtitlan

sources.cite: Matthew Restall, Seven Myths of the Spanish Conquest (2003)
Ross Hassig, Aztec Warfare (1988)

steps.title: Cortés: one man's gambles, 1519-1521
steps.text: Cortés personally changed three things: he scuttled his ships in 1519, disobeyed Governor Velázquez of Cuba to found Veracruz's own legal authority, and refused to quit after the Noche Triste (30 June 1520), when perhaps 600 of his Spaniards and many allies died. His second gamble was staying in Tlaxcala to rebuild rather than fleeing to the coast. The Epidemiologist will show how smallpox hollowed out Tenochtitlan, including the death of Moctezuma's successor Cuitláhuac; what the biography adds is that Cortés had the political skill to turn that luck into a coalition, and Cuauhtémoc, the last tlatoani, held out until 13 August 1521. Remove Cortés and the Spanish still come, but a different, probably slower, conquest follows, which is a judgment, not a fact.

whatifs.q: What if Tlaxcala had stayed neutral or sided with Tenochtitlan in 1519?

Smallpox would still have come later with other Europeans, but into an empire with its tribute web intact and time to adapt, so conquest would likely have been slower and different.

q: How did the Inca run an empire without writing or markets?

answer.short: The Inca replaced coins and contracts with a system where labor was the tax and hospitality was the wage. Households owed rotating mit'a turns, the state banked the product in stone storehouses (maize, freeze-dried chuño, cloth), and khipu cords carried counts up a decimal chain of command from 10 households to 10,000. Roads, runners and tambos moved goods, soldiers and news across vertical ecologies, and mitmaq resettlement scrambled local loyalties. It worked brilliantly for about a century, but its single road spine and thin loyalty made it fragile once disease and civil war hit in the 1520s.
answer.frame: The Inca ran a roughly 10-million-person Andean empire with no script and no markets, using knotted-cord records, labor tax and state storehouses, roads, and reciprocity instead.

plan.frame: The Inca ran a roughly 10-million-person Andean empire with no script and no markets, using knotted-cord records, labor tax and state storehouses, roads, and reciprocity instead.
