steps.title: A state stacked up the mountainside
steps.text: Start with the slope, not the state. Within about 150 km of Cusco (the map shows it founded from 1100) you can drop from Cordillera Oriental passes above 4,000 m to warm Urubamba valleys near 2,000 m. Each band grows something different: potatoes and llamas high, maize in the middle, coca and fruit below, cotton and fish on the coast. Andean communities already held scattered 'islands' of land in several bands, so goods moved by kin duty rather than by sale. In 1438, when the Inca polity begins in our index, the empire's real inheritance was this vertical ecology, which it scaled up from one valley to a continent. I'm going beyond the map data here, since it records only three places for the window.

pins.name: Lake Titicaca altiplano: potatoes, chuño, llamas

sources.cite: John Murra, The Economic Organization of the Inca State (1980)
Terence N. D'Altroy, The Incas (2002)

steps.title: The Royal Road spine and the runners
steps.text: Geography dictated the road plan: two long north-south trunks, one in the highlands past the Cordillera Blanca and the Altiplano, one along the coast through river oases and the Atacama's edge. The Inca network is usually put at about 40,000 km of road, with suspension bridges of grass rope over gorges that no cart could cross, since there were no wheeled vehicles anyway. Relay runners, the chaski, waited at huts roughly every 2 to 2.5 km (my estimate from chroniclers; spacing varied) and passed on cords and spoken messages; a message could cover on the order of 200 km a day, so Cusco could hear from far Quito in about a week. The Economic historian will show what filled the storehouses along these roads; what the terrain adds is that each tambo sat a day's walk apart, so grain, soldiers and news all moved on the same ladder of distances.

routes.label: Highland Capac Ñan (Qhapaq Ñan), Cusco to the north
Highland road south around Titicaca
Coastal road through desert valleys

sources.cite: John Hyslop, The Inka Road System (1984)
Terence N. D'Altroy, The Incas (2002)

steps.title: Conquering the coast, and a fragile spine
steps.text: Our data gives Chan Chan as the Chimú capital, the largest adobe city in the Americas, ending in 1470, which is when the Inca took the coast and with it the irrigated river valleys. A desert-bound state lives by canals off the Andean rivers, so whoever controls the mountain headwaters can also threaten the oases; the Inca simply came down the slope. Machu Picchu, a royal estate from 1450 on the ridge above the Urubamba, shows the other use of verticality: lowland maize and coca for the court, farmed on terraces. The weakness was the same spine: one road system with Cusco at its middle meant that when civil war split Huayna Capac's heirs in the 1520s, armies marched that road against each other, and the Spanish used it in 1532. The Demographer will count the people moved along it; I flag only that disease (smallpox likely ran ahead of Pizarro along these roads, though the date is debated) travelled at runner speed too.

routes.label: Inca armies down from the highlands to the Chimú coast

sources.cite: Michael E. Moseley, The Incas and Their Ancestors (1992)
Terence N. D'Altroy, The Incas (2002)

steps.title: An empire that taxed hours, not coins
steps.text: Where the Atlas sees Cusco in 1450, the potato is already there as a staple, and the economic puzzle is how a state fed and paid people with no money. The answer was mit'a: instead of coin, households owed rotating turns of labor, on state fields, roads, mines, bridges, or in the army. The state supplied food, chicha and tools while you served, so labor was the currency and hospitality was the wage. Scholars like John Murra argued this was an economy of reciprocity and redistribution, where the ruler's legitimacy rested on being a generous host. The Atlas data has no price series for the Andes (the Maddison figures cover England, India and others, not here), so the scale of output is something I'm reasoning toward, not reading off the map.

pins.name: Lake Titicaca basin (potato and chuño country)

sources.cite: John V. Murra, The Economic Organization of the Inca State (1980)
Terence N. D'Altroy, The Incas (2002)

steps.title: Storehouses: the Inca central bank was made of stone
steps.text: Storehouses (qollqa) were the system's buffer stock: thousands of round and rectangular stone buildings in rows, holding maize, freeze-dried potatoes (chuño), dried meat, cloth and weapons. They worked as granary, payroll, army commissary and famine insurance at once. Freeze-drying is the key technology: chuño keeps for years, which turns a perishable crop into a storable reserve, something the Mexica to the north, with potatoes absent, lacked in the same form. Cloth was the closest thing to money, since the state produced it in enormous quantity and gave it as reward, but it was a prestige and gift good rather than a market currency. Compare the Atlas's silver peso, which first appears at the Mexico City mint in 1536 and Potosí in 1545: silver arrived with the Spanish and had no monetary role under the Inca, only ornamental and sacred value.

routes.label: Provincial surplus (maize, chuño, cloth) flowing to Cusco

sources.cite: Terence N. D'Altroy, The Incas (2002)
John V. Murra, The Economic Organization of the Inca State (1980)

steps.title: The silver the Inca never spent
steps.text: The shock of 1532-33 is an economic category error: the Spanish demanded a room of gold and two of silver as Atahualpa's ransom, treasure the Inca valued for ritual and display but never used as money. Within about a decade Potosí (1545 in the Atlas) turned the same highlands into the engine of world silver, and the mit'a was repurposed into the Spanish mita draft, with the old reciprocity stripped out and wage-like obligations replaced by coercion. This is where my lens meets the Demographer's: the Inca moved and counted people, and the Spanish inherited that labor ledger as a supply of miners. How much of the later mita rested on Inca precedent versus Spanish invention is debated, so treat the continuity as real but overstated in some retellings.

routes.label: Ransom gold and silver toward the coast

Peter Bakewell, Silver Mining and Society in Colonial Mexico (1971)

steps.title: Ten thousand households, one chain of command
steps.text: Cusco (founded in the data from 1100) sat at the top of a decimal ladder: households were grouped into 10s, 50s, 100s, 500s, 1,000s, 5,000s and 10,000s (the hunu), each with a local official answerable upward, and four suyu (quarters) under governors, which is why Tawantinsuyu means 'four parts together'. Khipu, knotted cords with place-value knots in base 10, carried the counts of people, llamas and stored goods up this ladder, and khipukamayuq specialists read them back. The Cliopatria record shows the result: the Inca Empire from 1440, peaking at 2.095 million km² in 1497, with fragility of only 8% against a 14% base rate. That is a very calm score for a state that grew roughly 30-fold in about 60 years. Scholars still argue over whether khipu also held narrative, not only numbers; I'd say that is unresolved.

pins.name: Hanan and Hurin Cusco, the two halves of the capital

Terence D'Altroy, The Incas (2002)

steps.title: Gifts you cannot refuse: reciprocity as law
steps.text: With no market and no coin, the state's legal engine was a claim on labor framed as kin obligation: the ruler gave feasts, chicha and cloth, and communities gave mit'a turns of work. The Economic historian will show the storehouses and the flows of goods; what only the political lens sees is that this was a legitimacy contract, where refusing a gift-debt meant rebelling against a relationship, not just dodging a tax. Rulers also kept conquered gods' images in Cusco as honored hostages, and sons of local lords were schooled there. My law layer has nothing inside this window before the New Laws of the Indies (1542), so this is drawn from ethnohistory, not from a codified text, since the Inca left no written code.

pins.name: Hatun Xauxa, a provincial administrative center

sources.cite: John V. Murra, The Economic Organization of the Inca State (1980)
Terence D'Altroy, The Incas (2002)

steps.title: Moving the restless: mitmaq and the Chimú lesson
steps.text: Chan Chan (850 to 1470 in the index) was capital of the Chimú Empire, listed 1188 to 1481, with a fragility of 17%, on watch and near the 20% warning line, yet Inca conquest ended it around 1470. Rather than razing it, the Inca took Chimú metalworkers to Cusco and settled loyal mitmaq colonists among restive provinces, while moving suspect groups to loyal areas. The Demographer will count how many were moved; my point is that resettlement was a stability tool, scrambling local loyalties so no province held a single united population. The cost showed later: a hollow loyalty to Cusco meant that when civil war and Spanish arrival hit in the 1520s and 1530s, the empire ended in 1533 in the index, within a single generation of its 1497 peak.

routes.label: Chimú craftsmen resettled toward Cusco (approximate)

sources.cite: Michael E. Moseley and Alana Cordy-Collins (eds.), The Northern Dynasties: Kingship and Statecraft in Chimor (1990)
Terence D'Altroy, The Incas (2002)

steps.title: Counting a people with no numbers on paper
steps.text: Start in 1438, when Pachacuti's Inca Empire (polity:inca) begins, with Cusco as capital. The Atlas has no city figure for Cusco before 1533, which is honest: the Inca left no written census. What they did count, by khipu, was households grouped in decimal units of 10, 100, 1,000, 10,000 up to a huge hunu. Modern estimates for the empire's total population run from about 6 million to over 12 million, a wide band, and the contact-era figure of ~10 million is a scholar's reconstruction rather than a tally. Counting people was the empire's core technology, because a labor tax needs a headcount. The Political scientist will show how those khipu worked; what the demographer adds is that the count was the state.

sources.cite: Terence D'Altroy, The Incas (2002)
Noble David Cook, Demographic Collapse: Indian Peru, 1520-1620 (1981)

steps.title: Mitmaq: moving whole villages
steps.text: The Inca moved people as policy. Mitmaq colonists were resettled in two directions: loyal households planted in newly conquered lands, and restive populations pulled out and scattered. In the Cochabamba valley the state is reported to have settled on the order of 14,000 households to grow maize, per Wachtel's reading of the sources, though I treat that number as uncertain. After conquering the Chimu around 1470 (Chan Chan, place:chan_chan, in the Atlas until 1470), the Inca reportedly took Chimu metalworkers to Cusco. The Economic historian will show how the labor tax fed the storehouses; the demographic point is that mobility itself was the tax base, with perhaps a few percent of the population relocated. Routes drawn are schematic, not documented paths.

steps.title: 1533: Cusco at 122,000, then the fall
steps.text: By 1533 the Atlas shows Cusco (place:cusco) at 122,000, the only Andean figure in my data, and a plausible peak for a ceremonial capital that also hosted rotating mit'a workers and royal estates. Machu Picchu (place:machu_picchu, 1450 on) was a royal estate, not a city, with a population likely in the hundreds. The empire's death spiral began before Pizarro: Old World disease probably reached the Andes around 1524-1528, ahead of the Spanish, and is thought to have killed Huayna Capac and his heir, triggering the Huascar-Atahualpa war. The Atlas's slave-trade migration entry (from 1501) shows the Atlantic's forced movement, but its total is blank in my data, so I won't quote it; the Andes' own population fell by well over half within a century, per Cook's estimates. The plague layer is on, but the Atlas holds no Andean epidemic record, so this is outside my data.

sources.cite: Noble David Cook, Demographic Collapse: Indian Peru, 1520-1620 (1981)
Terence D'Altroy, The Incas (2002)

links.why: Vertical ecology gave each community goods from several altitudes by kin duty, which is the template the state scaled up into mit'a labor and redistribution instead of markets.
A labor tax needs a headcount, so the household counts the Demographer describes were the data that khipu and the decimal hierarchy carried upward.
Storehouses were useful only because roads, tambos and runners let grain, cloth and soldiers move between them, so the stone buffer and the road ladder were one system.
Resettling restive groups bought stability but left shallow loyalty, and the single Cusco-centered road spine then let rival heirs and the Spanish march straight through in the 1520s-30s.

views.name: John Murra
views.claim: The Inca economy ran on reciprocity and redistribution, with labor owed to the state and returned as feasts and goods, and without markets or money.
views.for: Mit'a service paired with state-provided food and chicha, large qollqa storehouses, and communities holding land in multiple ecological zones.
views.against: Some scholars argue the picture is too tidy and that exchange, local barter and coercion were more present than the reciprocity model allows.

sources.cite: John V. Murra, The Economic Organization of the Inka State, 1980

views.name: Gary Urton
views.claim: Khipu were a structured, binary-coded recording system that may have held more than numbers.
views.for: Numerical khipu are well decoded in base 10, and cord structure choices like knot type and direction suggest additional coded information.
views.against: No khipu has been convincingly read as narrative, and the Spanish record of khipu-based histories is filtered through colonial informants.

sources.cite: Gary Urton, Signs of the Inka Khipu, 2003

views.name: Terence D'Altroy
views.claim: Inca rule combined decimal administration, infrastructure, mitmaq resettlement and negotiated local rule, adapting to each province rather than imposing one model.
views.for: Archaeology of road sites, storehouses and provincial centers shows variable intensity of control across regions.
views.against: Chronicle accounts of uniform decimal organization may idealize a messier reality.

sources.cite: Terence N. D'Altroy, The Incas, 2002

whatifs.q: What if smallpox had not reached the Andes before Pizarro in 1532?
whatifs.a: Huayna Capac might have lived and the Huascar-Atahualpa war might have been avoided or delayed, leaving Cusco's road spine intact and the empire more unified. Pizarro's roughly 170 men would still have faced a large, organized state, though European steel, horses and local allies might still have won some footing. The collapse would likely have been slower and more contested.

unknowns: Whether khipu encoded narrative or only numbers
The true population of Tawantinsuyu, with estimates from about 6 to over 12 million

How much the Spanish mita rested on Inca precedent versus colonial invention

q: Why did a murder in Sarajevo start a world war?

answer.short: A local murder became a world war because Bosnia's mountain pockets and Serbia's rise made South Slav nationalism an existential threat to Vienna, while Russia, Germany and France had tied their credibility to clients and allies. Germany's open-plain geography had been converted by the Schlieffen timetable into a clock, so once Vienna issued its ultimatum (with Berlin's blank cheque) and Russia mobilized, restraint cost more than war in every capital. A handful of men (Conrad, Wilhelm, Nicholas's generals) set the tempo, and even Princip's success hung on a wrong turn, so the war was contingent in its trigger but structured in its spread.
answer.frame: A single assassination on 28 June 1914 escalated into global war because rigid alliances, Balkan rivalries, mobilization timetables and decaying empires turned a local crisis into a continental one.

steps.title: The Balkan Mountains That Never Made a State
steps.text: Look at the Dinaric Alps (44.0N, 17.6E) and Balkan Mountains: they run in ridges parallel to the Adriatic, so valleys are cut off from one another, and that is why this region never produced one big state, only many small peoples packed into pockets. When the Ottoman grip loosened, Vienna, St Petersburg and the new Balkan states all rushed to fill the vacuum. Austria-Hungary occupied Bosnia in 1878 and annexed it in 1908, which put Habsburg garrisons in the very mountains where Serb nationalists wanted their own state. By 1914 Sarajevo sat inside an empire whose Slavic subjects looked across a river to a free Serbia. Dates and the Bosnian details go beyond the Atlas layers, which show the Ottoman and Austria-Hungary polities but not the provincial borders.

routes.label: Austro-Hungarian occupation of Bosnia, 1878

sources.cite: Christopher Clark, The Sleepwalkers (2012)

steps.title: Straits, Rivers and Russia's Throat
steps.text: The Atlas chokepoints list the Bosporus (41.1N, 29.1E) and Dardanelles (40.2N, 26.4E): Russia's whole southern coast exits the world through those two narrow gates, and the Ottoman Empire at Istanbul (pop ~874,000 in our layer) held the key. A hostile power in Constantinople, or a Slavic one friendly to Russia in the Balkans, mattered enormously to St Petersburg, which is why it saw itself as Serbia's patron. For Austria-Hungary the opposite logic held: the Danube, which flows past Belgrade (45.0N, 20.3E) into Budapest and Vienna, was its lifeline, and Serbia sat on the upstream-downstream hinge. The Economic historian will show the trade flows, but what the map adds is that a customs dispute with Serbia, like the Pig War of 1906, was a fight over who controlled a river corridor. I am going beyond the Atlas data on the figures; the shipping share through the straits is often put at around a third of Russian exports, so treat it as approximate.

steps.title: Germany in the Nutcracker
steps.text: Berlin (52.5N, 13.4E) lay about 880 km from Paris and only about 520 km from Warsaw, with no mountain wall on either side: the North European Plain runs flat from the Rhine to the Urals, so Germany was a nutcracker with no natural shell. The Franco-German frontier was fortified and ridged by the Vosges, so German planners looked north through the open Belgian plain, and that geography is why a Balkan quarrel was bound to drag in Belgium and Britain, whose Strait of Dover (51.0N, 1.4E) is only 33 km wide. The Military historian will walk you through the timetables; the geographic point beneath them is that Germany could not afford to wait, because waiting meant Russia mobilizing across a plain. Sarajevo mattered because Vienna was Berlin's only dependable partner: if Austria-Hungary lost face to Serbia, Germany's southeastern flank would crumble. The distances are my rounded great-circle estimates, not Atlas data.

steps.title: Sedan 1870: the template and the grudge
steps.text: The map shows 40-odd Franco-Prussian War battles and sieges between Wissembourg and Belfort, almost all inside 300 km of the Rhine. Sedan (1 Sept 1870) captured Napoleon III, and Metz and Paris fell to siege. Moltke's lesson was that railways and prewar timetables win campaigns in weeks, which every general in 1914 took as gospel. The cost was a French grudge held for 40 years, and the Dual Alliance of 1879 and Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894 on the chronicle layer are that grudge turned into treaties. Confidence is high on the facts; 'every general took it as gospel' is my own interpretation.

steps.title: Two fronts, one timetable
steps.text: Germany sat between France and Russia (Franco-Russian Alliance, 1894), so Schlieffen's 1905 plan staked everything on beating France in about six weeks, sending the right wing through Belgium toward Paris before Russia finished mobilising. That meant no pause was possible: any Russian mobilisation forced German war on both. The Anglo-Russian Convention (1907) closed the ring. The chokepoint table gives the clue, since the Fulda Gap sat inside the German Empire while Belgium's roads and Liège's forts were the real gate. I add from outside the data that the plan needed Liège taken within days, and that the General Staff's 1914 rail schedules reportedly ran to thousands of trains, which I cannot verify precisely. The Geographer will show why Germany's position is so exposed; what the timetable adds is that geography became a clock.

steps.title: July 1914: the clock runs out
steps.text: The chronicle gives the dates: the blank cheque 5 July, Austria declares war on Serbia 28 July, Germany on Russia 1 August, Britain on Germany 4 August. Once Russia began partial then general mobilisation (30-31 July), German planners argued that waiting meant losing, so the Schlieffen timetable replaced diplomacy. Contrary to the popular story, mobilisation did not literally make war automatic, but it gave statesmen hours, not weeks, and military chiefs pressed that case. The map shows the result: Tannenberg destroyed a Russian army in East Prussia, but the Marne halted the German plan, and the quick war became trenches. Historians still argue about how much was planning versus choice; the Political scientist covers who chose what.

steps.title: Two empires, one dual bargain
steps.text: Austria-Hungary (1867-1918 in the polity index) was a compromise state: two parliaments, two governments, one army and foreign policy. The Atlas model scores its fragility at only 10% at 1892, 'calm', below the 14% base rate. That is the trap: a state that looked stable internally felt existentially threatened by one thing, South Slav nationalism. Serbia was an irredentist magnet, and Vienna's elites (Conrad, Berchtold) read a Serbian success as the start of the empire's unraveling. A model that sees calm and a ruling class that sees doom can both be right: the doom was about legitimacy, not territory. The Biographer will show Conrad's personal push for war; what my lens adds is that the Dual Monarchy's veto structure (Budapest's Tisza resisted war until mid-July) made any decision slow, then sudden.

sources.cite: Christopher Clark, The Sleepwalkers (2012)
Samuel R. Williamson Jr., Austria-Hungary and the Origins of the First World War (1991)

steps.title: The Serbian magnet
steps.text: The data lists 'Serbs' 1805-1915 with a peak of 0.091 Mkm² in 1912, fragility 18% (watch). That peak is the Balkan Wars: Serbia roughly doubled its area against the Ottomans and Bulgaria. Success made it more dangerous to Vienna, not less. Bulgaria (16%, watch) and Greece (17%, watch) are in the same watch band, so the Balkans were a region of many mid-risk states competing over Ottoman leftovers. The 1908 Austrian annexation of Bosnia (occupied since 1878) had already told Serbia that legal claims count for little; Russia, humiliated in 1908, promised itself not to back down again. The Geographer will show the terrain; the political point is that each power's credibility was now tied to a client.

sources.cite: Christopher Clark, The Sleepwalkers (2012)
Richard C. Hall, The Balkan Wars 1912-1913 (2000)

steps.title: Blank cheque, mobilized credibility
steps.text: On 5-6 July Berlin gave Vienna the 'blank cheque': Germany would back whatever Austria did. Germany, the new state of 1871 in the index, believed a quick Austro-Serbian war could stay local; Russia, with its 1905 October Manifesto still in memory and revolution a fear, could not abandon Serbia without losing great-power status. Notice what the law layer shows: no binding international rule stood in the way. The 1914 ultimatum of 23 July, with 48 hours to reply, was designed to be refused; Serbia accepted most points anyway and Austria declared war on 28 July. Alliance logic did the rest, since each ally feared that restraining a partner would lose it. The Military historian will show the railway clocks; I add that leaders chose to start the clocks, because each judged that backing down cost more than war.

steps.title: Princip's seven seconds
steps.text: Gavrilo Princip, 19, tubercular, was one of seven conspirators armed by the Black Hand network (Serbian officer Dragutin Dimitrijević 'Apis' stood behind it). The first bomb, thrown by Čabrinović at about 10:10, bounced off the car. Then the driver took a wrong turn onto Franz Josef Street, stalled at Schiller's delicatessen, and Princip, who had just given up, stood two meters away and fired two shots, killing Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie. Nothing about this was inevitable: one correct turn and the day likely ends as a failed plot. The Archduke himself had been a brake on war, and Franz Joseph, 84 and reigning since 1848, lost the one heir who opposed preventive strikes on Serbia. The Geographer will show why Bosnia mattered; what a biography adds is how thin the human thread was.

steps.title: Conrad's war, Wilhelm's blank cheque
steps.text: Franz Conrad von Hötzendorf, Austria's chief of staff, had urged war on Serbia some 25 times between 1906 and 1914 and been refused; Sarajevo finally gave him a pretext. On 5-6 July Wilhelm II, lunching in Potsdam with Austria's envoy Count Szögyény, promised unconditional German backing, then left on his annual Baltic cruise on 6 July, absent while the crisis hardened. Vienna waited until 23 July for its ultimatum to Serbia, largely because Hungary's Prime Minister Tisza had to be won over and the harvest let troops go home. The Military historian will show how timetables then bit; the point for people is that a few men, one of them on a yacht, set the tempo before any timetable mattered. Historians still argue over how much was design (Fischer) and how much drift (Clark), so I hold this with moderate confidence.

steps.title: Willy, Nicky and the telegrams
steps.text: Wilhelm and Nicholas were cousins who wrote to each other in English as 'Willy' and 'Nicky'. On 29 July Nicholas ordered general mobilization, then cancelled it that night after Wilhelm's telegram; his generals, notably Sazonov and Janushkevich, pressed him again and he signed on 30 July (effective 31 July). Wilhelm, reading Serbia's conciliatory reply on 28 July, famously said all reason for war had vanished, but it was too late: the machinery was moving. Two monarchs who personally wished to avoid war lacked control over their own militaries, which is the unsettling lesson. The Political scientist will explain why states chose this; the biographical answer is that kinship across thrones, once a safety net in Europe, had stopped working.

links.why: Germany's flat, two-front exposure on the North European Plain is what Schlieffen turned into a six-week timetable through Belgium, converting geography into a clock.
Serbia's doubling in the Balkan Wars (peak 0.091 Mkm² in 1912) made Vienna's elites read South Slav nationalism as doom even while the model scored the Dual Monarchy as calm at 10%.
Conrad's 25 refused calls for war and Wilhelm's 5-6 July promise are the personal decisions behind the political logic that each power's credibility was tied to a client.
The Willy-Nicky telegrams show two cousin-monarchs trying to stop what the mobilization timetables had already made hours-long, so kinship failed against the military clock.

views.against: Berlin hoped to localize the Austro-Serbian war and Wilhelm sought restraint on 28 July; Fischer's wider war-aims continuity thesis is contested.

whatifs.q: What if Princip's driver had taken the correct turn and the assassination failed on 28 June 1914?
whatifs.a: Vienna would probably have lacked a pretext, though Conrad and Serbian tensions would have kept pressure high, so a Balkan crisis later was likely. Franz Ferdinand, a brake on preventive war, would have stayed alive, making a continental war in 1914 less likely, but not impossible by 1916-17 as Russian military reforms matured.

q: How did Europe carve up Africa so fast after 1880?

answer.short: Europe partitioned Africa quickly because entry and rule became cheap while war between the powers stayed expensive and pointless. Quinine, steamers, the telegraph and the Maxim gun cut the cost of getting in and beating African armies (Omdurman, Ulundi), and rinderpest weakened many societies just as agents arrived. Rubber, gold and diamonds and the pull of investor capital gave claims a price, concession companies let small states hold land without paying for administration, and the Berlin rules plus bilateral treaties turned a race into notify-and-trade-borders paperwork. Where Africans had rifles and logistics (Ethiopia at Adwa) the model failed, and where rule stayed thin (tsetse, malaria) it was often more claim than control.
answer.frame: Why a continent about 10% European-held in 1880 was almost entirely partitioned by 1914, with few wars between the powers.

steps.title: Quinine opens the rivers
steps.text: Before 1850, West Africa killed Europeans at staggering rates: in Sierra Leone, mortality among European troops ran to roughly 400-700 per 1,000 per year (Philip Curtin's figures). The 1841 Niger expedition lost about a third of its Europeans to fever. In 1854 William Baikie took 12 men up the Niger-Benue on a steamer with regular quinine doses and lost none to fever. By the 1860s-70s, prophylactic quinine (bark from Andean Cinchona, then Javanese plantations under the Dutch) had cut mortality several-fold. My Atlas shocks layer for this window holds only 'industrial-era warming', so the disease evidence here is from outside the map data. The Economic historian will show the steamers and money; what disease data adds is that the river highways were closed to Europeans until the pharmacology arrived.

routes.label: Baikie's quinine-prophylaxis Niger expedition, 1854

sources.cite: Philip D. Curtin, Death by Migration (1989)

steps.title: Rinderpest sweeps the continent
steps.text: Rinderpest, a cattle virus likely brought with Italian army cattle landing at Massawa around 1887, reached the Zambezi by 1892 and the Cape by 1896-97. It killed an estimated 80-90% of cattle in many herds, along with buffalo and antelope. Pastoralists such as the Maasai, already hit by smallpox and drought, faced famine and collapse; farmers lost their draught animals and their wealth. German and British agents arrived in East Africa as these societies were at their weakest, and the same die-off let bush grow and tsetse flies spread, a cost to later colonial economies too. The Military historian will show the guns; what this adds is that some of the resistance was starved before the guns arrived. Mortality figures are rough and debated.

routes.label: Rinderpest spread, c.1887-1897

steps.title: Sleeping sickness: holding what you took
steps.text: Disease also limited what colonizers could hold. A sleeping sickness epidemic (Trypanosoma, carried by tsetse) hit Uganda from 1900: an estimated 200,000-300,000 died around Lake Victoria by 1905, and the Congo basin lost very large numbers too, though exact counts are unknown. Tsetse belts kept horses and oxen out of much of central Africa, so Europeans used human porters, which fed brutal labor demands. Partition was fast partly because quinine made entry cheap, yet effective rule stayed thin where tsetse, malaria and blackwater fever persisted. Disease let Europeans arrive; it did not let them govern.

pins.name: Lake Victoria shore, sleeping sickness epidemic

sources.cite: Maryinez Lyons, The Colonial Disease (1992)

steps.title: The cable and the canal shrink Africa
steps.text: The scramble was priced before it was fought. The Suez Canal opened in 1869 and Port Said appears in the Atlas steamship list that same year; a London to Calcutta letter fell from 154 days (1820) to 39 (1860), and the Atlantic cable of 1866 made London to New York same-day. Cheap steam and instant news meant a minister in Paris or Berlin could price a distant claim and see rivals move within hours. Egypt then became the first domino: Britain occupied it in 1882 largely to protect Suez-era finance and the route to India. The Military historian will show how the guns made holding ground cheap; what freight and telegraph data add is that ruling from 6,000 km away became affordable at all.

routes.label: London to India, steamers via Suez instead of the Cape

steps.title: Rubber, ivory and the Congo's price
steps.text: The 1880s were a price opportunity. Ivory had long paid for expeditions, but the rubber boom, driven by bicycle and then (from 1888 onward) pneumatic tyre demand, plus insulation for the very telegraph cables above, turned Congo vines into a commodity. Leopold II used a private company structure, not a state budget, to claim a basin of about 2.3 million km2, which Berlin recognised in 1885. The profits were brutal: forced quotas and hostage-taking, with widely cited estimates of millions of deaths, though the figure is debated. Antwerp, in the Atlas place index, became the rubber and ivory clearing port. Note the cheap model: concession companies let small states claim land without paying for administration, which is why so many partitions needed so little war. The Epidemiologist will show who could survive inland; the price signal says why anyone wanted to try.

steps.title: Gold, diamonds and the Rand
steps.text: South Africa shows the money pulling the flag. Diamonds at Kimberley in 1871 and gold on the Witwatersrand in 1886 drew deep-level mining capital from London; Cape Town's railway of 1862 in the Atlas tech list was the seed of the lines inland. Cecil Rhodes used De Beers profits to fund the Pioneer Column north in 1890, and the South African War (1899-1902) was fought over who would tax the Rand. The Atlas GDP series shows why British investors wanted outlets: UK GDP per head rose from 5,829 (1870) to 8,131 (1914, 2011 dollars), and surplus savings looked for high-yield mines and railways abroad. One caution: overall African trade was small in 1880, so the empire was not clearly profitable for most powers; it was speculative, and the Political scientist will show how rivalry, not ledgers alone, filled the map.

steps.title: Isandlwana: the exception that proves the rule
steps.text: The map's own record for Isandlwana in 1879 calls it the worst British defeat by an indigenous army in the colonial era. About 1,300 British and allied troops with Martini-Henry rifles were overrun by roughly 20,000 Zulu, who killed around 1,300 of them. Rifles alone did not guarantee a win: spread out, short of ammunition and without a defensive position, they lost. Six months later at Ulundi, Chelmsford formed a hollow square with Gatling guns and the Zulu kingdom was broken. The lesson the Europeans took was about formation and fire discipline, not about the superiority of their men. (Casualty and force figures are from memory and approximate. The Atlas record does not give them.)

steps.title: Omdurman: five hours, a gunboat river
steps.text: Kitchener went up the Nile on a railway built behind the army and steamers beside it, the Atlas's Omdurman record says it all: machine guns against massed infantry. Maxim guns and gunboats shelled the Mahdist army of tens of thousands on 2 September 1898. British dead were under 50, while Mahdist dead ran past 10,000. Gordon died at Khartoum in 1884, and Abu Klea in 1885 had shown that a square could break under a charge, so the lesson of 1898 was to keep the enemy at range. The chokepoint table shows the same logic: the First Cataract of the Nile went from the Khedivate to the British Empire, and the 1885 border change moved 5.1 million km² from Egypt into British Africa. The Economic historian will show the steamship and telegraph money; what the war layer adds is that the true cost was supply, not casualties. (Casualty figures are from memory.)

routes.label: Kitchener's river and rail advance up the Nile

steps.title: Adwa: when the rifles were on both sides
steps.text: The Atlas says Ethiopia kept its independence through the Scramble, and Adwa in 1896 shows why. Menelik II had imported perhaps 100,000 or more modern rifles, many bought from France and Russia, plus artillery, and his army of about 100,000 outnumbered Baratieri's roughly 17,000 Italians and colonial troops. The Italians marched at night on bad maps, split into columns, and lost several thousand killed. The Political scientist will explain why the powers accepted the result. The military point is that the 'cheap victory' depended on a gap in weapons and logistics, and where that gap closed, the conquest failed. (Figures are from memory and approximate.)

sources.cite: Harold G. Marcus, The Life and Times of Menelik II (1975)
Battle of Adwa, Wikipedia

steps.title: Berlin 1884: the rulebook for claiming
steps.text: The Berlin Conference (Nov 1884 to Feb 1885) did not divide Africa; no map was drawn there. What it did was write procedure. The 1885 General Act required a power taking a coast to notify the others, and required 'effective occupation', meaning enough authority to protect existing rights. Its real effect was to turn a vague race into a checklist: notify, plant a treaty, post an agent, and rivals had to either object or accept. Your data shows the result, with Belgian Congo (1890, peak 2.36 Mkm²) and British Africa (1885, 10.6 Mkm² at peak) appearing right after. Leopold II got recognition because Britain and Germany preferred a weak neutral owner of the Congo to a French or Portuguese one. Note the Act's occupation rule applied only to coasts, which left the interior open to paper claims. The Economic historian will show what made these claims worth the cost; I'm showing why they cost so little to make.

sources.cite: Thomas Pakenham, The Scramble for Africa (1991)
Berlin Conference

steps.title: Treaties that traded borders, not blood
steps.text: Between 1884 and 1914 the powers signed dozens of bilateral boundary treaties, usually drawn on maps with lines of latitude or rivers few had surveyed. The 1890 Anglo-German deal swapped German claims in Zanzibar for the North Sea island of Heligoland, treating Africa as a ledger. Even the closest call, Fashoda in 1898, ended when France backed down: Kitchener had just won at Omdurman, Britain had the naval and local advantage, and France wanted Britain's support against Germany. The 1899 convention then fixed the Nile-Congo watershed as the line. Peace held because the stakes were small next to Europe's own balance of power; colonies were bargaining chips, and a settled border was worth more than a contested one. The Military historian will cover how cheaply African armies were beaten; my point is that those wars were never fought between Europeans.

steps.title: Who was left standing, and why
steps.text: The map's fragility scores show the logic of who survived. Ethiopian Empire (1.13 Mkm² at 1908, fragility 29%) beat Italy at Adwa in 1896, which is why Italian Africa only appears from 1890 and peaks decades later in 1940. Liberia (1848, fragility 19%) lasted by US backing and rival powers' mutual vetoes. By contrast, Ashanti (ends 1897), Merina (1897), Sokoto (1904) and Bornu (1894) all had established institutions yet are gone in your data within about a decade of each other. Those states were not chaotic; they lost legitimacy in the eyes of the only audience that mattered in the Berlin rules, other Europeans. A surprising point from the law layer: Europeans often justified conquest as ending slavery, though the listed abolitions (Tunisia 1846, Ethiopia only 1942) show Africans and Ottomans had their own paths. I go beyond the data here on Adwa details; the pattern, not the precise numbers, is what to trust.

links.why: Quinine let Europeans survive inland, and combined with river steamers and a railway behind the army it made the Nile campaign to Omdurman logistically possible.
The rubber and ivory profits behind Leopold's Congo company gave Berlin a reason to recognise a cheap private owner, and the Act's notify-and-occupy checklist let such claims be made on paper.
Rinderpest weakened pastoral and farming societies in East Africa, so agents could sign treaties and the powers could trade borders without fighting either Africans or each other.
Adwa showed that imported rifles and a large army could beat Italy, and the powers' acceptance of Ethiopia's independence made it one of the few states left standing.

q: Why was British India partitioned in 1947, and why was it so violent?

answer.short: The Raj was partitioned because a state that had sorted Indians into religious blocs for decades (separate electorates, 1909 and 1935) ran out of legitimacy and force after the war, and the 1946 elections and Calcutta killings left no umpire for a shared India. It was so violent because the handover was compressed into ten weeks, the Radcliffe line cut through the most entangled province (Punjab, 53% Muslim, 30% Hindu, 15% Sikh) and was published after independence, and the army that might have policed it was itself being split by religion. About 14.5 million moved and perhaps 200,000 to 2 million died, with the roads and trains of Punjab as the killing grounds.
answer.frame: A colonial state built on divide-and-rule, communal electoral politics and wartime collapse was dissolved in a rushed 1947 handover that drew borders through Punjab and Bengal, leaving millions uprooted and no one to keep order.

plan.frame: A colonial state built on divide-and-rule, communal electoral politics and wartime collapse was dissolved in a rushed 1947 handover that drew borders through Punjab and Bengal, leaving millions uprooted and no one to keep order.

steps.title: Separate electorates: counting heads, not citizens
steps.text: The British Raj (1859-1947, peak 4.939 Mkm2 in 1917, 22% fragility, flagged fragile) ruled by sorting people into categories it could bargain with. The Morley-Minto reforms of 1909 gave Muslims separate electorates, after the 1906 Simla deputation led by the Aga Khan, and the Government of India Act 1935 extended the principle. Once seats are reserved by religion, a politician wins by speaking to one community, not across them, so the incentive to build a cross-communal party is weak. My data has no law record for this; the Rule & law layer shows abolition acts and constitutions elsewhere (the Ottoman Constitution of 1876, the Persian Constitution of 1906) but nothing on India, and I am going beyond it here. The Economic historian will show the canal-colony land and Bengal money that gave these communal blocs something concrete to fight over.

sources.cite: Ayesha Jalal, The Sole Spokesman: Jinnah, the Muslim League and the Demand for Pakistan (1985)
Government of India Act 1935

steps.title: 1946: the election that turned into a census of fear
steps.text: The 1945-46 provincial elections were the plebiscite the system was built to produce. The Muslim League won nearly all the Muslim reserved seats (about 425 of 495 by the usual count) and Congress swept the general seats, so each party could say it alone spoke for its community. The Cabinet Mission plan of May 1946 offered a weak centre with three provincial groupings, and it collapsed over how to read the grouping clause. Then the League's Direct Action Day on 16 August 1946 set off the Calcutta killings, with several thousand dead (estimates vary), and from that point the choice felt like partition or civil war. The Military historian will show why the police and army could not hold the line; what only my lens sees is that nobody had a legitimate umpire left.

sources.cite: Ayesha Jalal, The Sole Spokesman: Jinnah, the Muslim League and the Demand for Pakistan (1985)
Yasmin Khan, The Great Partition: The Making of India and Pakistan (2007)

steps.title: Mountbatten's deadline: exit as a political strategy
steps.text: Mountbatten arrived in March 1947 and on 3 June announced a handover for 15 August, about ten weeks away, where the earlier plan had been June 1948. Provincial assemblies in Punjab and Bengal voted on splitting, which turned a bargaining position into a legal procedure. The Raj ended on 14-15 August 1947, and the Republic of India and Pakistan, with its 1.022 Mkm2 peak in 1948, appear in the data as new states the same moment. The Radcliffe boundary was published on 17 August, after independence, so two new governments inherited a border and a panic at once. The Kashmir and Jammu record (1846-1947, 11% fragility, rated calm) shows how misleading a calm score is: a princely state's ruler held the decision, and accession fighting began in October 1947. The Demographer will show who fled across Radcliffe's lines.

sources.cite: Yasmin Khan, The Great Partition: The Making of India and Pakistan (2007)
Partition of India

steps.title: The ledger of a drained colony
steps.text: Maddison's series for India is a poor man's ledger: GDP per capita was 896 (2011 dollars) in 1861 and 843 in 1891, then 983 in 1948. Almost nothing was gained across 87 years, while the UK went from about 5,019 in 1857 to 10,753 in 1948. Population rose from 241.7 million in 1857 to 350 million in 1948 (a figure that already reflects the Partition-era loss of territory), so the pie barely grew while there were more mouths to share it. When income is flat and the state is the main prize, jobs, licences and land become zero-sum, and that is fertile ground for communal competition. This is the broad pattern, not proof of causation: Maddison figures for colonial India are reconstructions with wide error bars.

sources.cite: Maddison Project Database (2020), India and UK series
Tirthankar Roy, The Economic History of India, 1857-1947 (2011)

steps.title: Canal colonies: land as loyalty
steps.text: From the 1880s the British irrigated millions of acres of the Punjab doabs, building the Chenab, Jhelum and Lower Bari Doab canal colonies and settling them with loyal peasants, often Sikh and Muslim Jats and ex-soldiers, and wheat went by rail to Karachi for export. The land was a reward tied to military recruitment, so economic rights and army service were braided together. Meanwhile, Hindu moneylenders and traders in the towns held much of the credit, and the 1900 Land Alienation Act barred non-agricultural castes from buying farmland. Debt and land thus lined up with religion in a way that made grievances easy to read in communal terms. I am describing the structure from secondary literature, not from the Atlas layers, which don't carry Punjab land data.

steps.title: War prices and the Bengal famine
steps.text: In 1943 Bengal's famine killed roughly 2 to 3 million people, even though the rice harvest of 1942 was only modestly below normal. Burmese rice imports were cut off by Japan's conquest, the army and Calcutta's war workers were fed first, boats were seized under the 'denial policy', and wartime inflation priced landless labourers out of the market. Amartya Sen's entitlement argument is that people starved because their purchasing power collapsed, not because food was absent. Wartime strain drained the Raj's legitimacy and left Bengal's Muslim peasants and Hindu elites bitter about who ruled and who was fed. The Political scientist will show how this feeds into the 1946 elections; the Military historian can say what a depleted, overstretched army could still do in 1947.

steps.title: A province with no clean seam
steps.text: The 1941 census counted about 28 million people in undivided Punjab: roughly 53% Muslim, 30% Hindu and 15% Sikh. Almost no district was purely one group, and the Sikhs, the third party, were a majority nowhere. Any line had to cut through villages, canal colonies and the Sikh heartland around Amritsar. Lahore, the cultural capital, had a Muslim plurality, but Hindus and Sikhs owned much of its property and commerce. The Economic historian will show the silver and land behind that; what the head-count adds is that 'majority' was a district-level fiction, so a line that satisfied one group stranded millions of another. The Atlas city figures for Lahore (8.6 million in 1857) are far too high for a city of about 100,000 then, so I am using the census, not that series.

steps.title: Five weeks, two lines, one night
steps.text: Cyril Radcliffe, a London barrister who had never been to India, had about five weeks to draw two commissions' worth of borders. The lines were announced on 17 August 1947, two days after independence, so many villagers did not know which country they lived in. In Punjab the line fell between Lahore and Amritsar, and with it fell the old mixed districts. Lahore went to Pakistan, and its Hindu and Sikh population fled in weeks. My view of the numbers is that the speed was the killer: a population this entangled might have needed years to separate, and it separated in about three months. Estimates of the dead run from about 200,000 to 2 million, and we truly do not know. The Military historian will show why nobody could hold the roads while this happened.

steps.title: Fourteen million on the road
steps.text: The Atlas's migration layer puts the Partition at about 14.5 million people crossing the new borders from 1947 to 1951, roughly half in each direction. In Punjab the exchange was nearly total and nearly immediate: by about 1948 west Punjab had almost no Hindus or Sikhs left, and east Punjab almost no Muslims. Columns on foot, known as kafilas, stretched up to 40 miles long, which made them easy targets. Bengal differed: the movement was slower and went on for decades, with Calcutta's Direct Action violence of August 1946 (about 4,000 dead) as the early warning. Delhi's population jumped as refugees poured in, though the Atlas figure of 13.2 million for 1948 is far above the roughly 1.4 million of the 1951 census, so treat that series as a metro-scale estimate, not a city count. The Political scientist will explain why leaders accepted this; what only the census shows is that millions were moved by fear, not by the line itself.

steps.title: The army that won in Burma, 1944
steps.text: The Indian Army was the instrument that held the Raj together, and by 1945 it was about 2.5 million volunteers, the largest all-volunteer army in history. It won Kohima and Imphal in 1944 (both on this map) with Hindu, Muslim, Sikh and Gurkha units fighting side by side under mostly British officers. That is the paradox: the force was cohesive in war, but its loyalty ran through regiment and officer, not through a state that would outlive 1947. The Economic historian will show the Bengal famine strain behind this front; what the war record adds is that Calcutta was the logistics base for Burma, so the army was stretched thin and tired when peace arrived.

steps.title: Auchinleck's neutral army splits
steps.text: On 1 July 1947 Field Marshal Auchinleck began dividing the army, and the Supreme Commander's headquarters was to wind up by 30 November. The Punjab Boundary Force, created 1 August with roughly 23,000 men (my figure, from memory) under Maj-Gen Rees, had to cover 12 districts and could not. Its units were mixed in religion, so commanders feared mutiny if they fired on co-religionists, and the force was dissolved on 31 August. Troops were also split by religion as the lines were drawn, which meant the army was being partitioned while the killing was starting. The Demographer will show who fled along the Radcliffe lines; what I add is that roads and rail, not borders, were the killing grounds, and a few thousand soldiers could not guard hundreds of kilometres of refugee columns and trains.

steps.title: Princely armies and the Kashmir tripwire
steps.text: About 565 princely states had armies of uneven quality, and several became tools or victims of communal violence. In Kashmir the Maharaja's Dogra force collapsed in October 1947 when raiders from the northwest reached Muzaffarabad, and Hari Singh signed accession so that Indian troops were flown into Srinagar on 27 October. The same state forces that were supposed to keep order in places like Patiala and Faridkot are accused by historians of taking part in attacks on Muslims, though the scale is debated. The Political scientist will explain why leaders accepted partition; what only the military view sees is that once armies were divided by religion, the first interstate war began within weeks, so the borders were fought over before they were settled.

q: How did Tokugawa Japan stay at peace for 250 years?

answer.short: Tokugawa peace was a stack of reinforcing locks, not one cause. Mountains and sea made Japan hard to conquer from outside and easy to subdivide inside. Hideyoshi's sword hunt and status edicts had already monopolized force, and Ieyasu sorted about 270 domains by trust. Alternate attendance drained daimyo budgets into roads and Edo mansions, which built a national rice-and-credit market that made peace profitable. Neo-Confucianism, temple registration and the sakoku gateways made obedience feel natural and kept outside allies out of reach. It was a bargain that left the tozama armed, which is why it lasted 250 years but ended in 1868.
answer.frame: After a century of civil war (Sengoku), the Tokugawa shogunate held Japan in internal peace from 1603 to 1868 through a mix of geography, controlled armies, wealth, and ideology that needs explaining.

plan.frame: After a century of civil war (Sengoku), the Tokugawa shogunate held Japan in internal peace from 1603 to 1868 through a mix of geography, controlled armies, wealth, and ideology that needs explaining.

steps.title: A country that is mostly mountain
steps.text: About 73% of Japan is mountain, so farmland and people sit in small pockets: the Kinai basin around Kyoto, Nara and Osaka, the Nōbi plain, and the Kantō, the biggest lowland at roughly 17,000 km². The Ōnin War (1467) burned Kyoto, and the Sengoku century that followed was fought pocket by pocket, because every valley could be sealed by a ridge and held by one lord. Sekigahara (1600) sits at the narrow neck where the Kinai and eastern routes meet. Whoever held it held the land road between the two halves of the country. Mountains explain why war was so easy to start and so hard to finish; the Tokugawa had to turn that same fragmentation into a tool.

pins.name: Sekigahara (1600 battle, the gate between east and west)

sources.cite: Conrad Totman, Early Modern Japan (1993)
Sengoku period

steps.title: Edo: a capital placed on the biggest rice plain
steps.text: Ieyasu took the Kantō in 1590 and made a marshy fishing town, Edo, his seat, then shogun in 1603. The data lists Tokyo from 1457 and ~563,000 people; Edo reached about a million in the 1700s, in a place with no ancient court and no legitimacy except Tokugawa power. The Kantō's rice, rivers and a flat harbor fed it, while the Tōkaidō and Nakasendō roads ran west through checkpoints like Hakone (the 'guns in, women out' rule against hidden weapons and fleeing hostages). Edo is far enough from Kyoto and Osaka to keep the emperor and merchants at arm's length, yet its mountain rim made it hard to attack. The Economic historian will show the rice and silver moving through it; what geography adds is that every road to Edo funneled through a few gates a guard could count.

steps.title: Moat of water: Korea Strait and Nagasaki
steps.text: The Korea Strait is about 190 km from Busan to Fukuoka, roughly 50 km of it dotted with Tsushima, and the East China Sea adds hundreds more to China. That gap was wide enough to stop the Mongols twice (1274, 1281) and Hideyoshi's army had to retreat from Korea in 1598, so Japan's coast felt safe from land powers. After 1639 the Tokugawa funneled outsiders through four 'mouths': Dutch and Chinese at Nagasaki (Dejima, 1641), Korea via Tsushima, Ryukyu via Satsuma, and Ainu via Matsumae. With the sea doing most of the policing, the army could stay home, and the Economic historian's trade controls simply close those four gates. The Political scientist's alternate attendance leans on the same geography: the long roads to Edo were chosen paths, not open frontiers.

Joseon embassies to the shogun via Tsushima

sources.cite: Ronald Toby, State and Diplomacy in Early Modern Japan (1984)

steps.title: Hideyoshi's sorting of the sword
steps.text: The map's Warring States Japan (1468-1601) carries a 29% fragility score, and that is the problem Tokugawa inherited. Hideyoshi had already cut the first piece: the 1588 sword hunt disarmed peasants, and the 1591 status edicts froze samurai, farmer and townsman in place. Samurai were pulled off the land into castle towns, so a village could no longer raise an army. The Law layer lists 'Hideyoshi bans the slave trade (1587)', a sign of how far his edicts reached into ordinary life. Tokugawa did not invent peace. He inherited a state that had already monopolized the sword.

sources.cite: Mary Elizabeth Berry, Hideyoshi (1982)
Hideyoshi Toyotomi

steps.title: Sekigahara and the three kinds of daimyo
steps.text: After winning Sekigahara in 1600, Ieyasu sorted roughly 270 domains (han) by trust. Fudai were hereditary Tokugawa vassals and got the strategic spots, the Kanto and the Tokaido road. Tozama were 'outside lords' who had submitted only after the battle, such as Satsuma, Choshu and Tosa, and they were pushed to the far periphery. Shinpan were Tokugawa cousins. The shogunate itself held about 4 million of Japan's roughly 30 million koku, with the Economic historian to show what that rice meant. The design was to put the fudai in the middle and keep the tozama far from Edo and out of national office. This worked, but it also left the shogunate's future enemies with their own armies, tax bases and borders. I would call that a bargain rather than a conquest.

sources.cite: Conrad Totman, Early Modern Japan (1993)
Tokugawa shogunate

steps.title: Sankin-kotai: the road as a leash
steps.text: Iemitsu's 1635 revision of the Buke Shohatto made alternate attendance (sankin-kotai) mandatory for all daimyo: a year in Edo, a year at home, and wives and heirs left in Edo permanently as hostages. The cost was the point. Processions could run to hundreds or thousands of retainers, and a distant lord such as Satsuma spent a large share of his budget on travel and Edo mansions. Money that might have gone into castles and arms went into roads and inns. The Economic historian will show the commerce this created; what only the law lens sees is that this was a rule, not a favor. Castles could not be repaired without permission, marriages needed approval, and the 1615 'one domain, one castle' edict cut roughly 400 fortresses down to about 170. Surveillance (ometsuke inspectors) did the rest. The pitfall is that sankin-kotai alone did not keep peace; it worked because everyone's incentives had already been altered.

steps.title: Silver, guns and the end of the war economy
steps.text: Sengoku was an arms race that Japan's economy could afford: guns reached Tanegashima in 1543 and within decades Japanese smiths made them by the thousands. By 1590 Hideyoshi had disarmed the peasantry (the 'sword hunt') and surveyed the land in rice units (kokudaka). This turned wealth into a ledger: every domain's rank was its rice yield, roughly 18 to 20 million koku nationwide by the early 1600s (my figure, beyond the map data). The sharp point is that war stopped paying once the best land was surveyed and the guns were concentrated in few hands. The Political scientist will show how the daimyo were then bound; what money adds is that peace became the profitable option.

routes.label: Silver and silk, Ming China to Japan

sources.cite: Conrad Totman, Early Modern Japan (1993)
Noel Perrin, Giving Up the Gun (1979)

steps.title: Rice in Osaka, bills in Edo
steps.text: Alternate attendance forced every daimyo to keep a household in Edo, which therefore grew to about a million people by 1700, the biggest city on Earth, with no productive hinterland to feed it. Domains paid by selling tax rice in Osaka, the 'kitchen of the realm,' where the Dojima exchange even traded rice futures; coastal shipping carried the goods to Edo. So a peace-keeping rule created a national market: daimyo needed cash, merchants lent it, and many samurai sank into debt. The Political scientist will explain the rule; what only trade sees is that it made every lord a customer of Osaka and dependent on a network that the shogunate controlled. The Geographer's sea lanes are my arteries, but the volume figures are from memory, not the map data.

steps.title: Sakoku: a closed door with a peephole
steps.text: The 1630s edicts expelled the Portuguese in 1639 and confined the Dutch to Dejima in Nagasaki, but trade never stopped; it was rationed through four gateways (Nagasaki, Tsushima, Satsuma/Ryukyu and Matsumae). Early on, Japan exported enormous silver, and the map's Silver peso chain (Potosí, Manila, Canton) shows the same metal that ran the Ming economy. Closing the door denied rebel daimyo a western arms and Christian-alliance route and gave the shogunate a monopoly on foreign profit. Japan's food and copper-based economy was mostly self-sufficient, so it could afford isolation, and later on, domestic cotton, sugar and silk replaced imports. The Historian of faith and ideas will cover the ban on Christianity; what the ledger adds is that silk and silver kept flowing without letting any daimyo get rich on it. I go beyond the map data here; Maddison-style GDP for Japan is not in it.

steps.title: Zhu Xi arrives to order a samurai state
steps.text: The map's 'Zhu Xi sets the curriculum' relay (Mount Lu 1179, Beijing 1313, Seoul 1392, Tokyo 1607) lands in Edo just as Tokugawa Ieyasu wins at Sekigahara (1600) and takes the shogun title (1603). Neo-Confucianism gave a warrior class a moral job description: the samurai become scholar-administrators, and a fixed hierarchy of warrior, farmer, artisan, merchant is presented as the order of Heaven rather than the order of Ieyasu. Hayashi Razan, recruited by Ieyasu around 1605, made this the house ideology of the shogunate, and his family ran the official academy for generations. I'm going beyond the map's data on the details, but the key move is that obedience to a lord became a cosmic principle, not just a bargain. Sengoku had shown that loyalty could be bought and sold; Zhu Xi made it a virtue.

steps.title: Kagoshima 1549 to the temple ledger
steps.text: The map's 'Christianity leaves Jerusalem' chain ends at Goa 1542 and Kagoshima 1549, when Francis Xavier landed; by 1600 Japan probably had several hundred thousand Christians. After Shimabara (1637-38), where perhaps 30,000-37,000 largely Christian rebels and families died at Hara Castle, the shogunate treated the faith as a rebellion risk and not just a heresy. Its answer was the terauke system: every household had to register at a Buddhist temple and prove it was not Christian, with annual checks and fumi-e (stepping on images of Christ or Mary) as a test. Temples thereby became a census and police arm of the state, which is why a village priest knew who was born, married, moved and died. The Economic historian will show the sakoku trade controls; what the religion lens adds is that the Dutch at Dejima were let in because they traded without preaching. Numbers for hidden Christians (Kakure Kirishitan) who survived to 1873 are rough.

steps.title: Bashō walks a country at peace
steps.text: Matsuo Bashō (1644-1694) left Edo in 1689 on the trip that became The Narrow Road to the Deep North (1694), about 2,400 km on foot over roughly five months. A poet could wander the roads, stay at inns and visit ruined battlefields such as Hiraizumi, where he wept over warriors' dreams turned to grass, only because the roads were safe. Peace here is visible as literature: ukiyo-e from Edo (from about 1670 on the map) and haiku are products of a pacified urban culture. Bashō's own samurai-born past and his grief at old war sites also show how Tokugawa order turned fighters into readers. The Geographer will show the roads and barriers; this is the sound of them being quiet.

links.why: Hideyoshi's disarmament and the move of samurai into castle towns meant daimyo could be leashed through households and money rather than fought, which let sankin-kotai work.
The rule forcing daimyo to maintain Edo households created a million-person consumer city and pushed domains to sell rice in Osaka, so a political leash turned into a national market.
The Korea Strait and sea moat let the shogunate shut the door to four controlled gateways, so no daimyo could get foreign arms or allies.
The temple registry policed belief from below while Zhu Xi ideology justified hierarchy from above, so coercion and legitimacy reinforced each other.

views.name: John Whitney Hall and the bakuhan-system school
views.claim: Peace came from a carefully balanced structure: a central shogunate directly controlling about a quarter of the rice yield, with semi-autonomous domains held in check by law and surveillance.
views.for: Buke Shohatto, sankin-kotai, the one-castle-per-domain edict and the fudai/tozama placement all fit a deliberate design.
views.against: Revisionists point out that the shogunate was weaker and more negotiated than the design suggests, and that domains had much autonomy in practice.

sources.cite: John Whitney Hall, Japan: From Prehistory to Modern Times (1970)

views.name: Conrad Totman
views.claim: Peace was partly an ecological outcome: the construction boom of the early 1600s stripped forests, and the state's later management of land and timber and the shift to a stable, low-growth economy reduced incentives for conquest.
views.for: Deforestation and later forest regulation are well documented, and land was a binding constraint in a mountainous country.
views.against: Ecology does not explain why daimyo did not fight; politics and law carry more of the weight.

sources.cite: Conrad Totman, The Green Archipelago: Forestry in Pre-Industrial Japan (1989)

views.name: Mary Elizabeth Berry
views.claim: A shared information culture of maps, guidebooks and printed directories bound a dispersed country together, so peace rested on a public that could imagine the whole realm.
views.for: Edo-period printing, travel guides and commercial publishing flourished, as the Bashō step shows roads and inns in use.
views.against: Print culture followed peace as much as it produced it, so the causal direction is hard to prove.

sources.cite: Mary Elizabeth Berry, Japan in Print: Information and Nation in the Early Modern Period (2006)

views.name: Philip Brown
views.claim: Domains were strong and the shogunate relied on their cooperation, so peace was a negotiated equilibrium and not just top-down control.
views.for: Domains ran their own taxes, courts and armies, and the tozama stayed intact until 1868.
views.against: The shogunate's power to transfer, confiscate or reduce domains in the early decades shows real central leverage.

sources.cite: Philip C. Brown, Central Authority and Local Autonomy in the Formation of Early Modern Japan (1993)

whatifs.q: What if Tokugawa Ieyasu had lost at Sekigahara in 1600?
whatifs.a: Ishida Mitsunari's western coalition would likely have kept Toyotomi Hideyori as a figurehead over a regency council of rival daimyo. With the Kantō not consolidated and no sankin-kotai or fudai/tozama design, a return to civil war is plausible, but Hideyoshi's disarmament and surveyed land would still have favored a centralized peace by someone. Peace of 250 years looks much less likely than some form of unification.

unknowns: How much alternate attendance actually cost each domain; estimates for Satsuma and others vary widely and many are from later periods
Whether the shogunate was truly dominant or merely first among powerful domains, which is the central dispute between institutional and revisionist historians
How many Christians Japan had before the 1630s and how many hidden Christians survived
Whether a peace of this length was mainly designed, or an accident of Hideyoshi's disarmament, geography and the lack of an external threat until 1853

q: Why did Qing China lose the Opium War?

answer.short: Qing China lost because Britain could pick the point of contact and Qing institutions could not respond. Steam-powered, shallow-draught ships flanked fixed forts and reached the Yangtze and Grand Canal, where a small force threatened Beijing's grain supply without ever fighting the Qing army on land. Britain's borrowing and Indian opium revenue sustained a distant war, while the Qing had a fixed land tax, a silver drain, a divided court and no foreign-policy machinery to read what Britain had become. Size mattered less than whether a state could concentrate force, money and information at one chokepoint.
answer.frame: Why a vast empire with the world's largest economy and army was beaten by a small British expeditionary force in 1839-42: technology, logistics, state capacity and strategic blindness.

steps.title: Canton: a gate at the end of a funnel
steps.text: Guangzhou (Canton, pop ~2.1 million in the Atlas) sits at the head of the Pearl River estuary, which the Qing used as a single controlled door: from 1757 foreign trade was confined there. Ships had to pass the Bocca Tigris narrows near Humen, anchor at Whampoa, and deal only with the Cohong merchants. For the Qing this was a feature: one port to tax, watch and police. But a funnel works both ways. It put the empire's richest foreign trade at the end of a waterway the Royal Navy could learn well, and the Atlas's Xi River (23.1, 112.5) and the Pearl delta's web of channels meant the forts guarded one lane among many. The Hong Kong anchorage, 100 km downstream, was a free, deep-water base outside the gate.

steps.title: Going around the forts: steamers in the delta
steps.text: Forts are built to face the channel they know, and the Humen forts faced the main one. In January 1841 British ships took Chuenpi and Taikok, then in late February, Anunghoy and the Bogue forts fell in days. The iron steamer Nemesis (shallow draft, about 6 ft) could run through shoals and creeks where junks and sailing warships could not, and it towed ships against wind and tide. By late May 1841 British forces stood at Canton's walls. Walls and batteries fixed in place lose to a force that chooses which river branch to use each day. I go slightly beyond the Atlas here: the specific fort names and the Nemesis draft come from the standard literature, not from the map's index.

steps.title: The coast is a highway, the Grand Canal a throat
steps.text: China's coast is long, but its wealth is arranged in a line from the sea inland. The Yangtze (the Atlas marks it at 30.3, 108.1) is a navigable 1,000+ km road into the core, and the Grand Canal crosses it at Zhenjiang. In July 1842 the British took Zhenjiang and cut that crossing, which carried grain tribute north to Beijing (pop ~1.1 million in the Atlas). With Nanjing under their guns, the court sued for peace: the Treaty of Nanjing, August 1842. The Porcelain Tower, 32.0, 118.8, stood in sight of the fleet. The Economic historian will show the silver; what geography adds is that a few thousand troops, 100 km apart, could squeeze the capital's food supply without ever crossing the North China Plain, where Qing cavalry would have been strongest.

steps.title: The Bogue: forts that faced the wrong way
steps.text: The map's war layer lists a cluster at the river mouth: Chuenpee (1839), the Barrier (1840), then Second Chuenpee, the Bogue, First Bar, Whampoa and Canton (all 1841). Qing coastal forts were built in the age of sail to stop ships passing at close range, with fixed, often old cast-iron guns on masonry that could not be traversed and fired solid shot at a range that a ship could simply stand off from. On 7 January 1841 and again 26 February, British ships (the steamer Nemesis, an iron-hulled 2-gun paddle vessel, notably) shelled the Bogue forts from the flank and landed marines and troops behind them, so the guns never bore on the attackers. Admiral Kwan Tianpei died at Anunghoy. The point to take is tactical: a fort works only if the enemy must come at its guns, and steam let the British choose the angle and ignore the wind and tide. The Geographer will show the estuary's shoals and channels; what the gunnery adds is that those shallows did not matter once a shallow-draught steamer could ride them and flank the batteries. I am recalling details of the forts and the 1841 action from general knowledge, beyond the map's list.

steps.title: Chusan, Chinhai, Ningpo: sea power picks the ports
steps.text: The data records Amoy (1841), Chusan (1840 and again 1841), Chinhai (1841) and Ningpo (1842): the British hopped up a coast of 18,000 km they never needed to hold. Command of the sea meant a few thousand troops (roughly 4,000 to 10,000 at various points, going from memory) could appear anywhere, while Qing garrisons of Green Standard troops and bannermen were scattered across a country to police the interior and could not concentrate. At Chusan in July 1840 the island fell after a short bombardment. In 1841 the Qing counterattacked at Ningpo and Chinhai in early 1842 and failed, losing the garrison advantage to British firepower: percussion-lock muskets and rockets against matchlocks and spears. The Economic historian will show the funding that kept the fleet in being; the lens here is that each port taken threatened the Grand Canal and the grain tribute, not the capital by land, so the Qing had to defend everywhere with an army built to defend nowhere in particular. I am going beyond the map's list on troop numbers and weapons.

steps.title: Chinkiang: cutting the Grand Canal
steps.text: The last battles in the list are Chapoo, Woosung and Chinkiang, all 1842. Woosung (16 June) opened the Yangtze, and at Chinkiang in July the Manchu garrison fought hard, with many dying and families killing themselves, but the city fell and the fleet sat on the junction with the Grand Canal, choking the grain and salt barges that fed Beijing. The ships then anchored off Nanjing, home of the Porcelain Tower in the map index, and the Treaty of Nanking (29 August 1842) followed. This is the strategic lesson: Britain never beat the Qing army in a decisive field battle, it found the artery. The Political scientist will explain why the court read this threat late; the military point is that the Qing had no navy able to contest the river, and a single chokepoint, not conquest, ended the war. The map shows Qing holding Shanhai Pass and the Hexi Corridor, the land gates of the northern frontier, and both were irrelevant here. The pass-by-pass record shows strength that faced inland, and the war arrived from the sea.

steps.title: Silver in, tea out: the Canton bargain breaks
steps.text: Under the Canton System (the Atlas hub relay shows Guangzhou as the East's trade hub 1757-1842), foreigners could only trade there, and China wanted almost nothing but silver. The Atlas's silver peso journey ends at Canton in 1760, and the Manila galleon carried Spanish silver to buy Chinese goods. Britain's problem was tea: the Atlas has tea reaching London in 1658, and by 1790 Britain was a heavy buyer with little the Qing wanted in return. That is a structural drain of silver from Britain toward China, which is exactly what opium would reverse. Figures like the size of the early tea trade I am giving from general knowledge, not the Atlas.

steps.title: The drain reverses: Bengal opium for Chinese silver
steps.text: The East India Company monopolised Bengal opium (grown around Patna, which is in the Atlas index) and let private country traders sell it off Lintin, dodging the Qing ban. Roughly 4,000 chests a year around 1800 grew to some 30,000-40,000 by the late 1830s, which is general-knowledge scholarship, not Atlas data. The money came back as silver or bills, so the flow reversed: China, a net silver importer for two centuries, began losing silver, and since taxes were paid in copper cash but silver was the large-payment currency, the silver price rose and peasants' real tax burden jumped. The Military historian will show the guns and the Political scientist the court debate; what money adds is that the Qing treasury was being hollowed out just as the crisis arrived, and Britain's India revenue was financed by the very trade Commissioner Lin burned in 1839.

steps.title: Two treasuries, one war: why Britain could outspend
steps.text: The Atlas's Maddison series shows UK GDP per capita at 3,808 dollars in 1842 against India's 944, and UK total GDP of about 104 billion against India's roughly 215 billion; the UK's output was smaller in total but four times richer per head, and it was concentrated, taxable and borrowable through London's bond market. The Atlas tech layer dates the steam engine in Manchester in 1800 and the steamship in Glasgow in 1812 and Bristol in 1838; the iron steamer Nemesis of 1840 was built on that base and was financed through the Indian revenue. Qing China had no comparable Maddison entry in my data, so I cannot give its GDP here, but its land tax was low and fixed and it had no public debt market. The Geographer will show how steamers used the estuary; the economic point is that a state able to borrow and pay for coal, iron and sailors can sustain a distant war, whereas the Qing paid 21 million silver dollars of indemnity in a Treaty of Nanjing that opened Shanghai, which the Atlas hub relay shows taking over from Canton in 1842.

steps.title: Canton System: one port, one gatekeeper
steps.text: At its 1794 peak the Qing held 12.5 million km², and my data flags it at 17% fragility, 'watch', against a 14% base rate: strong, but not unusually safe. The court treated Britain as a tributary, not a peer. Under the Canton System (from 1757) all European trade ran through Guangzhou and licensed Hong merchants, which kept foreigners under control and fed the court's revenue. When Lord Macartney came in 1793 asking for diplomatic residence and more ports, Qianlong replied that China 'possesses all things in abundance'. The institution was built to manage barbarians, not negotiate with a rival state, and a regime that has no foreign ministry has no way to learn what Britain was becoming. I'd call this reading of the evidence fairly solid; the court's inner thinking is partly inferred.

steps.title: Ban or legalize? The 1836-38 memorial war
steps.text: In 1836 the official Xu Naiji proposed legalizing opium, taxing it and banning only official and soldier use, because the ban had failed and silver was leaving. Governors then split. Huang Juezi argued for harsher prohibition, and in 1838 the Daoguang Emperor sided with the hawks and sent Lin Zexu to Canton as imperial commissioner. The deeper problem was principal-agent. Canton officials, customs men and coast guard were bribed by smugglers, so the center had no honest information and no reliable enforcement. Lin was able and moral, but moral certainty is not policy: he seized and destroyed about 20,000 chests of opium in 1839 without a plan for the military answer. The Economic historian will show the silver; what my lens adds is that the court could see the drain but could not agree on a remedy, and the choice was made by a faction, not by a tested strategy.
