steps.title: Two legal worlds collide, then Nanjing
steps.text: The Qing saw itself ruling by Confucian moral order with imperial edicts, while Britain claimed equal sovereign states bound by treaty and by trade rights. After the 1839 Lin Weixi killing and the refusal to hand over the suspect, Britain demanded extraterritoriality. Beijing's real weakness was fiscal and administrative: Qing land tax had been fixed since 1713, with provincial armies funded locally and little central pool for a coastal war. The Military historian will show why the fleet won battles; what only my lens sees is that the court lacked the money, the coordination and the information to fight a long one. By August 1842 the Treaty of Nanjing ceded Hong Kong, opened five ports, imposed 21 million silver dollars in indemnity and later added fixed tariffs. The Qing read it as a pause, which may be why reform came so slowly. Whether the court truly saw it that way is debated.

links.why: The delta's shoals and branching channels, which the forts were built around, were neutralised by shallow-draught steamers like Nemesis, which then let ships flank guns that could not traverse.
The silver drain from opium imports created the fiscal crisis that set off the Xu Naiji versus Huang Juezi debate, and the hawkish outcome sent Lin Zexu to destroy the opium without a military plan.
Britain's borrowing capacity and Indian revenue paid for coal, iron steamers and a sustained campaign, which made possible the 1842 move up the Yangtze to cut the Grand Canal.

A court that managed foreigners through one port and had no means of learning about Britain left garrisons scattered for internal policing, so a mobile sea power could take coastal ports almost at will.

whatifs.q: What if the Qing had defended the Yangtze and Grand Canal junction at Zhenjiang with a substantial concentrated force and river defences?
whatifs.a: This could have delayed the fall of Zhenjiang and raised British costs, since the Manchu garrison there fought fiercely. It probably would not have changed the outcome, because the British could still blockade and strike elsewhere along the coast and Qing finances could not sustain a long war. The terms might have been somewhat less harsh, but opium and extraterritoriality would likely have come to a head anyway.

q: How did Islam spread so fast after 632?

answer.short: Islam's conquests were fast because a newly unified Arabian coalition, mobile across the desert, struck Byzantium and Persia just after their 603-628 war had drained them and the Ghassanid and Lakhmid buffers had gone. They held what they took because the terms were light: surrender for a tax, keep your faith, keep your officials. Conversion was slower, because garrison towns and a treasury built on non-Muslim taxpayers gave rulers reason to go gradually, and Arabic, coinage and monuments persuaded over centuries. The sweep stopped where the desert ended and stone and sea began, at the Taurus, Constantinople, the Atlas and the Hindu Kush.
answer.frame: A small Arabian polity conquered Persia, Syria, Egypt and North Africa within about a century, so we must explain both the speed of conquest and the slower spread of conversion.

plan.frame: A small Arabian polity conquered Persia, Syria, Egypt and North Africa within about a century, so we must explain both the speed of conquest and the slower spread of conversion.

angles.military: Why Yarmuk and Qadisiyya fell to mobile Arab armies against drained Byzantines and Sasanians
angles.political: How caliphal institutions, tolerant terms for subjects and tribal unity held conquests together
angles.scholar: How the Quran, early faith and dhimmi status shaped gradual conversion versus conquest

steps.title: The desert is a highway, not a wall
steps.text: Medina sits about 1,200 km from Damascus and about 1,300 km from Ctesiphon, but the Syrian Desert (and the Arabian interior) was home ground to the armies that crossed it. Camels carry a rider 50-70 km a day, go days without water, and eat desert scrub, so the ground that stopped Byzantine and Sasanian armies' supply trains did not stop Arab columns. Byzantium and Persia had long left the desert's edge to Arab client kingdoms (the Ghassanids and the Lakhmids), and both had been weakened or dismantled by about 602-630. So the Arabs met few buffers on the open frontier. I am confident of the broad logic; individual march distances here are my rough estimates.

Iraq front: Najd to the Euphrates near Hira

sources.cite: Hugh Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)

steps.title: Two empires, both cores on the desert's edge
steps.text: Here the map shows what only geography makes obvious: Damascus, Jerusalem, Antioch and Ctesiphon all lie within a few hundred km of the desert edge. Ctesiphon (33.1N, 44.6E) was a Sasanian capital on the Tigris, in flat alluvial plain with no mountain barrier between it and the Arabian steppe; the Zagros stood behind it, not in front. The Military historian will explain why Yarmuk and Qadisiyya were lost; what the terrain adds is that the loser had nowhere to fall back except into the mountains. Ctesiphon fell about 637, and the Sasanian court retreated east over the Zagros, losing the rich Mesopotamian tax base.

Euphrates to Ctesiphon, the Persian heart

Wikipedia: Muslim conquest of Persia

steps.title: Where the desert ran out: Nile, Atlas and Hindu Kush
steps.text: The same logic ran west along the dry Libyan and Maghreb coastal strip, with Alexandria falling around 641-642 and Kairouan founded in 670 as a desert-edge base for Ifriqiya. Carthage fell in 698. Armies crossed Gibraltar in 711, only about 14 km of water. East, the chain of oases (Merv, Herat, Bukhara, Samarkand) acted as stepping stones for camel and horse columns. Limits showed up where the desert ended: the Taurus and Cilician Gates stopped Syria-based armies from taking Anatolia, the Atlas and Pyrenees slowed the west, and the Hindu Kush and Central Asian steppe slowed the east. The Economic historian will show the silver that the oasis towns carried; what geography adds is that conquest followed the dry belt and stalled where it ended.

steps.title: Two empires bled each other dry
steps.text: The map shows 626 CE, Sasanians and Avars besieging Constantinople, then 627 Nineveh, where Heraclius broke Persian power. After 26 years of war (602-628) both empires were exhausted, and the Sasanians then tore themselves apart in a civil war (628-632), with the 629 Siege of Ctesiphon in our data. The Arabs did not beat two healthy giants. They hit two armies that had just beaten each other, with garrisons thinned, frontier Arab buffer allies such as the Ghassanids unpaid or disbanded, and treasuries empty. I'm going beyond the map in saying Byzantine pay arrears mattered; it is commonly argued, not measured.

sources.cite: Walter Kaegi, Heraclius: Emperor of Byzantium (2003)
Hugh Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)

steps.title: Yarmuk and Qadisiyya: mobility wins
steps.text: The records show a chain: Ullais, Ayn al-Tamr and al-Anbar in 633, then Ajnadayn, Damascus and Fahl in 634-635, before the big two in 636. Arab armies were perhaps 20-40,000 at Yarmuk, small, camel-borne, and able to retreat into desert where heavy Byzantine and Persian forces could not follow. They fought where they chose, and Khalid's reported march across the Syrian desert in 634 is the famous example. Sasanian cataphracts and war elephants needed fixed supply; at Qadisiyya the Arabs stood at the desert edge with a line of retreat and Ctesiphon fell in 637. Numbers in the sources are inflated and disputed, so treat them as order of magnitude. Nahavand in 642 finished the state, not the war.

steps.title: Where the sweep stopped: walls and sea
steps.text: The same system met limits. Constantinople in 717 held, because the Bosporus and Dardanelles stayed Byzantine in our chokepoint table at 622, 686 and 750 alike, and walls plus Greek fire neutralised an army with no navy of equal weight. Anatolia's Cilician Gates stayed Byzantine too, so mountains and fortress-themes stopped the raiders. In the west, Guadalete 711 collapsed a Visigothic kingdom, but Tours 732 was a raid at long range. Open ground favoured Arab mobility; stone and sea did not. The Economic historian will show the silver; what the plague data adds is whether depopulated frontiers made garrisons even thinner, which I cannot prove from battles alone.

steps.title: Two exhausted empires, one tribal coalition
steps.text: Muhammad's death in 632 left a polity that could have dissolved, and the first institutional feat was Abu Bakr's Ridda wars (632-633), which forced Arabian tribes back into a single tax-and-loyalty system. That unity is the core of the political case: the map shows Sasanian fragility at 20% (watch) and Eastern Roman 15%, both drained by their war of 603-628. The Ghassanids and Lakhmids, the two Arab client buffers that Rome and Persia used to police the desert, both end in 633 in the data, so the frontier guards vanished just as the armies arrived. The Military historian will show how Yarmuk and Qadisiyya were won; what this lens adds is that the winners had a fresh, unified command and the losers had lost their border buffers and their own legitimacy.

routes.label: Ridda wars then conquest of Syria and Iraq

sources.cite: Hugh Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)

steps.title: Surrender terms: pay, and keep your faith
steps.text: Conquest held because it was cheap to live under. Cities such as Jerusalem (c. 637) and Alexandria (642) surrendered on written terms: a poll tax (jizya) and land tax (kharaj) in exchange for protection and the right to keep worship and local officials. Rulers did not rebuild bureaucracies; Greek and Persian clerks kept the same registers for decades. Arab soldiers lived apart in garrison towns (Basra and Kufa in Iraq, Fustat in Egypt), paid from tax stipends under Umar's diwan, so they could not become landlords and local elites kept their estates. Converts at first still had to be attached to an Arab tribe as clients, so rulers had a fiscal reason to slow mass conversion. The Historian of faith and ideas will trace belief; the tax ledger shows why many subjects had little incentive to resist and why conversion came gradually over centuries.

routes.label: Terms of surrender and tribute

sources.cite: Hugh Kennedy, The Great Arab Conquests (2007)
Hugh Kennedy, The Prophet and the Age of the Caliphates (1986)

steps.title: From civil war to the Umayyad machine
steps.text: The system nearly broke in the First Fitna (656-661) after Uthman's murder, and again in the Second Fitna (680-692), yet it recovered because the state became more institutional. Mu'awiya made Damascus the capital in 661, and Abd al-Malik (685-705) introduced Arabic as the administrative language and minted Islamic coinage, replacing Byzantine and Sasanian types. The data shows the result: the Umayyad Caliphate peaks at 9.879 million km² in 732 with 4% fragility (calm), while the Sasanian Empire disappears after 643 in the map data. Yet the calm score hides the weakness: non-Arab converts (mawali) were still taxed and ranked below Arabs, and that grievance powered the Abbasid revolution of 750. Expansion was fast because the institutions were light; the empire ended because they were not inclusive enough.

steps.title: A prophet's town becomes a capital
steps.text: The Atlas dates Muhammad 570–632 and the Hijra of 622 as year 1 of the Islamic calendar. By his death most of Arabia had pledged allegiance, so the armies that left in 633 carried one shared creed and one shared obligation, not a loose raiding confederation. The Quran, gathered into a single codex under Caliph Uthman (about 650, the Atlas places it at Medina), gave the new community a fixed text that could be recited anywhere. That portability matters: a soldier in Syria and a soldier in Iraq heard the same words. The Political scientist will show how the caliphate held tribes together; what the faith adds is that unity was ideological as well as tribal.

routes.label: Hijra, Mecca to Medina (622)

steps.title: Conquest is not conversion
steps.text: The Sasanian Empire (224–651) ended and the Byzantines lost Syria and Egypt, yet the people stayed Zoroastrian, Christian and Jewish for generations. Arab garrisons lived apart in new towns such as Basra, Kufa and Fustat, so the faith spread slowly by contact rather than by force. Dhimmi status let Christians, Jews and Zoroastrians keep their worship in exchange for the jizya poll tax, which meant the state had a financial reason not to rush conversion. The Quran's recognition of 'People of the Book' made that arrangement religiously defensible. The Military historian will show why the armies won; what only this lens sees is that the Umayyad treasury, run on non-Muslim taxpayers, was a quiet brake on conversion. Estimates of when Muslims became a majority in Iran, Egypt or Syria (Richard Bulliet's conversion curve points to the 9th and 10th centuries) are modelled, not counted.

routes.label: Islam from Mecca to Jerusalem to Damascus

sources.cite: Richard Bulliet, Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period (1979)
Fred Donner, Muhammad and the Believers (2010)

steps.title: A new faith finds its own look
steps.text: The Atlas's Early Islamic style begins in 661 at Jerusalem, and its first great monument is the Dome of the Rock, finished in 691 under Abd al-Malik. Its inscriptions are among the earliest Quranic texts in public, and they argue with Christian belief about Jesus in the very city of the Holy Sepulchre. The Great Mosque of Damascus, built by al-Walid I in the early 700s on a Christian church precinct, used Byzantine mosaicists to say the new faith had arrived to stay. Around the same time Arabic replaced Greek and Persian in the administration, which tied prestige and careers to the language of the Quran. Buildings, coins and paperwork persuaded more slowly than armies, but they persuaded for longer.

sources.cite: Oleg Grabar, The Formation of Islamic Art (1973)

links.why: The Byzantine-Sasanian exhaustion of 602-628 left thin garrisons and unpaid buffers, so small camel-borne Arab armies could win decisive battles at Yarmuk and Qadisiyya.
The Ridda wars forced the tribes into one tax-and-loyalty system, and the shared creed and fixed Quran gave that unity an ideological core that the armies carried abroad.
Surrender terms taxing non-Muslims funded the garrisons, which gave the state a fiscal reason to slow conversion, so conquest produced a Muslim ruling class long before a Muslim majority.
Abd al-Malik's Arabic administration and Islamic coinage, with monuments like the Dome of the Rock, turned a conquering army into a lasting civilisation and tied careers to Arabic.

views.name: Fred Donner
views.claim: The conquests were driven by a monotheist movement of believers organised around piety and the Quran, not just by tribal booty-seeking.
views.for: Early sources stress a community of Believers that included Christians and Jews, and the Ridda wars restored a unified political-religious order.
views.against: Later Arabic accounts were written generations afterwards, and tribal and material motives are well attested.

sources.cite: Fred Donner, The Early Islamic Conquests (1981)
Fred Donner, Muhammad and the Believers (2010)

views.name: Walter Kaegi
views.claim: Byzantium fell short in Syria and Egypt through overstretch, weak finances and poor frontier arrangements after the Persian war, more than through Arab superiority in arms.
views.for: The 602-628 war, the loss of buffers and thin garrisons are well documented, and Arab armies were small.
views.against: Byzantium recovered Anatolia and held Constantinople, so collapse was not inevitable, and sources on numbers are weak.

sources.cite: Walter Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)

views.name: Richard Bulliet
views.claim: Conversion to Islam was gradual: Muslims became a majority in Iran, Egypt and Syria only around the 9th and 10th centuries.
views.for: His curve is built from name-change data in biographical dictionaries, and it fits the fiscal incentives for slow conversion.
views.against: Name-based dating is a model, not a count, and it is more reliable for Iran than for Egypt or Syria.

sources.cite: Richard Bulliet, Conversion to Islam in the Medieval Period (1979)

whatifs.q: What if Heraclius and Khosrow II had made peace in 603 and never fought the 26-year war?
whatifs.a: Both empires would likely have kept full treasuries, paid frontier allies, and held stronger garrisons, so the early Arab raids might have been repelled or limited to the fringe. Arabia's unity would still have projected power, but a conquest of Syria, Egypt and Iraq within ten years looks far less likely.

q: Why did Buddhism almost vanish from India but thrive in East Asia?

answer.short: Indian Buddhism was a monastery-centred faith that depended on merchant gifts and the favour of a few kings, with no state church and little village ritual to fall back on. Between about 500 and 1200 the trade hubs moved, Brahmin-and-temple Hinduism took over local patronage and absorbed the Buddha, and the last great patron (the Pala dynasty) shrank, so the Ghurid raids of the 1190s hit a thinned, concentrated institution. In East Asia the same religion met strong bureaucratic states that licensed and rebuilt it, a Chinese-language scripture tradition, cheap copying, and portable practices (Chan, Pure Land, Zen) that survived when estates were seized. Disagreement: the invasion-as-cause story is weaker than the slow loss of patrons, and the evidence favours the slow decline with the raids as the final blow.
answer.frame: Buddhism lost its institutional base in India (monasteries, royal patronage, merchant support) between roughly 500 and 1300 CE, while in China, Korea and Japan it won state patronage, adapted to local culture and gained new roots.

steps.title: Nalanda: a Buddhist heartland on a river plain
steps.text: Buddhism was born in the middle Ganges plain, and its geography was its weakness as well as its strength. Nalanda (25.1N, 85.4E, founded about 427 CE), Patna and Varanasi sit within roughly 200 km of each other on the Indo-Gangetic Plain, a rice-rich floodplain that fed thousands of monks. But that meant the faith's institutions were concentrated in one flat, reachable region, with no mountain redoubt. When Ghaznavid and then Ghurid cavalry came down through the Khyber Pass from the 1000s, and Nalanda fell around 1200, the whole core sat in the open. The Political scientist will explain who patronised it; what the map adds is that a faith clustered on one plain can be cut off by one invasion corridor.

steps.title: The Himalayan wall and the Silk Road conveyor
steps.text: The Himalayas and Tibetan Plateau (average about 4,500 m) blocked direct travel, so Buddhism went around them: from Gandhara through the Khyber Pass and Bamiyan (where Buddhas of 55 m and 38 m were carved about 570 CE), across the Pamirs and Tarim oases, through the Jade Gate and the Hexi Corridor to Chang'an, a trek of some 4,000 km. Oasis towns such as Dunhuang were strings of paid-for monasteries, and caravans needed monks as translators, bankers and safe lodging. The Economic historian will show the silver; geography's point is that each oasis was a cell that could be funded locally. Sea monsoon sailing (southwest winds out, northeast winds home) carried monks like Faxian, who returned from Sri Lanka by sea about 412 CE, to Guangzhou. I go beyond the data on Dunhuang and Kashgar coordinates, which are pinned, not indexed.

sources.cite: Xinru Liu, Ancient India and Ancient China: Trade and Religious Exchanges, AD 1-600 (1988)

steps.title: Seas that moved the faith, steppes that cut it off
steps.text: East Asia is a set of sea-connected, farmland-rich cores: from Gyeongju across the Korea Strait (about 200 km with Tsushima as a stepping stone) to Nara and Kyoto, Buddhism travelled with writing, tile and temple building, so each court could copy Chang'an's grid. India's northwest entry points were different: Khyber and Bolan passes work both ways, and Islam moved in, with Merv, Herat and Bukhara already Muslim by the 700s to 900s and Delhi a Sultanate seat from 1206. The Silk Road's Buddhist oases were Islamised and Bamiyan became a frontier statue. The Economic historian will show how trade shifted; the plague data I'd want to cross-check is the 1348 mortality, since the Black Death arrived along the same steppe-to-oasis corridors, but I have no direct Buddhist-monastery death figures. Geography's verdict: East Asia's coasts and straits made importing Buddhism safe; India's passes made losing it easy.

steps.title: Monasteries as merchant banks
steps.text: Early Indian Buddhism was a business partnership. Monks could not farm or trade, so they lived off lay gifts, and the biggest givers were merchants and guilds: inscriptions at Sanchi, Karle and other Western Ghats caves record traders, bankers and artisans paying for stupas and cells. Their money flowed along the Indian Ocean monsoon route (pepper, textiles, gold, ivory, with Muziris as hub from 100 BCE) and the Silk Roads, which the Kushan Empire (30-375 CE) straddled. Monasteries sat on those routes as warehouses, rest-houses and lenders, so Buddhism's footprint matched the map of trade. That works only while trade passes your door; the model carries its own weak point.

steps.title: When the hubs moved and the land grants went elsewhere
steps.text: Between 500 and 900 the money moved. Long-distance trade shifted to Baghdad (hub 800-1000), Palembang (680-1025) and Guangzhou (700-879), mostly carried by Arab, Persian and South-East Asian ships, and Muslim merchants gained ground in the western ports. Buddhist monasteries lost their merchant donors just as rulers rewarded Brahmins with land grants (a pattern historians see across post-Gupta India). Great monasteries like Nalanda (427-1200) came to live on royal village grants, which made them rich but dependent on a handful of kings. Hindu temples, by contrast, were embedded in local landholding and village life. The Geographer will show where the sea lanes ran; what the ledger adds is that a monastery tied to one king's revenue is a single point of failure. Evidence for the exact causal weight is debated, and I go beyond the data here.

steps.title: China: paper, printing and monastic capital
steps.text: In East Asia Buddhism grew its own economy. Chinese monasteries ran mills, oil presses, pawnshops and the inalienable estates that Tang and Song records describe, making them rich enough to draw hostile attention, such as the Huichang suppression of 845. Yet the technology layer shows the faith riding new tools: papermaking reaches Luoyang by 105, Seoul by 400 and Nara by 610, and the earliest dated printed book, the Diamond Sutra, comes from Dunhuang in 868, with printing at Kaifeng by 1040. A religion that could copy scripture cheaply had a durable base, while Indian Buddhism's centres, such as Nalanda, were concentrated and could be destroyed in one raid around 1200. The Political scientist will explain why the courts patronised it; the money view adds that diffusion across many local estates survived what concentration could not.

steps.title: Ashoka's edicts: a state discovers a moral language
steps.text: The Maurya Empire peaked at 3.946 Mkm² in 256 BCE, and the Edicts of Ashoka (-260) are the oldest case in the data of a ruler using Buddhist-flavored dhamma as a tool of governance. Ashoka ruled from Patna over a subcontinent of hundreds of peoples and needed a legitimacy language that no single caste or cult owned. The catch is that this was patronage, not establishment: Ashoka also supported Brahmans and other sects, and the Mauryas were gone by 171 BCE (model fragility 15%, 'watch'). So Indian Buddhism was born with a royal sponsor but never with a state church, which meant it lived on the goodwill of each successive dynasty.

steps.title: East Asian courts buy a bureaucratic religion
steps.text: Here the same religion met a different state type. After Han fell (237 CE in the data) China spent centuries divided, and rulers like the Northern Wei and Liang (510-560, peak 2.362 Mkm²) used monasteries for registering population, legitimizing non-Han rule, and ritual protection of the realm. Tang (peak 8.731 Mkm² in 661) then built the Tang Code (624) around a centralized bureaucracy that could license, tax and supervise the sangha rather than compete with it. Korea (Gyeongju) and Japan took the package whole: the Taiho Code (701) set up Nara (710) as a Tang-style capital with state-sponsored temples. The key is that a strong central state wanted a universal, literate, scripture-based institution and had the administrative reach to hold it in a harness. I'm going beyond the map data here for Northern Wei and Nara temple networks; the Historian of faith and ideas will show how Chan and Pure Land made it local.

routes.label: Buddhism as state technology: China to Korea to Japan

Erik Zürcher, The Buddhist Conquest of China (1959)

steps.title: India fragments, patrons scatter, raiders finish the job
steps.text: India never got a single Tang-style center after the Guptas (324-554, peak 2.495 Mkm², fragility 24%, 'fragile'). Pala (750-1168, 1.362 Mkm²) was the last big Buddhist patron, and its small Bengal-Bihar base meant Nalanda (427-1200) depended on one shrinking dynasty while Hindu courts endowed temples and Brahmans, who offered rulers caste-based legitimacy and rituals Buddhism could not. When Ghurid armies (1152-1209) and the Delhi Sultanate (1206) swept the Gangetic plain, monasteries, being walled, wealthy and conspicuous, were the targets, and a sangha with no lay ritual base had nowhere to retreat. The Economic historian will show the silver and land grants that dried up; what the plague data adds is a question of timing, which I flag rather than claim. Politically, a faith dependent on a few big institutions, with no state to rebuild them, dies when they burn, whereas in East Asia the state itself rebuilt them.

steps.title: Nalanda: the university that carried the faith
steps.text: Nalanda (founded 427 CE) is the whole Indian problem in one building. Xuanzang studied there from 637 and carried home 657 texts, so the knowledge was safe in China even as it became fragile at home. Indian Buddhism had concentrated its life in a few great monasteries that depended on kings and donors, so it had little roots in village ritual. Meanwhile Shankara (c. 700-750) and Advaita Vedanta, based at Kalady, answered Madhyamaka (Nagarjuna, c. 150-250) on its own ground of emptiness and non-dual reality. Hindu temple worship (the Hindu temple style begins c. 500 at Deogarh) absorbed the Buddha as an avatar of Vishnu, so a householder had no reason to leave for a separate faith. The Economic historian will show the monastery land grants; what the ideas lens adds is that when patrons moved, the rival schools already offered the same insights without the monks. Nalanda was sacked around 1197, but it was a deathblow to an already thinning body, not the cause.

steps.title: Translation made Buddhism Chinese
steps.text: Kumarajiva (344-413), from Kucha, reached Chang'an (Xi'an) in 401 and his Chinese Lotus Sutra of 406 became the best-loved scripture of East Asian Buddhism. Faxian had walked to India (399-412) to fetch monastic rules, showing that Chinese demand pulled texts east. Translation used Daoist vocabulary at first and gave Buddhism a home idiom, which India could not offer once Sanskrit scholasticism became specialist. The route runs on to Gyeongju (527) and Nara (552), where Buddhism arrived as a package of writing, temples and court ritual. The Political scientist will explain why courts wanted this package; what only the ideas lens sees is that the package had a local-language form.

routes.label: The Buddha goes east: Taxila, Kucha, Xi'an, Gyeongju, Nara

steps.title: Chan, Pure Land and Zen: faith without a monastery estate
steps.text: Chan (c. 520 at Shaolin, credited to the semi-legendary Bodhidharma) stressed meditation and teacher-to-student lineage over scripture and land. Then in the 840s the Tang crackdown destroyed monastic estates, yet Chan and Pure Land chanting survived because they needed only a teacher or a name. Eisai brought Rinzai Zen to Japan in 1191 and Dōgen founded Sōtō Zen after studying at Tiantong, so East Asian Buddhism renewed itself by moving. India's Buddhism, tied to a few big monasteries, had no equally portable practice. I am unsure how much Indian practice was ever as institution-bound as the sources suggest, since most Indian Buddhist records were lost. Nor can I say Pure Land numbers before 1300.

routes.label: Eisai and Dōgen bring Zen from Song China to Japan

links.why: Buddhism's merchant-funded model tied it to trade routes, so when long-distance trade shifted to Baghdad, Palembang and Guangzhou and the land-grant economy took over, its original donor base thinned and left it dependent on royal grants.
Reliance on a few royal land grants made Nalanda a single point of failure, so when the Pala shrank and the Ghurids arrived there was no wider patron base to rebuild it.

Tang-style states could license and supervise the sangha, which made monasteries rich targets (the 845 suppression), but Chan and Pure Land survived the seizure of estates because they needed only a teacher or a name.

A faith clustered on one open plain was exposed to the Khyber and Bolan corridors, the same passes through which Islam spread into the Silk Road oases, whereas sea-separated Korea and Japan could import Buddhism on their own terms.

views.name: Gradual decline thesis
views.claim: Indian Buddhism declined mainly through loss of lay and royal patronage and competition from Brahmanical temple Hinduism, and the Turkic raids only finished a weakened institution.
views.for: Merchant donations fell as trade routes moved; land grants favoured Brahmins and temples; Hindu traditions absorbed the Buddha as an avatar; Buddhism had few village rituals.
views.against: Regional evidence is patchy, and Buddhism persisted in Bengal, Kashmir and parts of the south long after 500, so a uniform decline is hard to show.

sources.cite: Richard Gombrich, Theravada Buddhism: A Social History from Ancient Benares to Modern Colombo, 1988
Romila Thapar, Early India: From the Origins to AD 1300, 2002

views.name: Invasion thesis
views.claim: The destruction of the great monasteries by Turkic armies in the 1190s-1200s broke a faith that relied on a few big institutions.
views.for: Nalanda, Odantapuri and Vikramashila fell around 1193-1203; Tibetan sources such as Dharmasvamin (about 1234) describe monks fleeing, and walled monasteries were conspicuous.
views.against: Decline was already under way, the dating of destruction rests on a few later sources, and Hindu temples were also looted, so raids alone do not explain why Buddhism did not recover.

sources.cite: Minhaj-i-Siraj, Tabaqat-i-Nasiri, c. 1260
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nalanda

views.name: Erik Zürcher
views.claim: Buddhism succeeded in China by translating itself into native idioms and gaining elite and state sponsorship.
views.for: Early Daoist-influenced translation, Kumarajiva's Chinese scriptures, and court sponsorship under the Northern Wei and Tang.
views.against: The Huichang suppression of 845 and Confucian hostility show that acceptance was limited and could be reversed.

sources.cite: Erik Zürcher, The Buddhist Conquest of China, 1959

whatifs.q: What if Nalanda had not fallen around 1200 and the Pala-style royal patronage had survived in Bihar?
whatifs.a: A university and a few monasteries would probably have survived longer, but the slow loss of village and merchant support suggests Buddhism would likely have stayed a minority tradition, perhaps like Jainism, which also lost royal backing but survived through lay merchant communities. I am less sure of the details, and this is an informed guess.

unknowns: How much each cause weighed (patronage loss, Hindu absorption, invasion), since the Indian evidence is thin and later Tibetan accounts are partly retrospective
Whether Buddhism had weaker village roots in India or if those records simply did not survive
Exact dates and extent of the destruction at Nalanda and other monasteries
The role of the Black Death or other epidemics in monastic communities, which cannot be measured with current data
Pure Land and Chan numbers before 1300

q: Did printing change Europe faster than it changed China and Korea?

answer.short: Yes in tempo, no in total effect. Europe's change was sharper over about 50 years (presses in some 250 towns by 1500) because an alphabet of dozens of sorts, paper made cheap after 1276, a labour shortage after the Black Death, a patchwork of rulers and a contested Bible all met at once. China and Korea had printed for centuries before (Diamond Sutra 868, Jikji 1377), so print deepened existing exam, Buddhist and state systems rather than shocking them; Korea's metal type was a ministry's tool with small runs, and Hangul (1446) met elite resistance.
answer.frame: Compare how fast movable-type printing (Gutenberg c.1450) versus older woodblock and Korean metal-type printing (Jikji 1377) reshaped literacy, books, religion and power in each region, and why the effects differed in speed.

plan.frame: Compare how fast movable-type printing (Gutenberg c.1450) versus older woodblock and Korean metal-type printing (Jikji 1377) reshaped literacy, books, religion and power in each region, and why the effects differed in speed.

angles.economist: Compare book costs, paper, press economics and market size: alphabet versus Chinese characters, Korean state versus commercial printing.

steps.title: Paper is the real cost cut
steps.text: Before any press, the economics of the book changed with paper. Parchment for one Bible took the skins of roughly 200 sheep or calves; rag paper, made at Fabriano from 1276 with water-driven stamping mills and gelatin sizing, cost perhaps a sixth as much as parchment per sheet by the 1400s (my estimate, not in the Atlas data). Paper had reached Baghdad by 794 and Xàtiva by 1056, so Europe was 1,100 years behind China (Luoyang 105) and Korea (Seoul c.400). Our map's year is 1348: the plague has killed a third or more of Europe, labour is scarce, and wages are rising, which makes copyists dearer and pushes towards a machine that replaces them. The Demographer will give the reader count; what my lens adds is that cheap paper had to come first.

routes.label: Paper west: Baghdad to Cairo to Xàtiva to Fabriano

sources.cite: Tsien Tsuen-Hsuin, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 part 1: Paper and Printing (1985)
Jonathan Bloom, Paper Before Print (2001)

steps.title: Why Gutenberg's alphabet paid and Cheongju's didn't scale
steps.text: Movable type is a fixed-cost bet: you cast a font, then amortise it over print runs. An alphabet needs about 50 to 100 sorts (letters, capitals, ligatures); a Chinese font needs thousands of characters, each in many copies, so the setup cost was far higher while carving one woodblock per page cost little and allowed cheap reprints on demand, with no standing type to store. Kaifeng 1040 (Bi Sheng) and Cheongju 1377 (the Jikji) came 70 to 410 years before Mainz 1450, but in Korea metal type served the state (the Joseon bureau for casting type, founded 1403), with small runs of tens of copies. Gutenberg's added pieces were an oil-based ink, a screw press and a hand mould for exact type, all aimed at selling many copies to a market. By 1500 an estimated 20 million books had been printed in Europe in about 1,000 presses' output (Febvre and Martin's figures; treat as approximate), while the Joseon state's output was tiny by comparison. Woodblock China, though, printed vast amounts cheaply: Song Hangzhou and Kaifeng publishers were commercial, so China was not slow, just on a different cost curve. The Political scientist will show who held the licences; I'm showing why the unit economics differed.

steps.title: Press towns follow the money
steps.text: The Atlas's press dates run Mainz 1450, Cologne 1465, Rome 1467, Venice 1469, Paris 1470, Kraków 1473, Westminster 1476: 20 cities in 26 years, following capital and credit, not courts. Venice, the trade hub from 1204 to 1500, had printed some 150 presses' worth of titles by 1500 (rough, from the Incunabula record) and drove prices down; Italian printers over-produced and several went bankrupt, including Gutenberg's own financier Fust's rivals. England's per-capita income stood at 1,683 dollars in 1450 and 1,697 in 1500 (Maddison), so books got cheaper while incomes were flat: a large real fall in price. Eastern Asia needed no such arbitrage because the cheap woodblock already existed. Dominant effect: Europe's change was faster in a short window of about 50 years, but China's had been running since 868 (Dunhuang), so total effect is not comparable cleanly. The Political scientist will tell why Venice's republic let it run free.

routes.label: Press spread: Mainz to Cologne to Rome to Venice to Paris

steps.title: Readers were in China's cities, not Europe's
steps.text: Before Gutenberg, the demand for print already sat in big cities. The Atlas records Xi'an at 3.1 million in 1234, Hangzhou at 1.3 million, and Luoyang at 1.7 million (these are model estimates and I treat them as rough, since Song-era census figures are contested). Paris, the largest city of the Latin West in my data, had 134,000 and London 60,000. Woodblock printing had been commercial in Song China since the 10th century, and the Song state printed the Confucian classics for an exam-taking class. So China had a dense urban reading public to serve a full 200 years before Europe did. Print here deepened an existing system; it did not start a new one.

pins.name: Song printing hubs: Hangzhou and Chengdu area

sources.cite: Tsien Tsuen-Hsuin, Paper and Printing, in Needham, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 part 1 (1985)
Chandler, Four Thousand Years of Urban Growth (1987)

steps.title: Gutenberg's Europe: small towns, huge speed
steps.text: Europe's cities were small, Paris 134,000 in 1234 and Venice 84,000, but they were close together and linked by trade. The Economic historian will show the silver and press costs; what the plague data adds is the demand side. The Black Death (the map is at 1348) killed perhaps a third or more of Europeans, which raised wages, pushed up literate urban craftsmen's share of the population, and left scribes scarce. From Mainz, presses reached Cologne by 1464, Venice by 1469 and Paris by 1470. Estimates of about 20 million volumes printed by 1500 are widely cited, though the exact figure is uncertain. That is a very fast spread among a small number of readers, with an alphabet of a few dozen letters to cast.

routes.label: Press towns spread from Mainz along Rhine and trade roads

sources.cite: Eisenstein, The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979)
Febvre and Martin, The Coming of the Book (1958)
Buringh and van Zanden, Charting the Rise of the West, Journal of Economic History (2009)

steps.title: Korea's early metal type, few readers to reach
steps.text: The Jikji, a Buddhist anthology printed with movable metal type at Heungdeok Temple in 1377, predates Gutenberg by about 70 years. Yet it did not trigger a mass shift. Print runs were small, work was done by temples and the state, and the Atlas gives no Korean city above the largest-city lists for this period, so I cannot give a reader count; I'd guess the literate population stayed a small elite until Hangul in 1446. The Historian of faith and ideas will show what was printed. My point is that speed depends on market size: Korea had early technology but a thin, state-bound readership. Rule of thumb: Europe's speed came from many small, competing city markets, China's from huge ones with an older print habit, Korea's from the state alone.

sources.cite: Jikji (Korean Buddhist text, 1377), en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jikji

steps.title: 868: a printed sutra, sealed in a cave
steps.text: The Diamond Sutra of 868 CE, found sealed at Dunhuang, is the oldest dated printed book in the world, and it is a religious object: printing in East Asia began as merit-making, with Buddhists multiplying sutras and charms by woodblock. By the Song, Confucian classics and examination texts were printed too, and Neo-Confucianism (Zhu Xi, White Deer Grotto 1179) rode on that supply. Korea carried the same logic furthest: the Tripitaka Koreana carved in the 13th century (some 80,000 blocks, from memory) and the Jikji of 1377, the oldest surviving book in metal movable type. So by 1348, the year on the map, East Asia already had five centuries of print, and the Black Death-year Europe still copied everything by hand. The Economic historian will show why characters favoured carved blocks over type; what only the ideas lens sees is that the first printed texts were fixed, sacred and canonical, which made print an instrument of orthodoxy rather than disruption.

steps.title: 1517: the Theses go viral
steps.text: Europe's printing was young and its effect was explosive because it landed on a contested text. The Gutenberg Bible (Mainz, 1455) was followed by Erasmus's Greek New Testament (Basel, 1516), which Luther used for his German version; the Ninety-five Theses of 1517 were reprinted across Germany within weeks, and Luther's New Testament of 1522 shaped modern German. Historians count several thousand Reformation pamphlet editions in the 1520s, with Luther the dominant author (my figure, from memory, not the map). Compare Korea: a Buddhist-Confucian state used print to copy sanctioned texts, with no rival church to answer. Printing in Europe split authority, in East Asia it mostly deepened it.

steps.title: 1443-1600: Hangul and the limits of print
steps.text: King Sejong's Hangul (promulgated 1446) was a literacy technology as radical as the press, a 28-letter alphabet in place of thousands of characters, yet elite yangban largely resisted it, and its wide use waited centuries. China meanwhile saw commercial woodblock publishing boom in the Ming: Journey to the West appeared in Nanjing in 1592, a vernacular comic epic for a mass market. So speed differed by what each system was doing: Europe's change was loud, quick and doctrinal; East Asia's was earlier, broader and steadier, but tied to examinations and the state. The Political scientist will show who held the censor's pen; the open question is whether a Hangul-style script, printed freely, could have produced a Korean Luther.

steps.title: Korea's state press: the Jikji and the ministry
steps.text: Korea shows the other pole of control: the state or its clients held the type. The Jikji was printed in 1377 at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju, a Buddhist monastery, but the Joseon court then took over metal type: the Bureau of Publication (Jujaso) was set up in 1403 and cast thousands of bronze characters. The Atlas's own Gwageo examinations (958) explain the demand: a literate bureaucracy recruited by exam needed standard texts, and the court was the main buyer. Printing was fast and sophisticated, but it was a ministry's tool, not a market's. Hangul (1443) fits the same pattern: a king's project, with officials like Choe Malli objecting. I am going beyond the map's records on Cheongju and the Jujaso; confidence is lower on exact dates.

sources.cite: Thomas Francis Carter, The Invention of Printing in China and Its Spread Westward (1925)
Jikji

steps.title: China's printers worked inside an empire
steps.text: Woodblock printing was old when Europe began: Tang-era print precedes 868, and the Northern Song (961-1138, peak 2.8 Mkm², fragility only 14%) used the state's Directorate of Education to print the classics and the Confucian canon. Printing there was cheap and already everywhere, so there was no sudden shock. The Ming (1368-1644) then wrote control into law: the Great Ming Code of 1397 sits on the Atlas's law layer, and it penalised certain forbidden writings. One empire meant one censor, one exam syllabus and one market of readers, which made printing an instrument of stability more than of challenge. The Economic historian will show why blocks beat type for Chinese characters; what the state layer adds is that the court had little reason to disrupt a system that already served it. The Ming figures come from the map; the censorship detail goes beyond it.

sources.cite: Tsien Tsuen-Hsuin, Paper and Printing, in Needham, Science and Civilisation in China vol. 5 part 1 (1985)
Great Ming Code

steps.title: Europe 1348: no one owns the press yet
steps.text: Here is what only the political lens sees: in 1348 Europe is the opposite of Ming China. The Holy Roman Empire is a patchwork of hundreds of princes, free cities and bishoprics, and Cologne, Venice, Paris and Florence answer to different laws. The Black Death of this year killed perhaps a third of the continent, which cracked guild and church monopolies on copying (the Demographer will give the labour numbers). When Gutenberg's press arrived about a century later, no single ruler could suppress it: a banned book moved one border over. By 1500 presses had spread to roughly 250 towns, and Venice alone was a major centre. Fragmentation made printing hard to control, and that is the real reason Luther's pamphlets of 1517 could turn into a political event. The Peace of Augsburg (1555) on the law layer is the price: princes eventually settled the chaos by choosing each territory's religion.

links.why: Cheap paper lowered the cost per sheet, so Gutenberg's fixed-cost font could be spread over large runs that parchment would never have made worthwhile.
Europe's fragmentation of authority meant a banned pamphlet moved one border over, so Luther's 1517 Theses spread before any single censor could stop them.
China's huge urban readership was already served by cheap blocks, and a single empire with one exam syllabus and one censor used that supply to stabilise rather than disrupt.
Korea's state-held type and the Jujaso gave small, controlled runs, which kept a thin readership thin despite metal type arriving 70 years before Mainz.

whatifs.q: What if Korea's Jujaso had licensed commercial presses and printed Hangul books for a mass market after 1446?
whatifs.a: A Korean print market might have grown a vernacular reading public a century or two early, with printed Buddhist and moral texts in Hangul. The yangban elite, who guarded Chinese-character prestige and exam careers, would probably have resisted, so I doubt a Luther-like rupture; a gradual widening is likelier.

whatifs.q: What if Gutenberg's press had been suppressed by a single Holy Roman Emperor with real power over all German cities?
whatifs.a: Printing would likely still have spread, since Venice, Paris and other cities answered to other rulers, but the Reformation pamphlet flood of the 1520s would have been harder to sustain. Europe would resemble Ming China more: slower, with a more controlled flow of texts.

q: Why did Gothic cathedrals rise in twelfth-century France?

answer.short: Gothic rose in the Ile-de-France because a farm-fed, growing population and a monetised economy could pay for huge building projects, while a weak but ambitious Capetian king and his allied bishops needed sacred prestige against richer rivals such as the Angevins. Abbot Suger at Saint-Denis (1137-44) supplied the decisive spark, a theology of 'new light' fused with existing structural tricks (pointed arch, rib vault) that Romanesque Durham and Burgundy already had. Relic-driven pilgrimage and the Paris schools gave the style its crowds, clients and vocabulary. Wealth enabled it, politics and religion explain why France led, and England and Germany had similar means but not the same push.
answer.frame: Why a new tall, light, pointed-arch style appeared in the Ile-de-France c.1140-1200, and why then and there, not elsewhere.

plan.frame: Why a new tall, light, pointed-arch style appeared in the Ile-de-France c.1140-1200, and why then and there, not elsewhere.

angles.economist: Medieval warm growth, agricultural surplus and town wealth that paid for stone cathedrals.
angles.demographer: Population and urban growth around Paris, Laon, Sens and Chartres demanding larger churches.
angles.political: Capetian kings, powerful bishops and communes using cathedrals to assert legitimacy and rivalry.
angles.scholar: Suger's light theology, Pseudo-Dionysius, relic cults and Saint-Denis shaping the Gothic form.

steps.title: The surplus behind the stone
steps.text: Start with the farm, not the church. Between about 1000 and 1200 the Medieval Warm Period, the heavy plough, the three-field rotation and the spread of watermills (the Atlas has Barbegal 110 and London 1086 on its energy layer) raised the yield of northern France's loam soils. Bigger harvests fed more mouths and left a tradeable surplus of grain and wine near Paris. I can't give you a precise French yield figure; the Atlas holds none, and the claim of rising surplus rests on general medieval economic history rather than the map data. The Demographer will show the people; what the farm accounts add is that those people could be fed without all of them farming.

sources.cite: Georges Duby, The Early Growth of the European Economy (1973)
Robert S. Lopez, The Commercial Revolution of the Middle Ages, 950-1350 (1971)

steps.title: Who could pay for a 100-year building site
steps.text: A cathedral was a capital project lasting decades: Chartres' main fabric rose in roughly 25 years after the 1194 fire, and Notre-Dame was begun c.1163. Money came from bishops' and chapter estates (tithes, rents, mills), from townspeople selling cloth and wine, and from donations tied to relic pilgrimage. Bruges (in the Atlas from 850) and the Champagne fairs fed cash into northern French towns. The Atlas's Paris-1470 compass and printing entries are later, so I go beyond the data here. Mason's wages and quarrying were paid in coin, which presumes a monetised economy. The Historian of faith and ideas will show why Suger wanted light; what the ledger adds is that he could afford to tear down and rebuild at Saint-Denis because the abbey's estates yielded a surplus.

Jean Gimpel, The Cathedral Builders (1958)

steps.title: Technology that made walls into windows
steps.text: Gothic is a labour-saving, stone-saving technology. Pointed arches and ribbed vaults channel weight to piers, so walls can be thin and glazed; flying buttresses appear c.1180s-1200 at Notre-Dame. That lets the same limestone and money produce more interior volume and light. Cranes, treadwheels and standard-cut stone templates sped work, and the Atlas shows waterpower (London mill 1086) and windmills (Weedley 1185) spreading in the same decades, so mechanical energy was cheap enough to run quarry and workshop support. Whether any economic force caused the style, as opposed to enabling it, is unclear: England and Germany had similar wealth and took longer to follow. The Political scientist's rivalry among kings and bishops is probably what decides why France led.

sources.cite: Robert Mark, Experiments in Gothic Structure (1982)

steps.title: Paris: the 124,000 problem
steps.text: Start at the end of the window. The Atlas shows Paris at 124,000 in 1220, with no figure at 1000 or 1110, and London at 55,000, up from 21,000. The Paris figure is a modelled estimate, and I would treat it as an order of magnitude: the true number may have been far lower, but the direction is not in doubt. Philip Augustus walled the city from about 1190, a sign that a large and crowded population needed enclosing. A city that size outgrew the old Romanesque cathedral of Paris, so Bishop Maurice de Sully began Notre-Dame around 1163 with a nave sized for crowds, not a monastic choir.

sources.cite: Josiah Cox Russell, Medieval Regions and their Cities (1972)
Notre-Dame de Paris

steps.title: Four towns, one crowd problem
steps.text: Sens (begun c.1135-40), Noyon, Laon (c.1155-60) and Notre-Dame all started within about 30 years of each other, in one belt around Paris roughly 150 km across. That is a clustering I would read as demographic: clearing of forest and drainage of land in the 11th and 12th centuries drew peasants into growing towns, and Chartres drew pilgrims to the Virgin's relic, the Sancta Camisa. Our map has no records for these towns, so I go beyond the data here: the Atlas indexes only Paris, and I rely on general scholarship and rough estimates rather than counts. The Economic historian will show the silver behind this growth. What I add is the crowd inside the walls: a rebuilt nave had to hold thousands at feast days, and the Romanesque churches were too small for that.

steps.title: What 1348 will take back
steps.text: The map is now at 1348, and that matters for the lens: the cathedral boom ran on a population that peaked just before the Black Death. France may have held somewhere near 15-20 million people by 1300, versus a few million around 1000; those are rough, widely debated figures. When growth stalled, building did too. Beauvais, the tallest choir attempt at about 48 m, fell in 1284 and was never completed. So the Gothic cathedral is a record of a population still expanding, and the plague finishes that record. We have no way to say how many people each cathedral was built for, and I won't pretend to.

sources.cite: Colin McEvedy and Richard Jones, Atlas of World Population History (1978)
Beauvais Cathedral

steps.title: A king with only an island of land
steps.text: When Louis VI took the throne in 1108, the Kingdom of France (990-1791) was a king's title more than a state: his real domain was a strip from Paris to Orléans, and local castellans defied him. The model rates France at 17% fragility around 1110 (watch, against a 14% base rate), so this was a precarious regime. The Duchy of Aquitaine and the Duchy of Burgundy each held more land than he did directly. Cathedrals and abbeys were among the few institutions that could make a weak king look anointed, which is why the royal abbey of Saint-Denis mattered so much. This is my inference from the political position, not something the data records.

sources.cite: Jean Dunbabin, France in the Making, 843-1180 (2000)
Louis VI of France

steps.title: Bishops as the king's allies, communes as his rivals
steps.text: The Capetians leaned on bishops: Louis VI and Louis VII could rely on episcopal support and sworn urban communes against local lords, and the Laon commune of 1112 ended with its bishop murdered, a reminder that cities were also rivals. The Abbey of Saint-Denis, consecrated in 1144 under Abbot Suger, who also served as royal adviser and regent in 1147-49, put royal prestige into stone. Sens, the archbishopric over Paris, began its cathedral in the 1140s, and Paris's own began around 1163. Competition among prelates and between Paris and Sens is plausible as a driver, but the sources tell us more about ambition than they prove a rivalry race. The Historian of faith and ideas will show what Suger thought the light meant; what only my lens adds is that the same man was managing the kingdom.

steps.title: Why there: the Angevin rivalry
steps.text: The Angevin Empire (1147-1209, peak 0.426 Mkm² in 1202) wrapped around the Capetian domain, and Henry II held far more land than the French king. Philip II (r. 1180-1223) answered with law and bureaucracy and then conquest: he took Normandy in 1204, and the Angevin state ended in 1209. In that contest, cathedrals in the Capetian zone, such as Paris, Reims where kings were crowned, and Chartres, rebuilt after the 1194 fire, signalled royal-church alliance against a richer rival. The Economic historian will show the silver and the Demographer the crowds; I add that a king short of land and army used sacred buildings to claim legitimacy. Gothic also spread to Angevin lands such as Canterbury (1174) and Le Mans, so style was no pure Capetian monopoly, and the political story explains emphasis, not origin.

steps.title: Suger's light: Saint-Denis, 1140
steps.text: The map's Gothic style (idea:style:gothic, 1140 to 1520) starts at Saint-Denis, just north of Paris, where Abbot Suger rebuilt the west front (c.1137-40) and then the choir (dedicated 1144). He wrote that the church should be flooded with 'new light', and he believed it because he thought Saint-Denis, patron saint of France, was the same man as Dionysius the Areopagite, whose writings (Pseudo-Dionysius, really c.500 CE) call God light and make material beauty a ladder to the divine. Saint-Denis housed the relics of the martyr and the royal tombs, so pilgrim crowds needed a bright ambulatory with radiating chapels, and a theology gave the pointed arches and ribbed vaults a purpose beyond engineering. The Economic historian will show the silver; what only this lens adds is that the money had an argument for why glass and height were worth buying. Honest caveat: the structural parts (pointed arch, rib vault) already existed in Romanesque Durham and Burgundy, so Suger's novelty is the combination and the stated meaning.

sources.cite: Erwin Panofsky (ed.), Abbot Suger on the Abbey Church of St-Denis and Its Art Treasures (1946)
Otto von Simson, The Gothic Cathedral (1956)
Abbot Suger, Wikipedia

steps.title: Why Paris, why then: schools and a shared Dionysius
steps.text: The style spreads along the very corridor where the schools were: the University of Paris (1150 on the map, the masters' guild) grew from the cathedral schools where Abelard (1079-1142) had taught his Sic et Non method of setting authorities against each other. Scholasticism (1100-1500) and Gothic share a habit of mind, laying out parts in a clear, logical order, which Erwin Panofsky argued in 1951 and which is suggestive but contested, since he gave no causal mechanism. Sens (begun c.1135), Noyon, Laon and Notre-Dame of Paris (begun c.1163) follow within a generation. Bishops who studied in these schools were the clients, and the Political scientist's bishops and kings supply the power; the ideas supply the vocabulary of light, number and order they built with. Note what the Aristotle road on the map shows: Toledo 1170 and Paris 1255 come after the first cathedrals, so Gothic is not a product of the Arabic Aristotle; it precedes it.

routes.label: Gothic from Saint-Denis to the great sees

sources.cite: Erwin Panofsky, Gothic Architecture and Scholasticism (1951)
Gothic architecture, Wikipedia

steps.title: Chartres 1194: relics made the glass
steps.text: In 1194 fire destroyed most of Chartres, but the Sancta Camisa, the tunic said to be worn by Mary at Christ's birth, survived, and the town read this as the Virgin's wish for a bigger church. Rebuilding went fast, mostly within about 30 years, with some 150 stained-glass windows, many paid for by guilds and nobles. Relic cults like this were the engine of the genre: a holy object brought pilgrims, pilgrims brought gifts, and gifts bought height and glass. Chartres also shows the Gothic theology of light made public, since the windows teach scripture to those who cannot read. The Demographer's growing towns supply the crowds; this lens says why they came. We cannot measure how many visitors, so the pilgrimage numbers stay unknown.

sources.cite: Otto von Simson, The Gothic Cathedral (1956)
Chartres Cathedral, Wikipedia

links.why: Surplus from the northern French loam soils created the cash and estate rents that let bishops and abbots fund decades-long building sites.
Suger's theology of light gave a purpose to the pointed arch and rib vault, and the engineering that thinned walls then made large windows possible.
A king with a tiny domain leaned on Saint-Denis, whose abbot Suger was also his adviser, so royal need for prestige pushed Suger's theology into stone.
Relic cults like Chartres' Sancta Camisa pulled pilgrim crowds into growing towns, which made bigger naves and more glass worth financing.

views.name: Otto von Simson
views.claim: Gothic was a deliberate expression of Pseudo-Dionysian metaphysics of light, first realised by Suger.
views.for: Suger's own writings on Saint-Denis describe the 'new light' and the Dionysian identification, and the choir was dedicated in 1144.
views.against: Pointed arches and rib vaults existed earlier, and later cathedrals were built without a clear Dionysian programme, so the link to theology is hard to prove.

sources.cite: Otto von Simson, The Gothic Cathedral (1956)

views.name: Erwin Panofsky
views.claim: Gothic architecture and scholastic thought share a habit of mind that orders parts into a logical whole.
views.for: Both flourished in the Paris region within a generation, and masters and bishops overlapped socially.
views.against: He gave no causal mechanism, and Gothic began before the Aristotelian revival reached Paris.

sources.cite: Erwin Panofsky, Gothic Architecture and Scholasticism (1951)

views.name: Georges Duby
views.claim: Agrarian growth and rising rents and tithes from c.1000 to 1200 created the surplus that financed cathedral building.
views.for: Northern French growth in clearing, towns and money coincides with the building boom, and cathedral chapters held large estates.
views.against: England and Germany had comparable wealth yet followed later, so surplus enabled the style without explaining its origin.

sources.cite: Georges Duby, The Age of the Cathedrals: Art and Society, 980-1420 (1976)

views.name: Political-prestige school
views.claim: Capetian kings and allied bishops used cathedrals to make a weak monarchy look sacred against rivals such as the Angevins.
views.for: Saint-Denis was royal, Suger served as regent in 1147-49, and Reims and Paris sat in the Capetian zone.
views.against: Gothic also appeared at Angevin Canterbury (1174) and Le Mans, and the sources show ambition more than a deliberate rivalry race.

whatifs.q: What if Suger had not rebuilt Saint-Denis in the 1140s?
whatifs.a: Some Gothic-like experimentation would probably still have happened, since rib vaults and pointed arches were already used in Durham and Burgundy, and Sens began about the same time. But the combination of light, height and theological meaning might have been slower to form and might have taken a different shape. Confidence is low because the structural ideas were in the air.

unknowns: How much Suger's own theology caused the Gothic style rather than justified it after the fact
Real population and wealth figures for twelfth-century Paris and the other Ile-de-France towns
Why England and Germany, similarly wealthy, adopted the style more slowly
Whether competition between prelates, such as Sens and Paris, was an active race or only coincidence

passes.political: Historian of faith and ideas: if Suger was both regent and theologian, can you separate his theology of light from his strategy for royal legitimacy, or were they the same project?
passes.scholar: Economic historian: how much of Saint-Denis and Chartres was paid by pilgrim offerings and relic income versus guild and noble gifts, and can any ledger or donation record separate them?
passes.economist: Political scientist: if England and the Rhineland were similarly rich in 1150, what incentive made Capetian-area bishops spend their surplus on height and glass rather than on castles or fairs?

q: Why did the Scientific Revolution happen in Europe and not in the Islamic world or China?

answer.short: Islamic and Chinese science led in 1000 and had paper, printing and wealth, so the gap was not means or ideas but who could say no. Latin Europe's geography (a mesh of seas, rivers and chokepoints, steps 10-11) sustained many jurisdictions (step 3), which sheltered chartered universities that owned their curricula and trained public dispute (steps 4-5). Plague-era dear labour, merchant demand for instruments and print then paid for the output (steps 7-9), whereas a single buyer or patron could end an observatory or a syllabus (steps 1-2). This is a convergence, not a single cause, and the evidence for the causal weights is much thinner than the narrative suggests.
answer.frame: Why the Scientific Revolution's institutional and intellectual breakthroughs (c.1543-1687) coalesced in Latin Europe when Islamic and Chinese science had led earlier and had the means.

plan.frame: Why the Scientific Revolution's institutional and intellectual breakthroughs (c.1543-1687) coalesced in Latin Europe when Islamic and Chinese science had led earlier and had the means.

angles.political: How Europe's fragmented competing states and autonomous corporations (universities, guilds) protected inquiry versus empires' centralized control.
angles.scholar: How madrasa, Confucian examination and Latin university traditions shaped natural philosophy, printing, translation and open challenge to authority.
angles.economist: Did Atlantic trade, printing costs, instrument-making and patronage markets make European experimental science pay?
angles.geographer: How coasts, rivers and distances shaped Europe's multi-centre networks versus unified Chinese and Islamic cores.

steps.title: One empire, one switch: the Ming and Yuan cores
steps.text: At 1348 the Yuan Dynasty (peak 14.252 Mkm² in 1352) is calm on the fragility model at 13%, a single court ruling a whole civilisation. That scale is the point: when one centre decides what counts as useful knowledge, a policy change applies to hundreds of millions at once. The Ming that replaced it (1375-1644, 6.273 Mkm² at peak) codified this in the Great Ming Code of 1397 and ran the exam system for a bureaucracy whose syllabus was Confucian classics, not mechanics. Calendar and astronomy stayed an imperial monopoly (private study of astronomy was restricted under the Ming). I am going beyond the map data here on the astronomy restriction; it is well attested but its enforcement varied. The result is not hostility to science but a single buyer for it, with no rival court to flee to.

sources.cite: Nathan Sivin, Science in Ancient China (1995)
Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China (1954-)

steps.title: The Abbasid hollow and the Ottoman patron
steps.text: The Islamic world did have competing states: the Abbasid Caliphate (750-1259) shows fragility 37%, the Fatimids a critical 47%, Seljuks 31%, Ghaznavids 38%. Plurality was not the missing ingredient. What differed was the form of the institution that held knowledge. Madrasa teaching rested on the waqf, a pious endowment tied to its founder's terms, and degrees were licences (ijaza) from individual teachers, not rights granted to a corporation. In 1258 the Mongols sacked Baghdad and ended the caliphate; by 1348 the Mamluks (fragility 15%, watch) and the rising Ottomans (5%, calm) were stable military states patronising scholars, but a patron's favour could end with the patron. The Historian of faith and ideas will show what the madrasa curriculum taught; what the state data adds is that nothing legally independent of ruler or founder could defend a heterodox teacher. Observatories like Maragha (1259) and Istanbul's Taqi al-Din observatory, demolished in 1580, depended on one sultan's mood.

sources.cite: George Makdisi, The Rise of Colleges (1981)
Toby Huff, The Rise of Early Modern Science (1993)

steps.title: Corporations that could say no
steps.text: Magna Carta (1215) and the Golden Bull of 1222 are the visible law tokens: rulers bound by charters, with estates and towns holding legal personality. Universities (Bologna, Paris, Oxford) were corporations with their own privileges, so a condemned thesis in Paris in 1277 did not stop work at Oxford or Padua. The Holy Roman Empire, with hundreds of jurisdictions, made exit cheap: Galileo left Pisa for Venetian Padua in 1592 and returned to Medici Florence in 1610, and when Rome condemned him in 1633, the Dutch printed his Discorsi in 1638 at Leiden. Copernicus (1543) and Vesalius (1543) published in Nuremberg and Basel, outside any single censor's reach. Cost was real: Bruno burned in 1600. But no single veto covered the whole market. The Economic historian will show what printing and patronage paid; the fragmentation here is what stopped one office from cancelling the output.

routes.label: Galileo's exit from Pisa to Venetian Padua, then to Medici Florence

sources.cite: Edward Grant, God and Reason in the Middle Ages (2001)
Toby Huff, The Rise of Early Modern Science (1993)

steps.title: The Commentator's road: Aristotle changes hands
steps.text: Before 1348 the Islamic world was the donor, not the laggard. The Atlas traces Aristotle from Baghdad (830) through Córdoba (1169) and Toledo (1170) to Paris (1255); Gerard of Cremona alone translated about 87 Arabic works, including Ptolemy's Almagest. Averroes became simply 'the Commentator' in Latin, and Avicenna's Canon was still taught in European universities into the 1600s. So the question is not who had the ideas but what each system did with them. Latin Christendom received them into corporations, Paris (1150) and Bologna (1088), that owned their own curricula and could fight over them.

routes.label: Aristotle and Avicenna into Latin

sources.cite: Dimitri Gutas, Greek Thought, Arabic Culture (1998)
Edward Grant, The Foundations of Modern Science in the Middle Ages (1996)

steps.title: Three ways to argue with authority, 1095 to 1348
steps.text: At 1348 the plague arrives in Latin Europe and the Black Death kills perhaps a third of it, yet the universities survive; the Economic historian will show what that did to labour and wages, while what the plague data adds from my side is that the corporate schools kept their charters and their disputations. Al-Ghazali's Incoherence of the Philosophers (1095) hit the Aristotelian project, though Averroes answered in 1180, and madrasas were endowed (waqf) to teach law, with natural philosophy a private side-subject. In China, Zhu Xi restored White Deer Grotto in 1179 and Neo-Confucianism made 'investigating things' a moral discipline, but the examination rewarded mastery of a fixed canon, so ambition flowed to commentary. Latin scholasticism, whatever its faults, institutionalised the quaestio: state a position, state the objection, answer it, in public. The Political scientist will explain why such corporations were protected; I note only that the habit of structured dispute was trained in every arts student. I hold this as interpretation, since historians such as George Saliba dispute the idea that Islamic science declined after Ghazali.

sources.cite: George Saliba, Islamic Science and the Making of the European Renaissance (2007)
George Makdisi, The Rise of Colleges (1981)

steps.title: Print, vernacular and the Chinese Euclid
steps.text: Gutenberg's Bible (1455) and Ratdolt's Venice Euclid (1482) put identical diagrams in many hands, and Luther's New Testament (1522) and the Ninety-five Theses show print turning dispute into mass events. The Economic historian will price the presses; what I add is that Europe's Reformation made challenging an authority a thinkable public act, which Galileo and Hobbes then borrowed. China had printing centuries earlier, so printing alone is not the answer. Tellingly, Euclid reached Beijing only in 1607 as Matteo Ricci and Xu Guangqi's Jihe yuanben, six books and a translation by outsiders. Leibniz's Novissima Sinica (1697) shows Europe still treating exchange as two-way, while Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah (1377) shows the Islamic world producing brilliant social theory without a matching institution to carry it.

routes.label: Euclid's Elements, Venice print to Beijing

sources.cite: Elizabeth Eisenstein, The Printing Press as an Agent of Change (1979)
Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China (1954-)

steps.title: Paper everywhere, presses nowhere (until Mainz)
steps.text: The Islamic world and China did not lack the means. Paper reached Samarkand in 751, Baghdad in 794, Cairo c.900, Xàtiva 1056, Fabriano 1276, and Bi Sheng-era Kaifeng had movable type by 1040 while Cheongju cast metal type in 1377. Paper made books cheap everywhere. Europe's edge was not the invention but who paid: Fabriano's mills ran on water power for a commercial market, and Italian merchants and universities already bought books in bulk. The Ideas colleague will show the madrasa and examination traditions; what cost data adds is that a 1348 Europe, about to lose perhaps a third of its people, would soon have scarce labour and dear scribes, which raises the return on any machine that replaces copying.

routes.label: papermaking west: Samarkand to Baghdad to Cairo to Xàtiva to Fabriano

sources.cite: Jonathan Bloom, Paper Before Print (2001)
Thomas Carter, The Invention of Printing in China and Its Spread Westward (1925)

steps.title: After the plague: dear labour, rich wages
steps.text: Maddison's UK series shows GDP per capita at 1,121 dollars in 1315, then 1,398 in 1379 and 1,808 in 1443, a rise of about 60% after the Black Death cut the labour supply. Higher wages and a demand for luxuries, cloth, books and clocks fed trade hubs: Venice (1204-1500) and Bruges (1280-1490) relayed goods between the Hanse, Italy and the Levant. Windmills spread (Amsterdam 1400) and gunpowder reached Paris by 1346, so a rich, war-prone patchwork of buyers paid for craftsmen who made lenses, clocks, cannon and measuring tools. I go beyond the data in the claim that wages drove labour-saving invention (Allen's argument for later Britain); for 1400s science it is plausible, not proven.

routes.label: Hanseatic cloth, grain and timber
Venetian spices and luxuries north

sources.cite: Robert C. Allen, The British Industrial Revolution in Global Perspective (2009)
Maddison Project Database

steps.title: Silver and spices tilt the Atlantic
steps.text: Hubs moved Venice, then Antwerp (1500-1585), then Amsterdam (1585-1795), as pepper reached Lisbon in 1499 and Antwerp in 1508, and Potosí silver, minted from 1545, reached Seville in 1585. UK GDP per capita fell from 1,760 in 1508 to 1,526 in 1636 before jumping to 2,412 by 1700, so the Atlantic windfall did not lift everyone evenly. What it did create was merchant demand for navigation, astronomy, instruments and accurate maps, and printed manuals; this is where the Economic historian's silver and the Geographer's coastlines meet. Counter-evidence: Ottoman Istanbul got a press in 1493 but its Muslim-language printing stayed minimal until 1729, which points back to the Political scientist's patronage and control, not to cost alone.

steps.title: Europe's coastline is a fractal; China's is a wall
steps.text: Look at the coastline, not the courts. Europe is a peninsula of peninsulas: the Baltic, North Sea, Atlantic, Adriatic and Mediterranean all bite deep, so a Lübeck cog or a Venetian galley is rarely more than a few hundred km from another sovereign's port. The Oresund, Dover and Brenner chokepoints were each controlled by someone different, so no single ruler could shut the whole system. The Rhine, Rhone and Po link these seas by water and short portages, which gave Europe a mesh of Venice, Bruges, Cologne, Lübeck and Paris rather than one capital. A scholar expelled from one city could be in another jurisdiction within weeks. That is the geographical root of what the Political scientist will call competition, and my claim is only that the map made it cheap to sustain.

Venice-Alps-Rhine overland corridor

Hall, John A. Powers and Liberties (1985)

steps.title: One river, one capital: the Chinese and Islamic cores
steps.text: The two great cores were geographically integrated in a way Europe never was. China's North China Plain and Yangtze, joined by the Grand Canal at roughly 1,800 km, let one bureaucracy feed one capital: Kaifeng (pop. ~1 million under the Song by my estimate, beyond the Atlas figure) then Hangzhou, then Beijing. Its sea frontier faced the Pacific, so no rival state sat across the water. The Islamic world ran along a desert-and-oasis spine from Córdoba to Samarkand, with Baghdad, Damascus and Cairo as rich hubs that were often rivals but shared one scripture, one learned language and one pilgrimage to Mecca. Both cores produced Ibn al-Haytham, Shen Kuo and Su Song, and both were ahead of Europe in 1000. But a single large market for scholars meant that the patronage of one court, or its fall, set the weather for all. Baghdad's sack by the Mongols in 1258 is the starkest case; the Atlas shows the Abbasids ending that year.

pins.name: Grand Canal (Hangzhou to Beijing, c.1,800 km)

Tigris-Nile-Mediterranean caliphal corridor

Pomeranz, Kenneth. The Great Divergence (2000)

steps.title: 1348: plague runs along the trade roads
steps.text: The map's date is the argument. In 1348 plague moves along exactly the trade arteries I have been describing, from Caffa to Constantinople to Genoa, Venice and Marseille, then north over the Alps and up the Rhone. The Economic historian will show the silver and the printing costs; what the plague data adds is that Europe's mortality, perhaps a third of its people, hit a continent with many independent labour markets, where wages rose and cities competed to attract skilled men, a pattern argued by historians but not settled. Egypt and Syria were struck as hard under a single Mamluk state that could tax and constrain what remained. I cannot prove the plague caused any science, and I would not claim it; I only note that the same geography that spread it also gave scattered European cities room to recover differently.
