steps.title: Tree rings hear the monsoon fail
steps.text: The Atlas's shock record, 'Angkor megadroughts' 1340-1420, comes from Vietnamese cypress (Fokienia hodginsii) tree rings, which Buckley et al. (2010) read as a 759-year monsoon reconstruction. The pattern is not one dry spell but decades of weak monsoon, with two especially severe droughts in the record, roughly the 1330s-1360s and the 1400s-1420s. Angkor is a rain-fed city: its barays, canals and embankments were engineered for a steady supply. Rice yields, reservoir levels and the canal network all depended on the monsoon arriving on schedule. Note the scale: this is a regional climate signal, not a plague. Notably, the Black Death dots on the map (Genoa, Venice 1348) stop in the west, and there is no documented plague at Angkor, so I will not blame disease here.

sources.cite: Buckley et al., Climate as a contributing factor in the demise of Angkor, Cambodia, PNAS (2010)

steps.title: Then the flood: a drought-dried system breaks
steps.text: The Atlas link from the megadroughts to polity:khmer cites Buckley et al.: 'Drought then flood damaged the hydraulic system.' That sequence is the killer. Dry years let channels silt and sediment accumulate; then violent monsoon pulses hit infrastructure with little maintenance capacity. Archaeology by Evans, Pottier and colleagues (2007, 2013) found evidence of breached and blocked channels, including damage around the Angkor water network. These point to a system with little slack, since a single failing node could starve or flood many fields at once. I'd put this at about 1400, though the dating of specific breaches is looser than the tree rings' year-by-year resolution. The Economic historian will show why the rice surplus mattered; what the climate data adds is that the surplus was most fragile exactly when the state needed it.

routes.label: Monsoon flood pulse into the canals

sources.cite: Evans et al., A comprehensive archaeological map of the world's largest preindustrial settlement complex at Angkor, Cambodia, PNAS (2013)
Buckley et al., Climate as a contributing factor in the demise of Angkor, Cambodia, PNAS (2010)

steps.title: 1431: a weakened city, a downstream retreat
steps.text: By 1431, the Atlas ends the Khmer polity and Angkor's span, after about 90 years of climate stress (1340-1420). The Political scientist will show Ayutthaya's sack; what the climate data adds is that the city fell to an enemy already weakened. I can't prove drought caused the relocation, since the tree rings show stress, not decisions, and Angkor's population was already dispersing. But the Mekong-Tonlé Sap floodplain around Phnom Penh sits on a river system that does not depend on Angkor's engineering. Think of the move as a retreat to a place where water arrives without a maintenance bill. Climate was a contributing factor, as Buckley et al. title it, rather than a sole cause.

steps.title: A capital built on a lake that breathes
steps.text: Angkor (13.4N, 103.9E) sits on a gentle plain just north of the Tonlé Sap, where the lake swells from roughly 2,500 km² in the dry season to 15,000 km² or more in the monsoon because the Mekong backs water up the Tonlé Sap river. That gave Khmer kings rich rice land, fish and a short haul to the lake, with sandstone from Phnom Kulen 40 km north. But the site had no large river of its own, only the small Siem Reap River, so everything depended on barays (the Western Baray is about 8 x 2 km) and canals that moved water across a nearly flat gradient. This is a hydraulic city: its power came from managing a nature-made pulse, and a managed system can fail when the pulse changes. Map data show the Khmer Empire (802-1431) with Angkor as its one marked capital, and nothing else of comparable size in the window, which tells you how concentrated the bet was.

steps.title: Four rivers meet: the pull south
steps.text: Follow the water south and you reach Chaktomuk, where the Mekong, the Tonlé Sap river and the Bassac meet, about 250 km from Angkor and roughly 300 km from the sea by river. The Mekong Delta (10.5N, 106.3E in the terrain index) is the exit to the Gulf of Thailand and South China Sea, so a capital at the junction controls both the lake's fish-and-rice interior and the river road to the coast. Angkor, by contrast, lies behind the lake and the Dângrêk Mountains (14.5N, 103.2E), better placed for the old overland and Khorat-plateau world than for ships. The Economic historian will show the trade silver pulling toward the coast; what the map adds is that the junction was already there, and the delta's wet land was the less drought-fragile rice base. At 1348 nothing in the place index marks a southern capital yet, so this pull is a geographic argument, and the move itself (around the 1430s-1470s) is documented in chronicles of uneven reliability.

steps.title: The rival upstream and the retreat out of reach
steps.text: Ayutthaya (founded 1351, 14.4N, 100.6E) sits on the Chao Phraya plain only about 400 km west of Angkor, with an open road across the Khorat plateau's southern edge and little mountain between them. Angkor, near the Siamese side of the Khmer realm, was the Khmer city most exposed to it, while Phnom Penh lies another 200 km southeast, behind the lake and flood plain. Geography made the retreat sensible: the flooded lake and Mekong give defensive depth to the south, and the 1431 end date in the index fits the traditional sack. The Climate historian will show why the water system was already failing; the Political scientist the Siamese politics. I add that a weakened hydraulic core, a rival 400 km away on easier ground, and a safer junction downriver all pointed one direction. I cannot separate the causes from the map alone, and the traditional 1431 date is a convention for a process.

steps.title: A rice empire on a rain-fed ledger
steps.text: Angkor's wealth was a land-and-labor economy: rice from the Siem Reap plain, stored and redistributed through temple estates. The map's rice record puts Central Thailand's farming back to about 2000 BCE, so the Khmer did not invent the crop, they engineered it with barays and canals. That worked while the court could mobilize labor for building and upkeep, and Angkor's 12th-13th c. temple boom (Angkor Wat, the Bayon) absorbed enormous surpluses. But an inland, rain-dependent core has a ceiling: more people meant more mouths, more maintenance, and a surplus that could not easily be sold. I'm confident about the temple-estate model; I go beyond the Atlas data on exact yields.

sources.cite: Michael Coe and Damian Evans, Angkor and the Khmer Civilization (2nd ed., 2018)
Angkor

steps.title: The wind shifts to the water's edge
steps.text: Here is what only the money lens shows. Under the Yuan and early Ming, Quanzhou (Atlas hub, 1000-1400) and Guangzhou fed a maritime network, and the Indian Ocean monsoon route carried pepper, textiles and porcelain; the Atlas porcelain record has Quanzhou shipping in 1340 and Kilwa receiving it by 1400. Southeast Asian polities that sat on water prospered, and Malacca (hub from 1400) became the new gateway. A capital on the Mekong-Tonlé Sap-Bassac junction could tax and ship forest goods and rice to coast and China; Angkor, a day or more from the lake, was a temple-city, not a port. The Epidemiologist will show how droughts and floods disrupted the baray system; what trade adds is why abandoning that costly system for a river-mouth capital paid off. Dates of Phnom Penh's rise are from later Khmer chronicles of uncertain reliability, so treat this as likely, not proven.

Forest products and rice down the Mekong

steps.title: Upkeep versus opportunity
steps.text: By 1431, the year the Atlas ends the Khmer polity, Angkor carried a fixed cost: maintaining thousands of kilometers of canals and embankments to feed a population no longer paid for by conquest tribute. Meanwhile Ayutthaya, founded 1351 on the Chao Phraya (also a rice delta but open to the Gulf), could tax maritime commerce, and Malacca was about to join it as a hub from 1400. Moving south cut the maintenance bill and put the court beside revenue. The Political scientist will tell the 1431 sack; I add that a king choosing between rebuilding a drying inland machine and taxing river trade had a clear fiscal incentive. We don't have price or customs data for either capital, so this is inference from geography and later Chinese and Iberian accounts.

steps.title: A fragile empire before Ayutthaya exists
steps.text: Start with the state, not the city. The Khmer Empire peaked at 0.953 Mkm² in 1206 under Jayavarman VII's building state, and by 1325 the Atlas model scores it 27% fragile against a 14% base rate and a 20% warning line. Its western neighbor Lavo (25% fragile, ending 1394) was the Khmer buffer toward the Chao Phraya basin. The Khmer court had also been losing its sacral glue: Theravada Buddhism was displacing the Devaraja cult that justified a god-king and his huge labor levies. I'd call this a cheap-to-challenge regime before any rival existed. Confidence is moderate because the fragility score is a statistical model, not a diagnosis.

sources.cite: Michael Vickery, Society, Economics, and Politics in Pre-Angkor Cambodia (1998)

steps.title: Ayutthaya fills the vacuum
steps.text: Ayutthaya appears in 1352 (founded 1351 by Ramathibodi I) and reaches 0.45 Mkm² only by 1600, so it started small but sat on the rice and river-trade core that Lavo had once screened for Angkor. Sukhothai, rated calm at 12%, was the other Tai power and was gradually absorbed into Ayutthaya's orbit by the 1400s. Thai-language chronicles say Ayutthaya took Angkor more than once, around the 1350s and again in the 1430s, but those accounts are late and dates conflict, so treat the sequence as contested. The Economic historian will show why Ayutthaya's river-and-sea access gave it revenue; what my lens adds is that a rival with a growing tax base needs only repeated raiding to force a rice-and-labor state into costly defense.

steps.title: 1431: the sack, then a court that does not return
steps.text: The Atlas ends Angkor and the Khmer polity entry at 1431, the traditional date of Ayutthaya's sack under Borommaracha II. The deeper political fact is what happened next: the kingship moved rather than being destroyed. Khmer rule continued (the dataset runs to 1867) from Phnom Penh, Longvek and later capitals, so 1431 marks a court choosing a safer, trade-facing seat after losing the ability to defend a vast inland temple city. The Epidemiologist and climate historian will show the drought and flood shocks that strained the water network; my addition is that a weakened king could neither pay the labor to repair it nor hold off raiders at once. The Geographer's Mekong pull then gave the court a place to go. Dates for the move vary across sources, so do not read 1431 as a single-day abandonment. Angkor itself was never fully empty: monks kept Angkor Wat.

links.why: Drought-then-flood damage to canals and barays raised the cost of upkeep, which made the fixed maintenance bill the economist describes harder to justify.
The Chaktomuk junction already gave access to river and sea, so when Indian Ocean and China trade grew, a capital there could collect revenue that inland Angkor could not.
Ayutthaya's repeated raiding hit a city whose hydraulic base was already weakened by climate stress, so the court could not both repair and defend.
A regime with a high fragility score and a fading god-king cult had little legitimacy or labor to hold Angkor, so the 1431 shock produced relocation, not recovery.

q: Who built Great Zimbabwe, and why was it abandoned?

answer.short: Great Zimbabwe was built by ancestral Shona (Karanga) speakers, whose sacral rulers turned cattle and Indian Ocean gold trade into c. 1100-1450 stone-walled power. It was probably abandoned by slow attrition rather than a single shock: a town of perhaps 10,000+ strained thin granite soils, pasture and fuelwood, while gold routes shifted north toward the Zambezi and rivals at Khami and Mutapa inherited the trade. Which factor weighed most is not settled.
answer.frame: Great Zimbabwe was built by ancestral Shona (Bantu-speaking Karanga) peoples of the Zimbabwe plateau, c. 1100-1450, on gold and cattle wealth tied to Indian Ocean trade, and was abandoned for reasons that were likely ecological, economic and political rather than any single cause.

plan.frame: Great Zimbabwe was built by ancestral Shona (Bantu-speaking Karanga) peoples of the Zimbabwe plateau, c. 1100-1450, on gold and cattle wealth tied to Indian Ocean trade, and was abandoned for reasons that were likely ecological, economic and political rather than any single cause.

steps.title: The cattle plateau above the fever lowlands
steps.text: Great Zimbabwe sits at about -20.3, 30.9 on the granite plateau between the Zambezi and the Limpopo, at roughly 1,000 m. That height matters: it lifts the site above the tsetse and malaria of the lowlands and gives it the reliable summer rains cattle need. The map's own record has the stone-walled capital alive 1100-1450. The soils are the catch: the sandy granite soils are good for grazing but thin for cereals, so the site lived on herds, and herds need fresh pasture. Rainfall on this plateau swings hard from decade to decade, so a town built on cattle was rich in good years and exposed in dry ones. To the south the Limpopo (-22.3, 30.8) was the older heartland of Mapungubwe; the Economic historian will show how its trade shifted north, and what the land adds is that the plateau had better rain and better pasture than the dry Limpopo valley.

sources.cite: Pikirayi, The Zimbabwe Culture: Origins and Decline of Southern Zambezian States (2001)

steps.title: Gold downhill to Sofala, then by sea to Kilwa
steps.text: In 1348, the year on the map, the gold had two steps. First came the overland leg of roughly 400 km east from the plateau to the Sofala coast, which crosses the lowlands near the Zambezi Delta (-18.4, 36.5). Then dhows carried it up the Mozambique Channel and the Swahili coast to Kilwa (-9.0, 39.5), about 1,300 km by sea, using the seasonal monsoon winds. Kilwa has a record from 900 CE to 1840 on the map, and its role as the shipper of Zimbabwe's gold is what made the stone capital rich. Great Zimbabwe controlled the plateau end of this chain, not the sea end, so its wealth depended on routes it did not own. The disease layer is switched on because the Black Death of 1347-1351 is not documented for this region, and I would not claim it hit here; the effect of the Indian Ocean trade is a question for the Economic historian.

steps.title: Why the herds left: an exhausted hill
steps.text: By 1450, the map's end date for the site, geography explains why leaving was plausible. A dense town on thin granite soils burns the nearby woodland for fuel and wears out its pastures, so herds and farmers must go further each year. Oral and archaeological accounts point to wood shortage and grazing pressure, but we do not have a precise count of the loss, so treat this as likely, not proven. The newer power centres sat where there was more to draw on: the Zambezi escarpment to the north, nearer other gold and ivory sources, and Khami to the west, about 200 km away. The Demographer will say how many people were involved and where they went; what only the land shows is that every successor sat on a different resource base from the cattle and gold balance of the old capital. The Political scientist will explain why the stone walls were left behind.

steps.title: Mapungubwe's gold dries up
steps.text: Before Great Zimbabwe there was Mapungubwe, a Limpopo valley capital that grew rich c. 1000-1290 on ivory and gold sold to the coast for glass beads and cloth. My data lists no Mapungubwe record, so this is beyond the map, but its rise matches the Swahili coast and Gulf route (800-1500), which the map says paid for Persian and Chinese goods with Zimbabwe gold. Archaeologists link its decline c. 1300 to a cooler, drier spell and to the trade moving north to the plateau, where gold was nearer. Read as economics: a trading hub loses when the supply and the buyers both shift away from it.

steps.title: Gold for cloth and beads, via Kilwa
steps.text: In 1348 Great Zimbabwe (in my index 1100-1450) is at its peak as the inland end of the Swahili coast and Gulf route, where gold left Sofala and was re-exported from Kilwa Kisiwani (index 900-1840). The map records porcelain reaching Kilwa by 1400, and Chinese and Persian ceramics and glass beads turn up in Zimbabwe's excavations. Cattle were the plateau's savings account, gold the export, and a ruling elite that controlled both could buy imports that confirmed its status. The same year the Black Death was killing perhaps a third of Europe, but there is no evidence it reached here, so this trade was running on its own cycle. I can't give reliable tonnage figures for the gold; estimates are guesses.

steps.title: The trade moves on
steps.text: By c. 1450 the index ends Great Zimbabwe's life, and the economist's suspects are the ones that eat a city of stone: a tight-packed elite living off tribute needs a surplus, and cattle herds plus fuelwood and fields probably strained a plateau supporting thousands. The Economic historian's price lens fits one more pull: gold fields and trade routes shifted north toward the Zambezi, and Khami in the southwest took over. Portuguese arrival (the empire starts in 1415, and Cape Route opens 1498) turned this gold into a European prize, but that is after the collapse, so it cannot be the cause. What the Geographer's rainfall and the Demographer's headcount show will decide whether this was a trade shift or an ecological squeeze; my lens suggests both, and I can't separate them yet.

steps.title: A town of perhaps 10,000 on the granite hills
steps.text: The Atlas's city-population table has no figure for this window, so these numbers go beyond the data and are archaeological estimates. The usual range for Great Zimbabwe at its peak, around 1300-1450, is roughly 10,000 to 18,000 people, which would make it the largest settlement in southern Africa and comparable to a mid-sized European town. Those people were mostly not inside the walls: the Great Enclosure's 250 m circuit (walls up to 11 m high) housed elite families, while commoners lived in daga (clay) houses spread across the valley. The wall count is solid; the headcount is soft and could be off by a factor of two. At 1348 the Atlas shows the city near its height, in the decades when the Black Death was emptying Europe and the Atlas disease layer is silent on the plateau.

sources.cite: Thomas Huffman, Snakes and Crocodiles: Power and Symbolism in Ancient Zimbabwe (1996)

steps.title: Why 10,000 people is a problem
steps.text: Demography is where the abandonment story gets concrete. A town of this size on cattle and sorghum needs steady grazing and fuel, and firewood and pasture within a few days' walk eventually run short. Many archaeologists propose that this strain, plus soil exhaustion and a drier spell, pushed people out. This is a hypothesis; the evidence is circumstantial and debated. The Economic historian will show the Kilwa gold and bead trade that fed the elite; what population adds is the cost side: the more traders and rulers the town drew in, the more mouths the surrounding land had to carry. Rather than a sudden collapse, a slow bleed of households is the likelier pattern.

sources.cite: Innocent Pikirayi, The Zimbabwe Culture: Origins and Decline of Southern Zambezian States (2001)

steps.title: Where the people went: north and west
steps.text: By about 1450 the Atlas marks Great Zimbabwe's end date, but people did not vanish; they relocated. Tradition and the archaeology of Khami (built from the 1450s) point to one stream moving west to the Torwa state and another north toward the Zambezi, where the Mutapa state emerged. The Political scientist will explain who ruled each; the demographic point is that the plateau's population stayed in the region and simply recentered. The population of Khami is much smaller than Great Zimbabwe at its height, which suggests dispersal into many homesteads rather than a single new city. Treat the two routes as inferred directions, not recorded marches.

steps.title: Who sat inside the walls?
steps.text: The Cliopatria layer records no state here, so the map shows a gap that is really a data limit: Great Zimbabwe (index: 1100..1450) was a polity with no written constitution we can read. The builders were ancestral Shona (Karanga) speakers, and the archaeology (Hill Complex first, Great Enclosure c. 1300-1450) points to a sacral ruler whose authority rested on cattle, gold and ritual rather than on a standing army. The dry-stone walls, with no mortar, used maybe 900,000 granite blocks and were built to be seen: they say 'this king can command thousands of laborers and the ancestors approve.' Those who ruled left no names; the earliest named rulers appear only in later Portuguese-era oral traditions. The Economic historian will show the gold and cloth that paid for this; what only the political lens adds is that the wall was a legitimacy machine, not a fortress. Everything about the ruler's title and succession rules is inference.

steps.title: A capital that outgrew its grazing
steps.text: The place index ends Great Zimbabwe at 1450, which matches the usual dating of its decline. For a political scientist this is a succession-and-scale problem: a sacral court of perhaps 10,000 or more people (the Demographer has the real estimate) drained fuel, grazing and food from its surroundings, while the Economic historian's Kilwa trade shifted toward routes further north on the Zambezi. Two heirs emerge: Khami, the capital of the Torwa state to the southwest, which kept dry-stone building with a new decorated style, and the Mutapa state in the north, whose rulers by the 1490s controlled gold and ivory routes. Oral tradition ties Mutapa's founding to Nyatsimba Mutota, with Nyanhehwe Matope expanding it, but those dates are uncertain. The pattern fits a familiar rule: when a capital's logistics fail, rivals nearer to the resource and the trade route inherit legitimacy.

steps.title: Why the 1348 plague tells us little here
steps.text: The map is set to 1348, the year of the Black Death in the Mediterranean, and it is tempting to read a plague cause into Zimbabwe's end. I would not. No evidence shows plague reaching the southern plateau then, and abandonment came roughly a century later. The Law layer also has nothing here: its recorded codes, such as the Kouroukan Fouga (1236) in Mali, are West African and written down only later, so the plateau's rules of succession and justice stay invisible. What the Demographer's data may add is whether the decline was a gradual drain rather than a shock. Treat 1348 as a control year: the court was probably at its height, which shows decline was not a global-crisis story but a local one of resources and rivals.

q: What do we actually know about why the Indus cities declined?

answer.short: We know the Indus cities declined gradually between about 1900 and 1700 BCE, with no evidence of invasion, massacre, or epidemic. The best-supported driver is a weakening monsoon that eroded the flood-fed farming surplus big river-edge cities relied on, possibly compounded by shifting rivers; the fading of Gulf trade looks like a symptom, not a cause. People did not vanish but dispersed east and south into many small villages with diversified crops, so 'decline' means the end of urbanism, not of the population. Exact weights of climate versus rivers are unsettled because dating errors of 100-200 years blur the sequence.
answer.frame: Between roughly 2600 and 1700 BCE the Indus cities shrank and urban life dissolved, but the cause is debated: monsoon weakening, river shifts, trade collapse, or a mix, with no evidence of invasion or a single catastrophe.

steps.title: A river that fed the cities, then lost its water
steps.text: At the mature phase, the Indus cities sat on very different water. Mohenjo-daro (27.3N, 68.1E) lay on the Indus floodplain itself, while Harappa (30.6N, 72.9E) sat beside the Ravi. Archaeologists have mapped thousands of sites along the dry Ghaggar-Hakra bed through Cholistan and Haryana, which is why many call it a 'lost river' of the civilization. Whether it was a large perennial river in that period is disputed: some geologists argue its water came from monsoon rains rather than Himalayan glaciers, and the Sutlej (31.0N, 76.5E) may have fed it earlier. Our evidence here is a patchwork of sediment studies and site surveys, not a single clean map.

routes.label: Ghaggar-Hakra course, roughly (debated)

steps.title: When the Sutlej and Yamuna changed course
steps.text: One long-running proposal is that the Sutlej and Yamuna shifted course, the Sutlej westward into the Indus system and the Yamuna eastward toward the Ganges, starving the Ghaggar-Hakra. The dating is the weak point: some studies place the Sutlej shift well before the cities, which would mean the Ghaggar-Hakra was already seasonal in the urban period. If so, Harappan settlements there were already adapted to monsoon-fed flows, and shrinking rains hurt them directly. The Epidemiologist and climate historian will show how the 4.2 ka weakening fits; what the map adds is that the same drying hit places very differently depending on whether a town stood on a snow-fed or rain-fed channel.

routes.label: Possible Yamuna diversion east to the Ganges (contested)

steps.title: Why the Indus floodplain was both gift and trap
steps.text: Mohenjo-daro's weakness was its position: on the low Indus plain the river can flood hugely or shift its bed, and the settlement was built on raised platforms against it. Mohenjo-daro's dated span in our index ends around 1900 BCE, and archaeology shows late decline there, not a single sudden destruction. Harappa, by contrast, is indexed to 1300 BCE, so some urban life lingered in the Punjab. The Demographer will trace where people went; geography suggests the move east toward the Yamuna-Ganges rainfall zone and south into Gujarat followed places where small-scale, flexible farming still worked. The Economic historian will show whether Gulf trade, via Dilmun, also faded, but the rivers alone suggest cities needing big grain surpluses were more fragile than villages that could shift crops.

steps.title: The 4.2 ka event: what the proxies say
steps.text: The Atlas has no shock recorded for this window, so I go beyond its data here. Around 2200 BCE a abrupt dry spell, the '4.2 ka event', shows in many records from Greece to China, and Akkad (2334-2154 BCE) falls in the same century. For South Asia the evidence is a monsoon that weakened gradually, not a single crash: lake and ocean-core records point to drying from about 2500 BCE, with Indian summer rainfall dropping by perhaps 10-30% in some reconstructions. The catch is dating. Many proxies have errors of 100-200 years, so 'drought hit, cities fell' is partly a trick of overlapping error bars. Harappa (founded about 2600 BCE) was still occupied after the event, so it was not a clean knockout.

steps.title: Drying that cities could outlast
steps.text: Mohenjo-daro (in the Atlas, 2500-1900 BCE) sat on a flood-fed river, so a weaker monsoon hurts it differently than a town on rain-fed fields. Giosan and colleagues argue that the Indus system was fed by strong monsoon floods that let farmers sow after the waters receded, and that as floods weakened, big river-edge cities lost their reliable surplus while smaller villages near the Himalayan foothills adapted. The Geographer will show where the Ghaggar-Hakra and Indus shifted; what climate adds is the reason the rivers mattered less and less. Notably the Harappans already grew summer and winter crops (millets and rice, wheat and barley), a hedge against rain failure that likely slowed, rather than prevented, the decline. This is an inference, and the evidence is regional and patchy.

sources.cite: Giosan et al., Fluvial landscapes of the Harappan civilization (PNAS, 2012)

steps.title: Plague? Mostly we cannot say
steps.text: Disease is the gap in this story. Mohenjo-daro's famous 'massacre' skeletons were reinterpreted decades ago as scattered burials from different times, so there is no evidence of epidemic or war there. Ancient pathogen DNA could settle it: Yersinia pestis was already circulating in Eurasia by about 3000 BCE, but no plague, or any epidemic, has been shown in the Indus cities, and tropical bones and heat preserve DNA poorly. The Economic historian will show whether trade routes to Dilmun (2300-1700 BCE in the Atlas) carried people and goods; what I add is that denser, drier, more crowded settlements could plausibly have raised infection (e.g. tuberculosis, found at Indus sites like Lothal-era sites), but that remains a hypothesis. The honest answer is: climate stress is supported, epidemics are not.

sources.cite: Kenoyer, Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (1998)
Robbins Schug et al., Climate change, human health, and resilience in the Holocene (PNAS, 2013)

steps.title: Lothal and Dilmun: the Gulf relay
steps.text: The Atlas records no named route here, only two hub records: Lothal (c. 2400-1900 BCE) as the eastern relay and Dilmun (c. 2200-1700 BCE) as the western one. Mesopotamian cuneiform texts name Meluhha, widely identified with the Indus, as a source of carnelian, ivory and exotic woods, and Indus-style seals and weights turn up at Ur and in the Gulf. Notice the trade's shape: Indus goods were luxuries and beads, a thin slice of an economy that rested on farming, so the Gulf link was a prestige and craft channel more than a lifeline. I cannot give tonnages; no one can. The ledgers survive only on the Mesopotamian side.

routes.label: carnelian, beads, timber, cotton textiles west; copper, silver, wool, oil back

steps.title: The Mesopotamian buyer goes quiet
steps.text: The Atlas dates Lothal's hub run to 1900 BCE and Dilmun's to 1700 BCE, so the eastern end stops first and the Gulf end lingers. Texts from Ur's merchants show direct Meluhha voyages fading in the early second millennium BCE, with Dilmun taking over as middleman, and Indus-style seals largely vanish from the west after about 1900 BCE. That sequence says the Indus cities were not simply cut off by a Mesopotamian collapse. Akkad (2334-2154 BCE) fell centuries earlier, long before the Indus cities shrank, so Akkad's end cannot be the trigger. Honest verdict: demand shifted and weakened, which probably hurt bead and craft towns, but it looks like a symptom beside the failing cities, not the cause.

steps.title: An economy that could turn inward
steps.text: What the money lens adds is resilience. Indus farmers grew wheat and barley in winter and millet and rice in summer, and the Atlas's wheat record at Mehrgarh (7000 BCE) shows how deep the farming base was. Cities lived off that surplus, so when long-distance luxury trade thinned, the countryside could keep going while the cities that depended on managing and exchanging it lost their purpose. The Geographer will show where rivers moved; the Epidemiologist and climate historian will show whether the rains failed. If either did, trade loss then amplified it, because merchants and craft quarters had no rural patron to fall back on. The Demographer's eastward flight to Punjab, Haryana and Gujarat fits small regional trading rather than a grand network.

sources.cite: Wright, The Ancient Indus: Urbanism, Economy, and Society (2010)

steps.title: Peak Indus: a million people, give or take
steps.text: The Atlas has no city population figures for this window, so I go beyond its records here. At maturity (about 2600-1900 BCE) the Indus zone covered roughly a million square km, with five big sites: Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Ganweriwala, Rakhigarhi and Dholavira. Mohenjo-daro (in the index from 2500 BCE) and Harappa (from 2600 BCE) are usually estimated at 30,000-40,000 people each, and the whole civilization at perhaps 1-5 million; those numbers are soft, built from site area and density guesses. The key demographic fact is that most people lived in small towns and villages, not the famous cities, which matters for what 'decline' means.

sources.cite: Jonathan Mark Kenoyer, Ancient Cities of the Indus Valley Civilization (1998)
Indus Valley Civilisation

steps.title: The great sideways shift: people leave the river
steps.text: Here is what the settlement surveys show. In the Ghaggar-Hakra region, Cholistan sites fall sharply after 1900 BCE, while Haryana and East Punjab sites increase in number but shrink in size. Gujarat gains post-urban sites too, and Mohenjo-daro's last phases show crowding and neglect, with Harappa's lower town thinning out by about 1900 BCE. Madhav Possehl and Cameron Petrie both read this as ruralization and dispersal into many small villages, not mass flight. Harappa remains in the index until 1300 BCE, as a smaller place. The Geographer will show why the rivers pulled settlements east, and the Epidemiologist and climate historian the drought; what my lens adds is that this looks like thousands of household decisions toward places with more reliable water, not a single exodus.

steps.title: New crops, smaller towns, and a DNA footnote
steps.text: By 1700 BCE urban features are gone: no standardized weights, fewer seals, and writing fades. Villages diversified crops, adding summer millets and rice alongside wheat and barley, which spreads risk when the monsoon is unreliable (Weber, Fuller). The Atlas's Indo-Aryan migration record (2000-1500 BCE) overlaps this window, but ancient DNA from Rakhigarhi (Narasimhan et al. 2019) shows no steppe ancestry in that individual, so steppe arrivals came after the cities' decline began and are not a cause. Population size after the collapse is unknown; I would not claim it fell as much as city abandonment suggests, since many people simply lived more dispersed.

q: Why did Columbus have to prove the Earth was round?

answer.short: Columbus never had to prove the Earth was round; educated Europeans had accepted a sphere since Aristotle and Sacrobosco's textbook. The 1490s quarrel was over size: Columbus used a small Earth and an overlong Asia (about 3,700 km to Japan by his figures, versus roughly 19,000 km in reality), and his critics were right. Spain's gamble was worth taking because Portugal held the African route and the spice chain ran through Venice and Cairo. An unknown continent in the gap rescued him, and Irving, Draper and White later turned the story into a myth about faith against science.
answer.frame: Educated Europeans already knew the Earth was round; the 1490s dispute was about its size and the Atlantic distance to Asia, and the 'flat Earth' story is a later myth.

steps.title: Aristotle's round Earth reaches the universities
steps.text: In 1348 the Scholasticism the Atlas places at Paris (1100–1500) taught the Earth as a sphere, and it was not controversial. Aristotle argued for it in On the Heavens from the curved shadow of the Earth in lunar eclipses and from stars that rise or vanish as you travel north or south. The Atlas's 'Aristotle's long road' (Baghdad 830, Córdoba 1169, Toledo 1170, Palermo 1225, Cologne 1248, Paris 1255) shows how the Latin West got these texts. Around 1230 the Paris teacher John of Sacrobosco wrote De sphaera, a short textbook on a round Earth that stayed in use for some 400 years. Dante's Divine Comedy (1315) has a spherical cosmos, with Hell's pit at the centre of the globe and Mount Purgatory rising from the southern hemisphere. A fourteenth-century student would have laughed at the idea that anyone doubted this. The route is the Atlas's own, apart from Toledo, which I have added as the Toledo school of translators.

steps.title: Euclid and printed books carry the globe to Venice
steps.text: By Columbus's day, mathematical geography was moving into print. The Atlas records Ratdolt's Venice Euclid (1482), reached via Baghdad (800) and Bath (1120), and the Gutenberg Bible (Mainz, 1455), which shows how fast presses were spreading in Europe. The Atlas lens does not list Ptolemy's Geography, but I know it was translated into Latin around 1406 and printed in the 1470s. That text gives a map with latitude and longitude on a globe, and educated readers saw an Earth that could be measured. The Atlas's Renaissance humanism (Florence, from 1350) is the setting: Petrarch's heirs hunted for lost classical texts, and the globe came back with them. That is why Columbus's advisers argued about numbers rather than about shape. The Geographer will show the size dispute, where Ptolemy's and Marinus's figures matter, and I stop at the point where the shape was settled.

steps.title: How a myth was manufactured: Irving, Letronne and Draper
steps.text: Columbus died in 1506, and the flat-Earth story about him is from the 1800s. Washington Irving's A History of the Life and Voyages of Christopher Columbus (1828) invented a scene of Salamanca churchmen insisting the Earth was flat. The Council of Salamanca did meet, but the dispute was over distance, and Columbus was wrong: he put Asia far too close, and his critics were closer to the truth. The anti-Church story was then taken up in John William Draper's History of the Conflict between Religion and Science (1874) and Andrew Dickson White's A History of the Warfare of Science with Theology (1896). Russell and others have shown that the 'flat Earth' tale grew from a conflict narrative, not from medieval sources. The few real flat-Earthers, such as Lactantius (c. 300) and Cosmas Indicopleustes (6th century), were marginal. The Biographer will show how Columbus's miscalculations shaped the court's verdict, and what my lens adds is that the 'proof' he supposedly needed was invented three centuries later.

pins.name: Washington Irving writes his Columbus life in Madrid (1828)

sources.cite: Jeffrey Burton Russell, Inventing the Flat Earth: Columbus and Modern Historians (1991)

steps.title: Eratosthenes' Nile, Ptolemy's long Eurasia
steps.text: The size of the Earth was measured, not guessed: around 240 BCE Eratosthenes took the Sun's angle at Alexandria (about 7.2 degrees, 1/50 of a circle) against a well at Syene and got roughly 250,000 stadia, within a few percent to 15 percent of the truth depending on which stadion you assume. Medieval scholars inherited that figure, and al-Farghani's 9th-century value of about 56 2/3 miles per degree, from Baghdad's caliphal surveys, gave a circumference near 20,400 km against the true 40,075. The trouble was Ptolemy: he shrank the degree to about 500 stadia and stretched Eurasia eastward, so on paper Asia ran far too far toward the Atlantic. The dispute was never round versus flat; it was which number you trusted for the degree, and how much of the globe the land ate.

routes.label: Eratosthenes' baseline, Alexandria to Syene (~5,000 stadia)

steps.title: Seven thousand versus twenty thousand kilometres
steps.text: Here is the real quarrel. Columbus used Ptolemy's small Earth, Marinus of Tyre's even longer Asia, and Alfraganus's degree read in shorter Italian miles, to place Japan about 3,700 km west of the Canaries. The true gap is roughly 19,000 km west, over ten thousand more than the other reading of the world, and the Portuguese royal advisers, working from a circumference near 40,000 km, were right to say no crew could carry food that far. Spain's commission at Salamanca and Santa Fe was arguing numbers; Columbus won only because a landmass he did not know about (the Americas, about 4,500 km out at these latitudes) sat in the gap. The Biographer will show how he sold the figures; what geography adds is that he was wrong about the Earth and lucky about the map.

steps.title: The spice toll booth: Venice, Cairo, Calicut
steps.text: Here is the economist's problem with 1348: pepper grown on the Malabar coast (Calicut) rode the monsoon to the Red Sea, crossed Mamluk Egypt (Cairo, Alexandria), and reached Venice with a toll or markup at nearly every hand-off. The Atlas has Venice as the Western trade-hub from 1204 and Calicut as the Eastern one from 1300, with the Mamluks sitting in the middle from 1250. That middle is the target: anyone who could avoid it would pocket the margin, which is why spice prices in Europe were many times the Malabar price (I can't give a precise multiple from this data). The Black Death of 1348 hit this chain hard, killing perhaps a third or more of Europe's people, yet demand for pepper, which was a luxury and a meat-preservation fashion item, rebounded, so the profit target stayed on the table.

steps.title: Portugal's gold and sugar rehearsal
steps.text: The Portuguese Empire starts in 1415, and its logic was commercial as much as holy: West African gold reached the Mediterranean by camel across the Sahara (the Atlas's Trans-Saharan route, with Timbuktu as its hub), and caravel captains wanted to intercept it at the coast. They tried sugarcane too: the tech layer dates Madeira cane to 1455 and São Tomé to 1500, an early plantation model that Spain would copy across the Atlantic. The Economic payoff was proof that Atlantic islands and coasts could make money, and that the sea could undercut the desert. The Biographer will show how Columbus learned this world while living in Lisbon and Madeira; what the ledger adds is that every Atlantic voyage was expected to pay for itself.

steps.title: Two bets on one prize: Cape route vs. western gamble
steps.text: By 1488 Bartolomeu Dias had rounded the Cape, so Portugal held a nearly proven route to Asia's pepper, and Da Gama's arrival at Calicut in 1498 would turn it into the Carreira da India. Castile was shut out of that Atlantic-African road by the Portuguese monopoly, and the Mamluk-Venetian chain was the only other way, so a western route was the one option left that could break the monopoly. That is the economic case: a cheap one-shot bet (three ships) against a prize worth the whole spice margin. The Geographer will show why the distance was misjudged; economics explains why the gamble was worth a king's money even at long odds. By 1493 the tech layer already shows horses landing at Santo Domingo, the start of an entirely different economy than the one Columbus sought.

steps.title: Genoese weaver's son with Marco Polo's numbers
steps.text: Columbus (b. Genoa 1451) never argued the Earth was flat; he argued it was small. He stacked favorable numbers: Marco Polo's (d. 1324) Asia stretching far east, Japan placed ~1,500 miles beyond China, and the shortest estimate of a degree of longitude, which let him put Asia roughly 2,400 nautical miles west of the Canaries. Modern figures are about 10,600 nm. Portugal's experts reportedly rejected him around 1484, and they were right on the arithmetic. He was sailing on a Marco Polo-sized error, not a flat-Earth fear. I am going beyond the map data on the exact figures, and they are debated.

steps.title: Salamanca and Santa Fe: a verdict by committee
steps.text: Isabella's commission of learned men, led by Hernando de Talavera, judged his figures too optimistic around 1490, because the distance looked far beyond any ship's supplies. The later story of clerics defending a flat Earth comes from Washington Irving (1828), not records. Columbus survived by being persistent and a courtier: he lingered for six years, and after Granada fell on 2 Jan 1492 the crown had money and attention to spare. Luis de Santángel, a royal financier, helped persuade Isabella, and the Capitulations of Santa Fe gave Columbus the title Admiral and 10% of profits. The Economic historian will show the silver and trade pressure; what a biography adds is that one stubborn, charming man outlasted correct experts.

routes.label: Columbus follows the Castilian court

steps.title: Right by luck: America as the rescue
steps.text: The experts were right and Columbus was saved by an unknown continent: the voyage took about 33 days from the Canaries, and ships likely could not have crossed to Asia. He died in 1506 still insisting he had reached Asia, while Vespucci (1454-1512) argued it was a new world, and da Gama (1460-1524) reached India by sea in 1498 on the Portuguese route. Magellan (1480-1521) later proved the real size. One life changed the world partly through a mistake that happened to be fortunate. The panel's open question is how much was him versus the many other captains who would have sailed soon.

links.why: Ptolemy's shrunken degree and stretched Eurasia, together with Marco Polo's Asia, gave Columbus the numbers he sold, so the Geographer's size error became the Biographer's argument.
Portugal's near-proven Cape route shut Castile out of the African road, so only a western route could break the monopoly, and that made Columbus's underestimated distance worth a king's money.
The experts' arithmetic was right and the voyage would have failed at open ocean, but the Americas sat in the gap and turned Columbus's mistake into success.

Columbus's lucky survival and heroic myth made him a ready figure for the 19th-century conflict narrative, in which Irving invented a flat-Earth scene that the real dispute about distance never contained.

whatifs.q: What if the Americas had not existed and Columbus had sailed west in 1492?
whatifs.a: His three ships would likely have run out of food and water long before the roughly 19,000 km to Asia, and the crews would probably have died or turned back. Spain's commission would have been vindicated, and the western route would have waited for better ships, with Portugal's Cape route staying the only practical way east.

q: Who was in Vienna in 1913, and could they have met?

answer.short: In 1913 Vienna the documented overlap is narrow: Hitler (until May) and Stalin (a few weeks in January-February) were both in the city, Trotsky was based there but often away reporting on the Balkans, Freud and Franz Ferdinand lived there too, and Tito is unconfirmed. They could have crossed paths only in the sense that a city of about 2 million, built from migrants arriving by rail, put them in the same place; poor hostels, exile circles, the Belvedere court and Berggasse 19 were separate social worlds, and no source documents any meeting between Hitler and Stalin or Trotsky. The Café Central and Schönbrunn encounter stories are legends.
answer.frame: In 1913 Vienna, a capital of 2 million held Hitler, Stalin, Trotsky, Tito, Freud and Franz Ferdinand's court, and the question is who overlapped in place and time and who could plausibly have crossed paths.

plan.frame: In 1913 Vienna, a capital of 2 million held Hitler, Stalin, Trotsky, Tito, Freud and Franz Ferdinand's court, and the question is who overlapped in place and time and who could plausibly have crossed paths.

steps.title: A city of 2 million, most of them from elsewhere
steps.text: The Atlas map shows Vienna at 1.7 million in 1897, 1911 and 1924, which is a rounded flat line. Going beyond that data: the census of 1910 counted about 2.03 million, and only around 45% of residents were born in Vienna. The rest came mostly from Bohemia and Moravia (Czech speakers were the largest group, perhaps a quarter of the city), then Hungary and Galicia. About 175,000 were Jewish, roughly 9%. This is the key fact for your question: in 1913 almost nobody famous was a native, so 'who was in Vienna' is really 'who arrived by rail from the empire's edges.' The rail termini (Nordbahnhof for Galicia, Westbahnhof for the west) were the front doors.

pins.name: Prague, a main feeder of Czech migrants

routes.label: Czech and Moravian migrants by rail to Vienna
Galician and Jewish migrants by rail to Vienna

steps.title: The poor men's map: hostels and a men's home
steps.text: Demographers read addresses as density. Hitler, a 24-year-old from Linz, lived in the Männerheim on Meldemannstraße in Brigittenau from February 1910 to May 1913, a charitable men's hostel for the poor, then left for Munich that month. Stalin stayed a few weeks in early 1913, around January to February, at Schönbrunnerstraße-area lodgings associated with Trotsky's circle, and the Stumpergasse address is traditionally cited. Both were poor in outer, crowded districts, while the court sat at Schönbrunn. Honestly, a 1913 overlap of Hitler and Stalin is possible by calendar (both there in early 1913) but there is no solid evidence they met. The Biographer will give the verified dates; what the headcount adds is that the odds were against it: a city of 2 million with about 20 districts, and the working-class lodging belts were not the same streets.

pins.name: Stumpergasse 29 (Mariahilf, 6th district), where Stalin lodged in early 1913

sources.cite: Brigitte Hamann, Hitler's Vienna (1996)
Simon Sebag Montefiore, Young Stalin (2007)

steps.title: After the empire: the city that kept its people but lost its hinterland
steps.text: The Atlas shows Vienna at 1.8 million in 1924 against 1.7 million in 1897. Austria-Hungary ended in 1918 and the city became the capital of a state of about 6.5 million, with almost a third living in Vienna. The Habsburg court dispersed, Czech and Hungarian officials and workers were pushed or pulled back to new states, and food and coal shortages hit hard in 1918 to 1921. The Political scientist will show how the court and the Reichsrat vanished; the population view adds that the 1913 crowd was already scattering. Hitler had gone to Munich, Stalin and Trotsky were in Russia's revolution by 1917, and Freud's circle stayed. The meeting-place of the empire became a city of migrants without an empire.

pins.name: Vienna 1924, capital of a rump republic

sources.cite: Wikipedia, Vienna

steps.title: Winter 1913: three future dictators' worlds in one city
steps.text: The documented overlap is Hitler and Stalin, both in Vienna in January and February 1913. Hitler (aged 23) was in the Meldemannstrasse men's hostel, which he had lived in since 1910, selling painted postcards. Stalin came for a few weeks, stayed with the Bolshevik Alexei Troyanovsky near Schönbrunn, and wrote 'Marxism and the National Question' before his arrest in St Petersburg in late February. The famous story that the two met or walked past each other at Schönbrunn is a legend with no contemporary evidence. They lived about 6 km and a whole social world apart. Trotsky's Vienna residence dates from 1907, but he spent much of 1912-13 as a war correspondent in the Balkans, so I would not assume he was home during Stalin's visit. The Demographer will show the hostels and districts, and what my lens adds is that being in the same city is not a meeting.

routes.label: Stalin's Vienna weeks (Jan-Feb 1913)

Wikipedia: Adolf Hitler
Wikipedia: Joseph Stalin

steps.title: Berggasse 19 and the Belvedere: who could cross whose path
steps.text: Sigmund Freud practised and lived at Berggasse 19 (from 1891), a short walk from the Ringstrasse, so Alfred Adler, who broke with him in 1911, was a plausible street-level neighbour in 1913. Franz Ferdinand, heir to Franz Joseph I (aged 82, at Schönbrunn and the Hofburg), lived at the Belvedere, but his world was court, army and hunting estates, and he travelled with heavy security and ceremony. Among the artists on my list, Klimt (51) and Schiele (23) were both working in Vienna, and Schoenberg's circle with Berg and Webern was active, though Schoenberg spent time in Berlin. Hitler admired the Ringstrasse as a pedestrian and could physically have seen the court's carriages, but I can only say 'could have', not 'did'. The Historian of faith and ideas will take Café Central, and what I add is that the plausible meetings were within professions and districts, not across them. We don't know of any documented encounter between these figures and Hitler.

sources.cite: Wikipedia: Sigmund Freud
Wikipedia: Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria

steps.title: May 1913: Hitler leaves for Munich
steps.text: Hitler left Vienna in May 1913 for Munich, partly, as he later claimed, from dislike of the multiethnic empire, and partly, as Hamann argues, to avoid Austro-Hungarian military service. So the 1913 'Vienna of the future dictators' was really a winter and spring one: Hitler there until May, Stalin there for weeks, and Tito, who in 1913 worked as a metalworker, was around Wiener Neustadt, south of Vienna, and I cannot confirm he was in the capital itself. The chair's list therefore fits the year but not the same weeks. The unanswerable counterfactual is what Vienna's 2 million inhabitants would have noticed, and the answer is probably nothing: none of these men was famous.

steps.title: The court that ruled from the Hofburg
steps.text: Austria-Hungary was two states under one monarch, and Vienna housed the machinery of both the Cisleithanian half and the joint ministries. Franz Joseph, 83, had reigned since 1848, the year the Rule & Law layer records Austria abolishing serfdom. Heir Franz Ferdinand ran a rival 'shadow court' from the Belvedere, with its own military chancellery, and was widely disliked by the old emperor's circle. The Reichsrat, elected by universal male suffrage since 1907, was paralysed by national blocs (Czech obstruction especially) and was effectively sidelined from March 1914 when it was prorogued. The data window has no Cliopatria fragility figure for these polygons, so I can't quote the model's collapse risk. My own view, beyond the data: the state looked stable to insiders, but its legitimacy rested on one old man.

steps.title: Exile politics: why radicals came to Vienna
steps.text: Vienna drew exiles because Cisleithania had the freest press and association law in central Europe after the 1867 constitution, while the Russian Empire (polity layer) policed dissent hard after 1905's October Manifesto (in the Rule & Law layer) was rolled back. Trotsky lived there from 1907 and edited the Pravda he published for Russian workers; Stalin stayed only a few weeks in January 1913, a stay generally dated to late January, and wrote 'Marxism and the National Question' under Bolshevik guidance, with Habsburg nationality politics as his case study. Hitler, a failed art student, left Vienna in May 1913 for Munich, partly to dodge Austrian military service. Meeting is plausible only in the sense of overlap in a city of 2 million. No reliable source documents a Stalin-Hitler or Trotsky-Hitler encounter, and the often-repeated Café Central story is a legend; the Biographer will test who was verifiably where. Tito's presence in 1913 is doubtful, and I would not put him on the map without a source: he was a young metalworker in Croatia and later in Austria-Hungary's army.

steps.title: The state they were all plotting against
steps.text: The same Vienna that sheltered Marxists and nationalists was the capital of a dual monarchy of about 51 million people and a dozen nationalities, bound by the Ausgleich of 1867. Franz Ferdinand reportedly planned federal reform (a 'United States of Greater Austria'), which Hungarian elites opposed; that is why he was both the empire's best hope and a target. His assassination in Sarajevo ended the order that held the 1913 cast together, and by 1918 the polity index shows Austria-Hungary gone. The Rule & Law layer's jump from 1910 to 1920 (Nineteenth Amendment) skips the real story here, which is the new republics' constitutions of 1918-20, which the data doesn't hold.

steps.title: Vienna's Ringstrasse stage set
steps.text: The Atlas's art layer has Beaux-Arts and imperial eclecticism (1850-1930, from Paris) and Art Nouveau (1893-1914, from Brussels), and Vienna sits where both meet. The Ringstrasse, begun in 1857, wrapped the old city in Beaux-Arts-style parliament, university, opera and town hall, a stage set for an empire of about 50 million. Then in 1897 Klimt and others broke away to form the Secession, and Olbrich's building (1898) carried the motto 'To every age its art, to art its freedom.' Beyond the Atlas's records: the Secession is in Vienna's own style story, and the Atlas has no Vienna-specific entries, so this is my own reading. A 1913 visitor walked between two architectural arguments in one afternoon.

sources.cite: Carl E. Schorske, Fin-de-Siecle Vienna: Politics and Culture (1980)

steps.title: The coffeehouse as a university
steps.text: The Atlas has no thinkers recorded for this window, so I speak from outside its data. Cafe Central was the best-known coffeehouse of Vienna's intellectual world; Trotsky is widely reported as a regular there, playing chess, in his Vienna years (1907-1914). Freud lived and practised at Berggasse 19 from 1891 to 1938, and his Wednesday Psychological Society, founded in 1902, became the Vienna Psychoanalytic Society in 1908. By 1913 Jung had broken with Freud (the split dates from 1912-13), so the circle was already fracturing. Schoenberg's atonal Second String Quartet (1908) and Klimt's Secession painting shared the same few square kilometres. The Biographer will confirm who was verifiably in the city; what my lens adds is that cafes, not institutions, were where such strangers could overlap.

steps.title: Ideas that left Vienna by 1938
steps.text: The Atlas's idea journeys (Marx from Trier to Havana, non-violence from Vaishali to Montgomery) show how thoughts travel through people, and Vienna's ideas fit the pattern. Freud left for London in 1938 and died there in 1939; Schoenberg moved to Berlin in 1911, returned, and ended in Los Angeles in 1933-34. So 1913 is a snapshot of a crowd that was about to scatter. The Atlas's journeys show Marx's idea took power where he least expected; Vienna's ideas likewise travelled further than the city that made them. Whether Hitler, then in Vienna's men's hostels until May 1913 (then Munich), ever met any of these figures is not documented; the Political scientist and Demographer can place the radicals, while my lens finds only a shared city, not a shared room.

whatifs.q: What if Hitler had stayed in Vienna past May 1913 and been drafted into the Austro-Hungarian army?
whatifs.a: He would likely have faced medical examination and service in a multiethnic army, and he was in fact judged unfit when examined in Salzburg in 1914. His path into the Bavarian army in 1914 might never have happened, but we cannot say how his politics would have developed.
